  • For experienced developers: for a plain stack or queue, ArrayDeque is almost always faster and uses less memory. Choose LinkedList mainly when you need both List and Deque behaviour, or null elements in a queue.

Use LinkedList or something else?

Use LinkedList whenUse something else when
You add and remove at both ends (queue, deque)You only need a queue or stack: ArrayDeque is faster
You insert many times while walking with an iteratorYou read by index a lot: use ArrayList
You need one object that is both a List and a QueueMemory is tight: use ArrayList
The list is small and the code stays simpleElements need priority order: use PriorityQueue
You must store null in a queueMany threads share the queue: use ConcurrentLinkedDeque

intermediate.content:
Adding elements

LinkedList gives you many names for "add at an end". The names come from the three roles the class plays: List, Queue and Deque.

1. add, addLast and offer

  • Signature: boolean add(E e); void addLast(E e); boolean offer(E e)
  • Returns: add and offer return true; addLast returns nothing
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: All three put the element at the end of the list. Use add when you think "list", offer when you think "queue", and addLast when you think "deque".

For experienced developers: They all call the same internal linkLast: create a node, point the old last node's next at it, and update last. A LinkedList has no capacity limit, so offer never returns false here (it can for bounded queues).

2. addFirst, push and offerFirst

  • Signature: void addFirst(E e); void push(E e); boolean offerFirst(E e)
  • Returns: nothing / nothing / true
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: These put the element at the front. Adding at the front is where LinkedList beats ArrayList: no shifting. push is the name used when the list acts like a stack (last in, first out).

For experienced developers: push(e) is just addFirst(e). Together with pop() (which removes the first element) you get a stack that is consistent with the Deque contract. Note: the legacy Stack class works at the other end and is synchronized.

3. add(int index, E e)

  • Signature: void add(int index, E element)
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: O(n) to reach the index

For freshers: Inserts the element at a position. Linking the new node is instant, but Java must first walk to that position, one node at a time.

For experienced developers: The walk starts from whichever end is closer (index < size/2 goes from the front, otherwise from the back), so the average cost is about n/4 steps. For an insertion that is far from both ends an ArrayList is usually still faster because its shifting is a native block copy.

4. addAll(Collection c) and addAll(int index, Collection c)

  • Signature: boolean addAll(Collection c); boolean addAll(int index, Collection c)
  • Returns: true if the list changed
  • Time: O(m) / O(index + m)

For freshers: Adds all elements of another collection, at the end or starting at an index, keeping their order.

For experienced developers: It converts the argument to an array, then links the new nodes in one pass, so it is efficient even for the indexed version (only one walk to the index).

Reading elements

Reading the ends is O(1). Reading in the middle walks the chain. Pick the variant by what you want when the list is empty: an exception or null.

5. getFirst, getLast and element

  • Signature: E getFirst(); E getLast(); E element()
  • Returns: the element at that end
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Read the first or last element without removing it. On an empty list they throw NoSuchElementException. element() is the queue name for getFirst().

For experienced developers: They read the first / last pointers directly. If an empty list is normal in your program, use the peek family (next card), which returns null instead of throwing.

6. peek, peekFirst and peekLast

  • Signature: E peek(); E peekFirst(); E peekLast()
  • Returns: the element, or null if the list is empty
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Look at an end without removing it; if the list is empty you get null, not an exception. peek() and peekFirst() look at the front, peekLast() at the back.

For experienced developers: These are the "safe" counterparts of getFirst/getLast. Because LinkedList allows null elements, a null result is ambiguous: it could be "empty" or "the element is null". Check isEmpty() if you store nulls.

7. get(int index) and set(int index, E e)

  • Signature: E get(int index); E set(int index, E element)
  • Returns: the element / the replaced element
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Read or replace by position. It works, but remember the list has to walk to the index: reading the 500th element touches up to 250 nodes.

For experienced developers: The cost is why a for (int i...) list.get(i) loop over a LinkedList is O(n²). Use a for-each loop or an iterator instead: they move from one node to the next in O(1) per step.

8. contains, indexOf and lastIndexOf

  • Signature: boolean contains(Object o); int indexOf(Object o); int lastIndexOf(Object o)
  • Returns: true / the index / the index (or -1)
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Search by value from the front (indexOf, contains) or from the back (lastIndexOf). Matching uses equals().

For experienced developers: Linear scans, identical in behaviour to ArrayList. Override equals in your element class (or use a record) so the search works for your objects.

Removing elements

Removing an end is O(1). The names differ again by what happens on an empty list.

9. remove(), removeFirst, pop and removeLast

  • Signature: E remove(); E removeFirst(); E pop(); E removeLast()
  • Returns: the removed element (throws on an empty list)
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: remove(), removeFirst() and pop() all take the first element out and return it; removeLast() takes the last. If the list is empty they throw NoSuchElementException.

For experienced developers: The no-argument remove() is the Queue method and must not be confused with remove(int) / remove(Object). Removing an end only updates one or two links, with no shifting.

10. poll, pollFirst and pollLast

  • Signature: E poll(); E pollFirst(); E pollLast()
  • Returns: the removed element, or null if empty
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Like remove, but safe: when the list is empty you get null instead of an exception. poll() is the standard way to take the next item from a queue in a loop: while ((x = queue.poll()) != null).

For experienced developers: Prefer poll in queue-style code and removeFirst when an empty list would be a bug that you want to see as an exception.

11. remove(int index) and remove(Object o)

  • Signature: E remove(int index); boolean remove(Object o)
  • Returns: the removed element / true if found
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Remove by position or by value (the first equal element). Both have to walk the chain to find the node, then unlink it.

For experienced developers: The same overload trap exists as in ArrayList: on a LinkedList<Integer>, remove(2) removes index 2; use remove(Integer.valueOf(2)) for the value. removeFirstOccurrence and removeLastOccurrence (next card) make the direction explicit.

12. removeFirstOccurrence and removeLastOccurrence

  • Signature: boolean removeFirstOccurrence(Object o); boolean removeLastOccurrence(Object o)
  • Returns: true if an element was removed
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Remove the first or the last element equal to the value, when the list holds duplicates.

For experienced developers: removeFirstOccurrence is the same as remove(Object). removeLastOccurrence scans from the back, which is the only direct way to remove the last match in a list.

13. removeIf, removeAll, retainAll and clear

  • Signature: boolean removeIf(Predicate); boolean removeAll(Collection); boolean retainAll(Collection); void clear()
  • Returns: true if changed / nothing
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Remove by a rule, remove everything found in another collection, keep only what is found in another collection, or remove everything.

For experienced developers: These are inherited from Collection; they work with an iterator, unlinking nodes as they go. clear() unlinks every node (setting their fields to null to help the garbage collector).

Using LinkedList as a Queue, a Stack and a Deque

Because LinkedList is also a Deque, the same object can be used three ways. Choose the interface type that matches your use so the code says what you mean.

The same LinkedList as Queue, Stack and Deque

RoleAddRemoveLookOrder
Queue (line at a ticket window)offer(e) at the backpoll() from the frontpeek()First in, first out (FIFO)
Stack (pile of plates)push(e) on top (front)pop() from the top (front)peek()Last in, first out (LIFO)
Deque (both ends)offerFirst / offerLastpollFirst / pollLastpeekFirst / peekLastBoth ends

For pure queue or stack work, ArrayDeque is usually even faster (no node objects), but it does not allow null and has no index methods.

Changing, converting and walking

The rest of the List API works exactly as in ArrayList, so only the LinkedList-specific points are shown here.

14. iterator, listIterator and descendingIterator

  • Signature: Iterator iterator(); ListIterator listIterator(); Iterator descendingIterator()
  • Returns: an iterator
  • Time: O(1) per step

For freshers: Walk the list element by element. iterator() goes forward, listIterator() also goes backward and can add or replace, and descendingIterator() walks from the last element to the first. Iterators are the right way to loop a LinkedList because each step is O(1).

For experienced developers: The iterators are fail-fast (they check modCount). A ListIterator can insert in the middle in O(1) at the cursor: this is the one case where LinkedList truly beats ArrayList for middle insertion, because you are already standing on the node.

15. sort, replaceAll, forEach, stream, toArray, subList

  • Signature: inherited from List and Collection
  • Returns: as for ArrayList
  • Time: O(n) or O(n log n)

For freshers: These work just like on an ArrayList: sort orders the list, replaceAll changes every element, forEach runs an action, stream starts a pipeline, toArray copies into an array and subList gives a range view.

For experienced developers: sort copies the nodes into an array, sorts it with TimSort and writes the values back, so there is no benefit from being a linked list. If you sort a lot, you probably wanted an ArrayList.

16. clone, equals, hashCode, toString and reversed

  • Signature: Object clone(); boolean equals(Object); String toString(); LinkedList reversed()
  • Returns: a shallow copy / comparisons / text / a reversed view
  • Time: O(n) / O(1)

For freshers: clone() makes a shallow copy (the new list has its own nodes but shares the elements). Two lists are equals when they have the same elements in the same order, whatever the list class. In Java 21 reversed() gives a view that walks from the back.

For experienced developers: Prefer the copy constructor over clone(). A reversed view is not a copy: changes through it change the original.

Master program: every LinkedList method in one place

One single program that uses all the LinkedList methods you learned above, step by step. Read the numbered comments from top to bottom, run it, and match each output line with its step.

Module: Sorting methods

A LinkedList can be sorted with the same tools as an ArrayList, but the work happens differently inside.

  • In place: list.sort(...), Collections.sort(...), Collections.reverse(...), Collections.shuffle(...).
  • New result: stream().sorted(...), or descendingIterator() / reversed() to read backwards.
  • For experienced developers: a linked list cannot be sorted in place by index. The default List.sort copies the nodes into an array, sorts the array with TimSort, and writes the values back. So it is still O(n log n), plus O(n) extra memory. The classic alternative, merge sort on nodes, is not available in the public API.

17. List.sort(Comparator)

  • Signature: void sort(Comparator<? super E> c)
  • Returns: nothing (the list is sorted in place)
  • Time: O(n log n) plus an O(n) temporary array

For freshers: Sorts the list with the rule you give. Pass null for the natural order. It works just like on an ArrayList, so your code looks the same.

For experienced developers: The default method copies to an array with toArray(), sorts, and then replaces the values one by one through a ListIterator (using set). The nodes themselves are not moved.

18. Collections.sort(List)

  • Signature: static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> void sort(List<T> list)
  • Returns: nothing (list is sorted in place)
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Sorts numbers or text in natural order. Because it works on any List, the same call works for ArrayList, LinkedList and Vector.

For experienced developers: It delegates to list.sort(null). Since LinkedList has no fast index access, never write your own bubble sort with get(i) and set(i, x): that would be O(n cubed) in the worst case.

19. Comparator.comparing(...) with LinkedList

  • Signature: static Comparator<T> comparing(Function<T,U> key)
  • Returns: a Comparator
  • Time: O(n log n) when used to sort

For freshers: To sort a list of objects (such as groups waiting at a gate), say which field to compare. Add thenComparing for ties.

For experienced developers: A good use for a LinkedList is a waiting queue. Sorting it once by priority and then taking from the front with poll() works, but if priority changes often a PriorityQueue is a better fit.

20. Collections.reverse(List) and descendingIterator()

  • Signature: Iterator<E> descendingIterator()
  • Returns: an iterator that walks from the last element to the first
  • Time: O(n) to walk

For freshers: Collections.reverse flips the list itself. If you only want to read backwards without changing anything, use descendingIterator() (or reversed() in Java 21).

For experienced developers: A doubly linked list can walk backwards just as fast as forwards, which is why descendingIterator is cheap. The reversing is done with a ListIterator from both ends.

21. Collections.shuffle(List, Random)

  • Signature: static void shuffle(List<?> list, Random rnd)
  • Returns: nothing (list is mixed in place)
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Mixes the elements randomly, for example to play a playlist in random order. Use a seeded Random when you need the same result every time (for tests).

For experienced developers: For a list that is not RandomAccess, shuffle first copies the elements to an array, shuffles the array and writes the values back, so it stays O(n) and never uses slow get(i) calls.

22. stream().sorted(...)

  • Signature: Stream<E> sorted(Comparator<? super E> c)
  • Returns: a sorted stream (collect it to a list)
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Makes a sorted copy and keeps your LinkedList exactly as it was. Good for reports.

For experienced developers: The stream copies the elements into its own buffer, so the extra memory is O(n). The original nodes are not touched.

Which sorting method should I pick?

I want to...UseNote for LinkedList
Sort in place with a rulelist.sort(comparator)Copies to an array internally, still O(n log n)
Sort numbers or textCollections.sort(list)Same as sort(null)
Read backwards, no changedescendingIterator() or reversed()Cheap, the list is doubly linked
Really flip the listCollections.reverse(list)O(n)
Random orderCollections.shuffle(list, new Random(seed))O(n)
Keep the original, get a sorted copystream().sorted().toList()O(n) extra memory
Always take the smallest nextPriorityQueue instead of sortingO(log n) per insert

Module: Finding (searching) methods

Finding in a LinkedList always means walking the chain. The special thing is that it also has cheap peeking at both ends, which an ArrayList does not offer as a method family.

  • Look at the ends (O(1)): getFirst, getLast, peek, peekFirst, peekLast, element.
  • Is it there / where is it: contains, indexOf, lastIndexOf (all O(n)).
  • Best / count: Collections.max, min, frequency.
  • By condition: stream().filter(...).findFirst(), anyMatch.
  • For experienced developers: Collections.binarySearch works on a LinkedList but uses an iterator-based search with O(n) steps and only O(log n) comparisons, so it is rarely better than indexOf.

23. peek, peekFirst, peekLast, element, getFirst, getLast

  • Signature: E peekFirst() / E peekLast() / E getFirst()
  • Returns: the end element (peek returns null when empty; get/element throw)
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: These "look but do not remove" methods tell you who is at the front or at the back. The peek family returns null on an empty list; getFirst, getLast and element throw NoSuchElementException.

For experienced developers: Because the list keeps direct references to its first and last node, all of them are O(1). That is why a LinkedList is a good queue.

Watch out: On an empty list getFirst() throws an exception while peekFirst() returns null. Pick the one that fits how you want to handle "empty".

24. contains(Object)

  • Signature: boolean contains(Object o)
  • Returns: true if an equal element exists
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Asks "is this value somewhere in the list?". It checks one node after the other with equals.

For experienced developers: Same as indexOf(o) != -1. Pointer chasing makes it slower in real time than the same call on an ArrayList of equal size.

25. indexOf and lastIndexOf

  • Signature: int indexOf(Object o) / int lastIndexOf(Object o)
  • Returns: position or -1
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: indexOf returns the position of the first match, lastIndexOf of the last. If the value is missing you get -1.

For experienced developers: indexOf starts at the first node; lastIndexOf starts at the last node and walks backwards, so it is quick when the match is near the end.

26. removeFirstOccurrence and removeLastOccurrence (find and remove)

  • Signature: boolean removeFirstOccurrence(Object o)
  • Returns: true if something was removed
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: These find a value and remove it in one step. The first version removes the first match, the second removes the last match. They are handy when the same value appears more than once.

For experienced developers: Both are Deque methods. remove(Object) is the same as removeFirstOccurrence.

27. Collections.max, Collections.min and Collections.frequency

  • Signature: static <T> T max(Collection<? extends T> c)
  • Returns: the biggest / smallest element, or a count
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Find the biggest or smallest value, or count how often a value appears, without sorting.

For experienced developers: They use the collection iterator, which is the efficient way to traverse a LinkedList (never index loops).

28. Collections.binarySearch(List, key)

  • Signature: static <T> int binarySearch(List<? extends Comparable<? super T>> list, T key)
  • Returns: index or -(insertion point) - 1
  • Time: O(n) steps, O(log n) comparisons on a LinkedList

For freshers: Works only on a sorted list. On a LinkedList it still returns the right answer, but it gains little, because it must walk the chain to reach the middle.

For experienced developers: For lists that do not implement RandomAccess (and have 5000 or more elements), the JDK switches to iteratorBinarySearch. Comparisons are O(log n), but moving the iterator is O(n).

Watch out: For a big LinkedList that you search often, copy it to an ArrayList (or use a TreeSet) instead.

29. stream().filter(...).findFirst() and anyMatch

  • Signature: Optional<E> findFirst() / boolean anyMatch(Predicate p)
  • Returns: an Optional or a boolean
  • Time: O(n), stops early

For freshers: Find the first group that fits a condition, or ask whether any group does. The Optional answer reminds you to handle "nothing found".

For experienced developers: Because the stream iterates the list once and stops at the first hit, no extra index access is needed.

Which finding method should I pick?

I want to know...UseCost
Who is at the front / back?peekFirst() / peekLast()O(1)
Is the value there?contains(x)O(n)
Where is the value?indexOf(x) / lastIndexOf(x)O(n)
Find it and remove itremoveFirstOccurrence(x)O(n)
Biggest, smallest, how manyCollections.max / min / frequencyO(n)
First element passing a conditionstream().filter(...).findFirst()O(n), early stop
Sorted data, many searchesUse ArrayList + binarySearch, or a TreeSetO(log n)

expert.content:
How LinkedList works inside

A short tour of the source code explains every cost in the tables.

  • The class keeps transient int size, Node<E> first and Node<E> last. Each Node has item, next and prev.
  • linkLast(e): create a node whose prev is the old last; set last to it; link the old last's next; size++; modCount++. No arrays, no copying, so no "amortised" caveat.
  • node(index) picks the nearest end: if index < (size >> 1) it walks from first via next, otherwise from last via prev. That is why access in the middle is the slowest.
  • unlink(node) reconnects the neighbours and clears the node's fields so the garbage collector can reclaim it.
  • Memory: on a 64-bit JVM with compressed pointers a node is 24 bytes (12 header + 3 references x 4). A million elements cost 24 MB of nodes on top of the elements themselves, versus 4 MB of references in an ArrayList.
  • Cache behaviour: nodes are scattered in memory, so walking a LinkedList causes many CPU cache misses, while an ArrayList reads contiguous memory. This is why ArrayList often wins even where Big-O suggests otherwise.

Time complexity summary

OperationLinkedListArrayList (for comparison)
get(i), set(i, e)O(n), up to n/2 stepsO(1)
add at the endO(1)O(1) amortised
add / remove at the frontO(1)O(n)
add(i, e), remove(i) in the middleO(n) to reach i, then O(1) to linkO(n) shift (fast block copy)
Insert / remove through a ListIterator at the cursorO(1)O(n)
contains, indexOfO(n)O(n)
Memory per element~24 bytes node + element~4 bytes reference + element
Iteration speedSlower (cache misses)Faster

Trap: indexed loops are quadratic

  • A for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) list.get(i) loop calls get n times, each costing up to n/2 steps: O(n²).
  • Use a for-each loop, an Iterator, or forEach: O(n) in total.
  • The program below counts node visits to make the difference visible without timing.

LinkedList vs ArrayList vs ArrayDeque: which one?

NeedBest choiceWhy
A general list you read by indexArrayListO(1) get, compact, cache-friendly
A queue or a stackArrayDequeNo node objects, faster than LinkedList; no nulls
A queue that must hold null, or needs both the List and Deque APIsLinkedListThe only class that is both a List and a Deque
Many inserts/removals through an iterator in the middle of a big listLinkedListO(1) at the cursor
Thread-safe queueConcurrentLinkedDeque / LinkedBlockingDequeLinkedList is not synchronized

Rule of thumb: start with ArrayList, and move to ArrayDeque for queues and stacks. LinkedList is a niche choice.

Best practices

Habits that keep LinkedList code correct and fast.

  • Declare the variable as the interface you use: Queue<T>, Deque<T> or List<T>.
  • Never loop with get(i); use for-each, an iterator or a stream.
  • Use the poll/peek/offer family when "empty" is a normal state, and remove/get/add when it would be a bug.
  • Avoid null elements, because peek()/poll() use null to mean "empty".
  • For thread safety use ConcurrentLinkedDeque or wrap with Collections.synchronizedList; remember to lock while iterating.
  • Do not use LinkedList only because "insertion is O(1)": measure first; ArrayList is faster for most sizes.

Real example: a ticket counter with undo

A queue of travellers and a stack of cancelled tickets, both built on LinkedList.

Real-time examples

A LinkedList shines when things happen at the front and at the back: playlists, waiting lines and history. Each program below is complete.

Example 1: Music playlist (play next, add to end)

For freshers: "Play next" puts a song at the front, "Add to queue" puts it at the back, and playing takes the first song. For experienced developers: all three operations are O(1) on a linked list.

Example 2: Support desk with VIP lane

For freshers: normal customers join the back of the line, VIP customers jump to the front. For experienced developers: this is a deque with two insertion points. If there were many priority levels, a PriorityQueue would be the right tool.

Example 3: Recent activity list that keeps only the last 3 items

For freshers: a "recently viewed" box shows only the newest three forts. New one goes to the front; if there are more than 3, the oldest at the back is dropped. For experienced developers: a bounded history with addFirst and removeLast is O(1) per step.

Sample project: Fort Gate Queue Simulator

What we build: a console simulation of a fort gate where groups wait in a line.

  • Step 1: create a Group record (name, people, vip).
  • Step 2: groups arrive; normal groups join the back, VIP groups join the front.
  • Step 3: the gate lets in at most 20 people per round; a group that is too big for the remaining space waits at the front of the next round.
  • Step 4: a group waiting more than 2 rounds is moved out ("gave up") using an Iterator.
  • Step 5: print what happened in each round and a final summary using peekFirst, size and a stream.

Practice questions

Now test yourself. Each question is harder than the examples above: read the problem, write your own solution, then compare it with the one shown. Every solution was compiled and run, and its output is real.

Practice question 1: Tour route planner (insert stops, skip, queue of waiting groups)

Level: Medium

Problem: A guide plans a day tour as a LinkedList of forts. Stops are added at both ends and in the middle, visited stops are dropped from the front, and the same object also acts as a queue of groups waiting at the gate.

Your task:

  1. addFirst / addLast / add(index, e) to build the route.
  2. A ListIterator inserts a stop right after a chosen fort while walking.
  3. removeFirst as each fort is visited, peek to see what is next.
  4. offer / poll to serve waiting groups in first-come-first-served order.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 2: Round-robin guide scheduler

Level: Hard

Problem: Three groups need a guide for different numbers of hours. The guide serves each group 2 hours at a time, then the group goes to the back of the line if it still needs more time. Find the order in which groups finish.

Your task:

  1. Store each group as a small record (name, hours left) in a LinkedList used as a queue.
  2. Repeat: poll() the first group, give it min(2, hoursLeft) hours, and add() it to the back if hours remain.
  3. Print each turn, and the finish order with the clock time at which each group finished.

Hints:

  • poll() takes from the front, add() adds to the back: that is a queue.
  • A record is immutable: create a new one with the reduced hours.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 3: Reverse a LinkedList by hand and rotate it

Level: Easy

Problem: Without using Collections.reverse, reverse a LinkedList of stops using only the deque methods. Then rotate it left by 2 positions (the first two stops go to the back).

Your task:

  1. Reverse: take elements with removeFirst() and put each at the front of a new list with addFirst().
  2. Rotate: repeat 2 times: addLast(removeFirst()).
  3. Print the list at each step.

Hints:

  • Each move is O(1), so the whole reverse is O(n).

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 4: Josephus game: who is left?

Level: Medium

Problem: Nine trekkers stand in a circle. Counting from the first, every 3rd trekker is sent out, and counting continues from the next person. Print the order in which they leave and the last one standing.

Your task:

  1. Put numbers 1 to 9 in a LinkedList.
  2. Keep an index; move it by 2 each time and use % size() to go around the circle.
  3. Remove with remove(index) and print the name.

Hints:

  • Because remove(index) shifts the next person into the same index, do not add 1 afterwards.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 5: Merge two sorted queues with ListIterator

Level: Medium

Problem: Two gates each have a sorted LinkedList of arrival times. Produce one merged sorted list by taking the smaller front each time (a merge), and also insert a late arrival (time 25) at the right place in the merged list using a ListIterator.

Your task:

  1. Compare peekFirst() of both lists, poll() the smaller one and add it to the result.
  2. When one list is empty, add all of the other with addAll.
  3. Walk the result with a ListIterator; before the first element bigger than 25, call add(25).

Hints:

  • A ListIterator inserts in O(1) once it stands at the right place.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 6: Sliding window maximum with a Deque

Level: Hard

Problem: Heights of forts along a trail are given. For every window of 3 neighbouring forts, print the tallest one. Do it in O(n) with a LinkedList used as a Deque that stores indexes.

Your task:

  1. Keep indexes in the deque so that the heights are in decreasing order from front to back.
  2. Before adding index i, remove indexes from the back while their height is smaller than height i.
  3. Remove the front if it has left the window; the front is the maximum.

Hints:

  • Every index enters and leaves the deque at most once, so the total time is O(n).

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

interviewQA: What is a LinkedList and how is it different from an ArrayList?

LinkedList is a doubly linked list: each element sits in a node with prev and next references. It gives O(1) insertion and removal at both ends and via an iterator, but O(n) index access. ArrayList uses an array: O(1) index access, O(n) insert/remove in the middle and at the front.
Which interfaces does LinkedList implement?
List, Deque (and so Queue), Cloneable and Serializable. It does not implement RandomAccess.
Time complexity of get(i), add at the end, add at the front, remove in the middle?
get(i) O(n) (walks from the nearer end); add at end O(1); add/remove at the front O(1); remove(index) O(n) to find the node, then O(1) to unlink.
When would you actually choose LinkedList?

When you need both List and Deque behaviour in one object, need to store nulls in a queue, or do many insertions/removals through a ListIterator in a large list. For plain queues and stacks ArrayDeque is better; for general lists ArrayList is better.
Why is a for loop with get(i) slow on a LinkedList?
Each get(i) walks the chain, so n calls cost O(n^2). Use for-each, an Iterator or streams, which move node to node in O(1).
Difference between remove(), poll() and pop()?
remove() and pop() take the first element and throw NoSuchElementException when empty; poll() takes the first element and returns null when empty. pop() is the stack name for removeFirst().
What is the difference between peek() and element()?
Both read the head without removing it; peek() returns null for an empty list, element() throws NoSuchElementException.
How do you use LinkedList as a stack?
Declare Deque<T> stack = new LinkedList<>(); use push(e) to add on top, pop() to remove from the top and peek() to look. They all work at the front of the list.
Does LinkedList allow duplicates and null?
Yes. Be careful with null because peek() and poll() return null to signal an empty list.
Is LinkedList thread-safe?
No. Use ConcurrentLinkedDeque or LinkedBlockingDeque for concurrent use, or wrap with Collections.synchronizedList and synchronise manually while iterating.
What is the memory overhead of LinkedList?
Each element needs a Node object: about 24 bytes (object header plus three references) on a 64-bit JVM with compressed pointers, compared with a 4-byte reference slot in an ArrayList.
How does node(index) decide where to start walking?
If index is less than size/2 it walks forward from first, otherwise it walks backward from last, so it needs at most about n/2 steps.
What does descendingIterator() do?
It returns an iterator that visits the elements from last to first, without creating a reversed copy.
Why can ListIterator.add() be O(1) on a LinkedList?
The iterator already holds a reference to the neighbouring nodes, so inserting a new node only changes the links around the cursor; no search is needed.

topics.name: Vector

beginner.content:
What is a Vector?

A Vector is a resizable array, just like ArrayList, with one big difference: every method is synchronized, so only one thread at a time can use it. It is one of the oldest classes of Java (from version 1.0, before the Collection Framework existed) and was later retrofitted to implement List.

  • Package java.util. Implements List, RandomAccess, Cloneable, Serializable.
  • Keeps insertion order, allows duplicates and null, and reads by index in O(1).
  • Thread-safe because each method locks the vector. This makes it slower than ArrayList when only one thread is used.
  • Default capacity is 10. When full it doubles its capacity (or grows by a fixed capacityIncrement if you set one).
  • Has many old-style methods (addElement, elementAt, removeElement, elements()) next to the modern List methods.
  • Modern advice: use ArrayList for single-threaded code, and CopyOnWriteArrayList or Collections.synchronizedList when you need thread safety. Learn Vector mainly to read old code and for interviews.

Where Vector sits in the Collection Framework

Iterable
(I)
← extends
Collection
(I)
← extends
List
(I)
← implements
AbstractList
(c)
← extends
Vector
(c)
← extends
Stack
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. Stack is a subclass of Vector, so it inherits all the Vector methods and the synchronization.

Creating a Vector: four constructors

  • new Vector<>(): empty, capacity 10, doubles when full.
  • new Vector<>(int initialCapacity): empty with the given capacity, doubles when full.
  • new Vector<>(int initialCapacity, int capacityIncrement): grows by that fixed amount instead of doubling.
  • new Vector<>(Collection c): a copy of another collection.

All Vector methods at a glance

n is the number of elements. The first group is the classic Vector API; the second is the List API that Vector shares with ArrayList.

MethodWhat it doesTime
addElement(e)Adds at the end (old name of add)O(1) amortised
insertElementAt(e, i)Inserts at index iO(n)
elementAt(i) / firstElement() / lastElement()Reads by index / first / lastO(1)
setElementAt(e, i)Replaces the element at iO(1)
removeElement(o) / removeElementAt(i) / removeAllElements()Removes by value / index / everythingO(n)
capacity() / ensureCapacity(n) / trimToSize() / setSize(n)Capacity management (setSize pads with null or truncates)O(1) / O(n)
elements()An old-style Enumeration (not fail-fast)O(1)
copyInto(Object[])Copies the elements into an arrayO(n)
indexOf(o, from) / lastIndexOf(o, from)Search starting at a given indexO(n)
add, get, set, remove, contains, size, clear, addAll, removeAll, retainAll ...The ordinary List methods, all synchronizedas ArrayList
sort, forEach, removeIf, replaceAll, stream, subList, iterator, listIteratorInherited List helpersas ArrayList

Benefits and advantages

Vector is the older cousin of ArrayList. It is still found in many old projects and exams, and it has a few real strengths.

  • Thread-safe methods. Every method such as add, get and remove is synchronized, so two threads cannot break the internal array.
  • Grows automatically like an ArrayList, and you can even choose how much it grows with a capacityIncrement.
  • Fast index access. It is an array inside, so get(i) is O(1).
  • Works with old code. Old APIs return a Vector or an Enumeration, and a Vector is a full List today, so it works with every modern collection tool.
  • Simple model for beginners: one object, safe even if you forget about threads for a small program.
  • For experienced developers: its methods are individually atomic, which prevents a corrupted array. That is a weaker promise than it sounds; see the disadvantages.

Disadvantages and when NOT to use it

For new code, Vector is rarely the best choice. Here is why.

  • Slower. Every call takes a lock, even if only one thread is running. A plain ArrayList is faster in that case.
  • Doubles in size by default. When full, a Vector grows to twice its capacity (unless you set an increment), which wastes more memory than ArrayList (1.5 times).
  • Old and wordy API. Methods like addElement, elementAt and removeAllElements duplicate the modern List methods.
  • Safe methods, unsafe sequences. "Check then act" (if (!v.contains(x)) v.add(x)) is two calls, and another thread can sneak in between. You still need your own synchronized block.
  • Iterators are still fail-fast. Looping over a Vector while another thread changes it can throw ConcurrentModificationException.
  • For experienced developers: for shared data use CopyOnWriteArrayList (read-heavy), Collections.synchronizedList (when you control the lock), or a concurrent queue. The class is not deprecated but is considered legacy.

Use Vector or something else?

Use Vector whenUse something else when
You maintain old code that already returns a VectorYou write new single-threaded code: use ArrayList
An old API needs a Vector or an EnumerationMany reads and few writes by many threads: use CopyOnWriteArrayList
You need a simple thread-safe list and speed is not a worryYou need atomic multi-step actions: use synchronized blocks or a concurrent collection
You want to control the growth step with capacityIncrementYou need a queue between threads: use BlockingQueue

intermediate.content:
Adding and reading with the classic Vector methods

These names come from before Java 1.2. They still work and you will meet them in older code.

1. addElement, insertElementAt and add

  • Signature: void addElement(E obj); void insertElementAt(E obj, int index); boolean add(E e)
  • Returns: nothing / nothing / true
  • Time: O(1) amortised / O(n)

For freshers: addElement(x) and add(x) both append at the end. insertElementAt(x, i) puts x at index i and shifts the rest right. Note the argument order: element first, then index (the opposite of add(int, E)).

For experienced developers: addElement is the original method; add was added for the List interface and simply calls the same code. Each call takes the vector's lock, so a loop of a million adds pays for a million lock operations (the JVM can often optimise this away, but the lock is still part of the contract).

2. elementAt, firstElement, lastElement and get

  • Signature: E elementAt(int index); E firstElement(); E lastElement(); E get(int index)
  • Returns: the element
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Read an element by position (elementAt = get) or read the first or last. firstElement() and lastElement() throw NoSuchElementException on an empty vector; a bad index throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

For experienced developers: Note the exception type: Vector throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (a subclass of IndexOutOfBoundsException), while ArrayList throws a plain IndexOutOfBoundsException.

3. setElementAt and set

  • Signature: void setElementAt(E obj, int index); E set(int index, E element)
  • Returns: nothing / the old element
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Replace the element at an index. setElementAt(element, index) returns nothing; set(index, element) returns the element it replaced.

For experienced developers: Again the classic method has the argument order (element, index), while the List method has (index, element). Mixing them up compiles when both are int and Integer-compatible types are used: be careful with Vector<Integer>.

Removing elements

Remove by value, by index, or everything.

4. removeElement, removeElementAt and removeAllElements

  • Signature: boolean removeElement(Object obj); void removeElementAt(int index); void removeAllElements()
  • Returns: true if found / nothing / nothing
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: removeElement(x) removes the first element equal to x and says whether it found one. removeElementAt(i) removes by index. removeAllElements() empties the vector (same as clear()).

For experienced developers: removeElement is the same as remove(Object). Later elements shift left. An invalid index throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Capacity

A Vector has a size (elements stored) and a capacity (room available). Unlike ArrayList, Vector lets you read the capacity.

5. capacity, ensureCapacity, trimToSize and setSize

  • Signature: int capacity(); void ensureCapacity(int); void trimToSize(); void setSize(int)
  • Returns: the capacity / nothing
  • Time: O(1) / O(n)

For freshers: capacity() tells how many elements fit before growing. ensureCapacity(n) makes room for n. trimToSize() shrinks the room to the size. setSize(n) changes the size itself: extra slots are filled with null, or elements beyond n are dropped.

For experienced developers: The growth rule is double the capacity (when no increment was given), not 1.5x as in ArrayList. setSize is a rare tool; it can create a vector full of nulls.

Searching

Besides the List search methods, Vector can start the search from a chosen index.

6. indexOf(o, from), lastIndexOf(o, from) and contains

  • Signature: int indexOf(Object o, int index); int lastIndexOf(Object o, int index); boolean contains(Object o)
  • Returns: the index (or -1) / true or false
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Search for a value starting at a position you choose: indexOf("Pune", 2) looks for Pune from index 2 onwards; lastIndexOf("Pune", 3) looks backwards from index 3.

For experienced developers: These two-argument searches exist only on Vector (not on ArrayList). Matching uses equals().

Walking through a Vector

Vector has two ways to walk that ArrayList does not mix: the old Enumeration and the modern Iterator.

7. elements() (Enumeration) versus iterator()

  • Signature: Enumeration elements(); Iterator iterator()
  • Returns: an Enumeration / an Iterator
  • Time: O(1) per step

For freshers: An Enumeration is the old way: hasMoreElements() and nextElement(). An Iterator is the new way: hasNext(), next() and remove(). Prefer Iterator (or for-each).

For experienced developers: The Vector Iterator is fail-fast (throws ConcurrentModificationException if the vector changes), but the Enumeration is not fail-fast and cannot remove. Both individual calls are synchronized, but a whole loop is not atomic: to iterate safely across threads you must synchronize on the vector yourself.

8. copyInto, toArray and clone

  • Signature: void copyInto(Object[] anArray); Object[] toArray(); Object clone()
  • Returns: nothing / an array / a shallow copy
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: copyInto(array) copies the elements into an array you provide (it must be big enough). toArray() creates a new array. clone() makes a shallow copy of the vector.

For experienced developers: copyInto is the classic method; toArray(new String[0]) is the modern equivalent that allocates the right array for you.

9. The inherited List methods

  • Signature: add, get, remove, contains, addAll, removeAll, retainAll, removeIf, replaceAll, sort, forEach, stream, subList, listIterator
  • Returns: as ArrayList
  • Time: as ArrayList

For freshers: Everything you learned for ArrayList also works on Vector: the same names, the same results. The only difference is that each call is synchronized.

For experienced developers: Because Vector implements List, you can swap new Vector<>() for new ArrayList<>() in most code by changing one word, provided you only used List methods (declare the variable as List to make that easy).

Master program: every Vector method in one place

One single program that uses all the Vector methods you learned above, step by step. Read the numbered comments from top to bottom, run it, and match each output line with its step.

Module: Sorting methods

A Vector is a List, so it can use all the normal sorting tools. The difference is that its own sort method is synchronized, so the lock is held for the whole sort.

  • In place: v.sort(...), Collections.sort(v), Collections.reverse(v), Collections.shuffle(v, rnd).
  • New result: v.stream().sorted() gives a sorted copy.
  • For experienced developers: Vector.sort sorts the internal array under the lock, so other threads wait until it finishes. A stream, in contrast, is not synchronized: if other threads write while you stream, you may see a ConcurrentModificationException. To stream safely, copy first under a lock: synchronized (v) { copy = new ArrayList<>(v); }.

10. Vector.sort(Comparator)

  • Signature: synchronized void sort(Comparator<? super E> c)
  • Returns: nothing (the vector itself is sorted)
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Sorts the vector in place with your rule. Pass null for natural order. While it sorts, other threads that use this Vector must wait.

For experienced developers: It is overridden in Vector as synchronized and sorts the elements array directly with Arrays.sort, then bumps modCount.

11. Collections.sort(List)

  • Signature: static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> void sort(List<T> list)
  • Returns: nothing (list is sorted in place)
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Sorts numbers or text in natural order. It works on a Vector because a Vector is a List.

For experienced developers: It calls v.sort(null), so you get the synchronized version for free.

12. Comparator.comparing(...) with Vector

  • Signature: static Comparator<T> comparing(Function<T,U> key)
  • Returns: a Comparator
  • Time: O(n log n) when sorting

For freshers: Sort objects by a field, then by another field if there is a tie.

For experienced developers: The Comparator itself has no state, so it can be shared by threads safely. The Vector protects the list, not your comparison logic: do not change an object while it is being compared.

13. Collections.reverse and Collections.shuffle

  • Signature: static void reverse(List<?> list) / static void shuffle(List<?> list, Random rnd)
  • Returns: nothing (changed in place)
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: reverse turns the order around; shuffle mixes it randomly. A fixed seed makes the shuffle repeatable.

For experienced developers: Each element swap goes through the synchronized get/set, so the lock is taken and released many times. Hold it yourself with synchronized (v) {...} if you want the whole reorder to be one atomic step.

14. stream().sorted(...)

  • Signature: Stream<E> sorted(Comparator<? super E> c)
  • Returns: a sorted stream
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Makes a sorted copy and leaves the Vector unchanged.

For experienced developers: The stream is not locked. In a multithreaded program, copy the Vector inside a synchronized block first, then stream the copy.

Which sorting method should I pick?

I want to...UseThread note
Sort in place with a rulev.sort(comparator)Whole sort holds the lock
Sort numbers or textCollections.sort(v)Same as v.sort(null)
Reverse or shuffleCollections.reverse / shuffleLock taken per element; wrap in synchronized for one atomic step
Sorted copy, keep the originalstream().sorted() on a snapshotCopy under a lock first

Module: Finding (searching) methods

Searching a Vector is a scan (O(n)), like an ArrayList, but each call is synchronized. A Vector also has its own older names for some jobs.

  • Is it there / where: contains, indexOf(x), indexOf(x, fromIndex), lastIndexOf(x).
  • The ends: firstElement() and lastElement() (old names; getFirst() and getLast() in Java 21).
  • Sorted data: Collections.binarySearch (O(log n) because Vector is RandomAccess).
  • Best / count: Collections.max, min, frequency.
  • By condition: stream().filter(...).findFirst(), anyMatch.
  • For experienced developers: a search followed by a change is not atomic. Wrap "find, then act" in synchronized (v).

15. contains(Object)

  • Signature: boolean contains(Object o)
  • Returns: true if an equal element exists
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Tells you whether a value is in the Vector. It uses equals.

For experienced developers: Implemented as indexOf(o, 0) >= 0 and synchronized. The answer can be out of date a moment later if other threads are changing the Vector.

16. indexOf(Object, int) and lastIndexOf(Object)

  • Signature: int indexOf(Object o, int index) / int lastIndexOf(Object o)
  • Returns: position or -1
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Vector has an extra form of indexOf that starts searching from a given position. Use it in a loop to find every match, not just the first.

For experienced developers: The two-argument versions exist only on Vector (ArrayList has just the one-argument forms).

17. firstElement() and lastElement()

  • Signature: E firstElement() / E lastElement()
  • Returns: the first or last element
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Quickly read the first or last item. On an empty Vector they throw NoSuchElementException.

For experienced developers: These are the legacy names. Since Java 21 you can also use getFirst() and getLast() from SequencedCollection; the behaviour is the same.

Watch out: Check isEmpty() first when the Vector may be empty.

18. Collections.binarySearch(List, key)

  • Signature: static <T> int binarySearch(List<? extends Comparable<? super T>> list, T key)
  • Returns: index or -(insertion point) - 1
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Very fast lookup in a sorted Vector. A negative result means "not found".

For experienced developers: Each probe calls the synchronized get, so under heavy sharing the lock is taken about log n times. The result is only meaningful if nobody changes the Vector between your sort and your search.

19. Collections.max, min and frequency

  • Signature: static <T> T max(Collection<? extends T> c)
  • Returns: biggest, smallest or a count
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Find the best value or count a value without sorting.

For experienced developers: They iterate with the Vector iterator, which is not synchronized as a whole. Hold synchronized (v) around the call when other threads write.

20. stream().filter(...).findFirst() and anyMatch

  • Signature: Optional<E> findFirst()
  • Returns: an Optional or a boolean
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Find the first element that fits a condition, or ask if any element does.

For experienced developers: Streams do not take the Vector lock. For a stable result in threaded code, stream a snapshot copy.

21. Enumeration search (legacy)

  • Signature: Enumeration<E> elements()
  • Returns: an Enumeration that walks the elements once
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: The old way to look through a Vector. hasMoreElements() asks if there is more, nextElement() gives the next one. Old code uses it, so you should be able to read it.

For experienced developers: Enumeration is not fail-fast and cannot remove. For new code use an Iterator or a for-each loop.

Which finding method should I pick?

I want to know...UseCost
Is the value there?contains(x)O(n)
Where is it (all places)?indexOf(x, from) in a loopO(n)
First or last elementfirstElement() / lastElement()O(1)
Quick lookup in sorted dataCollections.binarySearchO(log n)
Biggest, smallest, how manyCollections.max / min / frequencyO(n)
First element passing a teststream().filter(...).findFirst()O(n)
Old API gives an EnumerationhasMoreElements / nextElementO(n)

expert.content:
How Vector works inside

Vector and ArrayList are close relatives; the differences explain the behaviour.

  • Data lives in protected Object[] elementData with elementCount as the size. Both are protected, so subclasses (like Stack) can touch them.
  • Growth: newCapacity = oldCapacity + (capacityIncrement > 0 ? capacityIncrement : oldCapacity): it doubles unless you set an increment. ArrayList grows by half instead, so Vector may waste more memory.
  • Thread safety: methods are synchronized on the vector object. Single calls are atomic; compound actions are not: "if not contains then add" can still race between two threads.
  • Iterators are fail-fast via modCount; the old Enumeration is not.
  • Vector is never null-hostile: null elements are allowed.

Vector versus ArrayList

VectorArrayList
Thread safetyYes: every method is synchronizedNo
Speed (single thread)Slower (lock on each call)Faster
Growth when fullDoubles (or fixed increment)Grows by 50%
SinceJava 1.0 (retrofitted to List in 1.2)Java 1.2
Old methodsaddElement, elementAt, elements() ...None
IteratorsIterator (fail-fast) and Enumeration (not fail-fast)Iterator (fail-fast)
Read capacitycapacity()Not possible
TodayLegacyDefault list

The compound-action trap

  • Each Vector method is atomic, but a sequence of calls is not.
  • Checking contains and then calling add leaves a gap in which another thread can add the same value.
  • Lock around the whole sequence: synchronized (vector) { if (!vector.contains(x)) vector.add(x); }.
  • The sample shows the safe version (single-threaded, so it only proves the code runs; the point is the locking pattern).

Which list should you choose today?

SituationUseWhy
One thread (almost always)ArrayListNo locking cost
Read often, write rarely, shared by threadsCopyOnWriteArrayListReaders never block; no ConcurrentModificationException
Shared by threads with ordinary writesCollections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>())Same locking as Vector, but a modern API
Old code that already uses VectorKeep it, or migrate carefullyCheck for elements() and the Stack class

Best practices

Practical advice for the Vector you meet in real projects.

  • In new code avoid Vector and Stack; use ArrayList, ArrayDeque or a concurrent collection.
  • Declare variables as List so you can switch the implementation later.
  • Lock the vector (synchronized (v) {...}) around loops and check-then-act sequences that other threads can interleave.
  • Prefer iterator() or for-each to elements(); the Enumeration cannot remove and is not fail-fast.
  • Set the initial capacity if you know the size, to avoid repeated doubling.

Real example: a shared list of visited forts

Two worker threads add fort names to one Vector; the final size is always correct because each add is synchronized.

Real-time examples

Where does a Vector really appear? In old libraries, in simple shared logs, and in code that grows in fixed steps. Three small programs follow.

Example 1: Legacy API that hands you a Vector

For freshers: some old code gives you a Vector and an Enumeration. You read it with the old methods, then copy it into a modern list. For experienced developers: Collections.list(enumeration) converts any Enumeration to an ArrayList in one call.

Example 2: Shared notice board written by two threads

For freshers: two helpers post notices to the same board at the same time. A Vector keeps the board safe; no notice is lost. For experienced developers: only the count is deterministic here; the order of the notices depends on thread timing, so we print the count and sorted content.

Example 3: A buffer that grows in fixed steps

For freshers: you can tell a Vector how much room to add each time it is full. For experienced developers: with capacityIncrement 0 the capacity doubles, with a positive value it grows by that amount; a fixed step gives predictable memory but more frequent copying.

Sample project: Legacy Fort Register Migration

What we build: a console tool that reads an old Vector-based register, safely adds records from two threads, and migrates the data to a modern list with a report.

  • Step 1: a legacy class fills a Vector<String> with text lines such as Raigad,Pune,120.
  • Step 2: two threads add more lines at the same time (the Vector keeps them safe).
  • Step 3: read the lines with Enumeration, and parse each into a FortRow.
  • Step 4: migrate to an ArrayList, sort by visitors (largest first) and find the best fort with Collections.max.
  • Step 5: print the report with totals per city (a TreeMap) and a check that nothing was lost.

Practice questions

Now test yourself. Each question is harder than the examples above: read the problem, write your own solution, then compare it with the one shown. Every solution was compiled and run, and its output is real.

Practice question 1: Shared ticket counter log (many threads, one Vector)

Level: Medium

Problem: Four counters at a fort gate record each ticket they sell into one shared list at the same time. A Vector is synchronized, so no ticket is lost; a plain ArrayList could lose some or even throw an error.

Your task:

  1. Start four threads; each adds 1000 tickets to the same Vector.
  2. After join, the size is exactly 4000.
  3. A check-then-add on a Vector is not atomic, so it is wrapped in synchronized (list).

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 2: Thread-safe leaderboard

Level: Medium

Problem: Three judges enter scores for the same contest at the same time into one shared Vector. After all judges finish, print the top 3 scores, the total and the average.

Your task:

  1. Start 3 threads; each adds 5 scores (use judgeNumber * 10 + i so the result is predictable).
  2. Wait for all threads with join().
  3. Sort the vector in descending order and print the top 3, the number of scores, the sum and the average.

Hints:

  • Do the sorting after join(), when no thread is writing any more.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 3: Move old Enumeration code to modern List code

Level: Easy

Problem: An old method returns a Vector of city names. Print them with an Enumeration, then show the same result with a for-each loop, a stream that keeps only names with 5 or more letters, and count them.

Your task:

  1. Use elements() with hasMoreElements and nextElement.
  2. Rewrite it with a for-each loop.
  3. Use a stream to filter names whose length is at least 5, sort them and print them.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 4: Predict the capacity

Level: Medium

Problem: A Vector starts with capacity 3 and capacityIncrement 4. Add 12 elements and print the capacity every time it changes. Then do the same with the default doubling Vector starting at capacity 3 and compare the number of growth steps.

Your task:

  1. Create new Vector<>(3, 4) and new Vector<>(3).
  2. After each add, if the capacity changed, print the size and the new capacity.
  3. Count how many times each Vector grew.

Hints:

  • The default doubling Vector goes 3, 6, 12.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 5: Safe unique registration with two threads

Level: Medium

Problem: Two registration desks try to register the same 100 visitor IDs into one shared Vector. IDs must be unique. First show why "check then add" with only a Vector is not enough, then fix it with one synchronized (vector) block, and print the final size.

Your task:

  1. Both threads loop over IDs 1 to 100 and do: if the vector does not contain the ID, add it.
  2. Put the check and the add together inside synchronized (registered).
  3. After both threads finish, the size must be exactly 100 and there must be no duplicates.

Hints:

  • Vector locks on itself, so synchronized (registered) uses the same lock as its methods.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 6: Producer and consumer sharing a Vector

Level: Hard

Problem: A producer thread adds 5 ticket numbers (1 to 5) into a shared Vector, one every few milliseconds. A consumer thread removes them as they appear and sums them. Use wait and notifyAll on the Vector so the consumer sleeps when it is empty. Print the total.

Your task:

  1. Producer: in a synchronized block add the number and call notifyAll().
  2. Consumer: in a synchronized block, while the vector is empty call wait(); then remove index 0 and add it to the sum.
  3. Join both threads and print the total (15).

Hints:

  • Always use while, not if, around wait().

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

interviewQA: What is a Vector? Why is it called a legacy class?

Vector is a growable array from Java 1.0 whose methods are all synchronized. It was retrofitted to implement List in Java 1.2 but keeps old methods like addElement and elements(). It is called legacy because ArrayList and the concurrent collections replaced it.
Difference between Vector and ArrayList?

Vector is synchronized (thread-safe, slower), doubles its capacity when full and has the old Enumeration API; ArrayList is unsynchronized, grows by 50% and is the default choice for single-threaded code.
What is the default capacity of a Vector and how does it grow?
Capacity 10. When full it doubles, or grows by capacityIncrement if you passed one to the constructor.
Is Vector fully thread-safe?
Individual methods are atomic, but compound operations (check-then-act, iteration) are not, so you must lock the vector yourself around such sequences.
Enumeration versus Iterator on a Vector?
Enumeration (elements()) is the old read-only cursor and is not fail-fast; Iterator is the modern one, supports remove() and is fail-fast.
How do you make an ArrayList thread-safe instead of using Vector?
Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>()), or CopyOnWriteArrayList for read-mostly workloads.
What does setSize(n) do?
It changes the size of the vector: if n is larger the new slots are filled with null, if smaller the extra elements are discarded.
How does Vector relate to Stack?
Stack extends Vector, so a Stack is also synchronized and inherits every Vector method. Use ArrayDeque for a modern stack.
Does Vector allow null and duplicates?
Yes to both, and it keeps insertion order.
Which exception does elementAt(i) throw for a bad index?
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, a subclass of IndexOutOfBoundsException.

topics.name: Stack

beginner.content:
What is a Stack?

A stack is a pile where you only touch the top. The last item you put on is the first item you take off: LIFO (Last In, First Out). Think of a pile of plates, or the Back button of a browser: the page you visited most recently is the first one you go back to.

  • The class java.util.Stack extends Vector, so it is a growable array in which the end of the array is the top of the stack.
  • Only five methods are special: push, pop, peek, empty and search.
  • Because it extends Vector, it is synchronized (thread-safe, slower) and also exposes all Vector/List methods (get(i), add(i, e), ...), which can break the LIFO discipline.
  • Allows duplicates and null. Starts with capacity 10 and doubles when full.
  • Modern advice: the Java documentation itself recommends Deque<E> stack = new ArrayDeque<>() for new code. Learn Stack for interviews and to read old code.

Where Stack sits in the Collection Framework

Collection
(I)
← extends
List
(I)
← implements
AbstractList
(c)
← extends
Vector
(c)
← extends
Stack
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class.

The five Stack methods at a glance

MethodWhat it doesOn an empty stackTime
push(e)Puts e on top and returns it-O(1) amortised
pop()Removes and returns the top elementthrows EmptyStackExceptionO(1)
peek()Returns the top element without removing itthrows EmptyStackExceptionO(1)
empty()true if there are no elementstrueO(1)
search(o)Position of o counted from the top (1 = top), or -1-1O(n)

Your first Stack program

  • Items go on top with push; the printed list shows the bottom first and the top last.
  • pop takes the top item off, so the order of removal is the reverse of the order of adding.

Benefits and advantages

A Stack follows one simple rule: last in, first out (LIFO). Think of a pile of plates: you put a plate on top and you take the top plate first.

  • Very easy to learn. Only a few methods matter: push, pop, peek, empty, search.
  • Perfect for "undo" thinking. The most recent thing is always the first to come back: undo, back button, nested brackets, function calls.
  • Fast core operations. push, pop and peek work at the top and cost O(1) (amortized for push).
  • It is also a Vector. So you can still use get(i), contains, size and loops over it.
  • Thread-safe methods (inherited from Vector, every call is synchronized).
  • For experienced developers: stacks turn recursion into loops (depth-first search, expression evaluation, parsing) and avoid StackOverflowError on deep inputs because the explicit stack lives on the heap.

Disadvantages and when NOT to use it

The Stack class has a good idea but an old design. Java itself recommends something else for new code.

  • It is a legacy class. The Javadoc says to prefer Deque (for example ArrayDeque) for LIFO work.
  • It exposes too much. Because it extends Vector, anyone can call add(0, x) or remove(2) and break the stack idea.
  • Slower. Each call is synchronized even when you use one thread.
  • Strange order. Printing a Stack shows bottom to top, and iteration also goes bottom to top, the opposite of the order pop returns. An ArrayDeque used as a stack iterates top to bottom.
  • Pop on empty throws. pop() and peek() throw EmptyStackException when nothing is there; always check empty() first.
  • For experienced developers: use Deque<E> stack = new ArrayDeque<>() with push/pop/peek. It is faster, has no locks, and its interface only allows stack-like operations when you type the variable as Deque. It does not allow null elements.

Use Stack or something else?

Use Stack whenUse something else when
You learn the idea of LIFO, or maintain old codeYou write new code: use ArrayDeque as a stack
You need the last item first (undo, back, brackets)You need first-in first-out: use a Queue
A small program where speed does not matterSpeed matters or you need millions of pushes: use ArrayDeque
You want a thread-safe stack with minimal effortReal concurrency: use ConcurrentLinkedDeque or LinkedBlockingDeque

intermediate.content:
The Stack methods

Each method with a runnable example.

1. push(E item)

  • Signature: E push(E item)
  • Returns: the item that was pushed
  • Time: O(1) amortised

For freshers: Puts the item on the top of the stack. It also returns the item, which is handy in expressions.

For experienced developers: Internally it calls addElement(item), so the "top" is the last index of the underlying array (the opposite of Deque.push, which adds at the front). The vector grows by doubling when it is full.

2. pop()

  • Signature: E pop()
  • Returns: the removed top element
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Removes the top element and returns it. If the stack is empty it throws EmptyStackException, so check empty() first when the stack might be empty.

For experienced developers: Implemented as peek() then removeElementAt(size - 1): no shifting because the top is the last slot. EmptyStackException is an unchecked RuntimeException.

3. peek()

  • Signature: E peek()
  • Returns: the top element (not removed)
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Look at the top element without removing it. Use it to decide whether to pop. Throws EmptyStackException when empty.

For experienced developers: Unlike Deque.peek(), which returns null for an empty deque, Stack.peek() throws. Do not assume the two behave alike when you migrate.

4. empty()

  • Signature: boolean empty()
  • Returns: true if the stack has no elements
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Tells whether the stack is empty. It is the classic Stack name; isEmpty() (inherited from Vector) does exactly the same.

For experienced developers: The two names exist for historical reasons. Prefer isEmpty() in new code so the call works with any collection.

5. search(Object o)

  • Signature: int search(Object o)
  • Returns: the 1-based distance from the top, or -1
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Finds an element and tells how far it is from the top: the top element is at position 1, the next at 2, and so on. If the element is not there you get -1. If it appears several times, the one closest to the top is reported.

For experienced developers: It is size() - lastIndexOf(o). Note the two quirks: positions are 1-based and counted from the top, unlike indexOf which is 0-based from the bottom.

Inherited Vector methods

A Stack is a Vector, so every Vector method works. Be careful: the ones that touch the middle break the "only the top" rule.

6. Walking a Stack

  • Signature: for-each, iterator(), listIterator(), forEach(), stream(), get(i)
  • Returns: elements from the bottom to the top
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Iterating a Stack visits the elements from the bottom up (insertion order), which is the opposite of the order pop would return them. To print "top first" iterate backwards or use a ListIterator.

For experienced developers: This surprises people who switch to ArrayDeque or LinkedList used as a stack, where iteration goes from the top down. Do not rely on iteration order when you change the class.

7. Methods that break the LIFO rule

  • Signature: get(i), add(i, e), remove(i), set(i, e), insertElementAt(e, i)
  • Returns: work on any position
  • Time: O(1) / O(n)

For freshers: Because Stack inherits the Vector (List) methods, nothing stops you from reading or removing in the middle. That is legal, but then it is no longer a true stack.

For experienced developers: This is a design flaw of java.util.Stack (inheritance instead of composition) and a main reason that Deque/ArrayDeque is recommended: it exposes only the end operations.

8. Stack as the modern Deque

  • Signature: Deque stack = new ArrayDeque<>(); push, pop, peek
  • Returns: LIFO with a clean API
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: The recommended replacement is ArrayDeque used through the Deque interface. It has the same push, pop and peek names but offers only end operations, is not synchronized (so faster) and returns null from peek() on an empty stack.

For experienced developers: Differences to remember: Deque.pop() throws NoSuchElementException (not EmptyStackException), peek() returns null, ArrayDeque forbids null elements, and iteration goes from the top down.

Master program: every Stack method in one place

One single program that uses all the Stack methods you learned above, step by step. Read the numbered comments from top to bottom, run it, and match each output line with its step.

Module: Sorting methods

A Stack is a Vector, so it is also a List and can be sorted like one. The important point is what the order means: index 0 is the bottom of the stack and the last index is the top.

  • Sorting changes the stack. After Collections.sort(stack) ascending, the largest value is on top, so the next pop() gives the largest.
  • Reverse flips top and bottom. The old bottom becomes the new top.
  • Real stack-style sorting uses only push/pop/peek and a second helper stack.
  • For experienced developers: sorting a Stack with list methods is allowed, but it bypasses the LIFO discipline. If your design is strictly a stack, keep the sorted view in a separate list or use stream().sorted() on a copy.

9. Collections.sort(List) on a Stack

  • Signature: static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> void sort(List<T> list)
  • Returns: nothing (the stack is reordered in place)
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Sorts the stack from bottom to top in ascending order. So the biggest number ends up on top. Pop gives the biggest first.

For experienced developers: It calls Vector.sort (synchronized) and rewrites the internal array. To have the smallest on top, sort with Collections.reverseOrder().

10. Vector.sort(Comparator) and Comparator.comparing

  • Signature: synchronized void sort(Comparator<? super E> c)
  • Returns: nothing (the stack is sorted in place)
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Use it when the stack holds your own objects, for example tasks. The Comparator says which task should be nearer the top. Remember: the last element in the order is the top.

For experienced developers: The method is synchronized on the Stack. Equal elements keep their relative order (stable sort).

11. Collections.reverse(List) on a Stack

  • Signature: static void reverse(List<?> list)
  • Returns: nothing (the stack is reversed in place)
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Turns the stack upside down: the old bottom becomes the new top. A classic way to reverse a stack when you only need the final result.

For experienced developers: The "pure" way is to pop everything into a second stack (and again into a third). The list method swaps elements by index and is much shorter, but it is not stack-like.

12. Sorting with a helper stack (only push, pop, peek)

  • Signature: Stack<Integer> sortStack(Stack<Integer> in)
  • Returns: a new stack with the smallest on top... or biggest, as you choose
  • Time: O(n squared)

For freshers: Sometimes a question says "sort a stack using only another stack". Take each item out of the input; move bigger items from the helper back to the input until the right place is found; then push the item.

For experienced developers: This is an insertion sort using two stacks, O(n squared) time and O(n) extra space. It is a good interview exercise about how stacks behave.

13. Collections.shuffle and stream().sorted()

  • Signature: Stream<E> sorted(Comparator<? super E> c)
  • Returns: a sorted stream (copy)
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Collections.shuffle(stack, new Random(1)) mixes the cards in a deck. stack.stream().sorted() gives a sorted copy and keeps the stack as it was. A stream reads from the bottom to the top.

For experienced developers: A stream over a Stack is not locked. Copy first in threaded code. The shuffle with a seeded Random gives the same order on every run.

Which sorting method should I pick?

I want to...UseEffect on top of stack
Biggest on topCollections.sort(stack)Top = biggest
Smallest on topCollections.sort(stack, Collections.reverseOrder())Top = smallest
Sort objects by a rulestack.sort(Comparator.comparing(...))Last in order = top
Turn the stack upside downCollections.reverse(stack)Old bottom = new top
Sort with only stack operationsHelper-stack insertion sortTop = biggest (as coded)
Sorted copy, stack untouchedstack.stream().sorted().toList()No change

Module: Finding (searching) methods

A Stack has one finder of its own, search, plus everything it inherits from Vector and List.

  • Look at the top: peek() (O(1), does not remove).
  • How far from the top? search(x) counts from the top and starts at 1; the result is -1 when missing.
  • Position from the bottom: indexOf(x), lastIndexOf(x) start at 0 at the bottom.
  • Is it there: contains(x). Best and count: Collections.max/min/frequency.
  • By condition: stream().filter(...).findFirst(), anyMatch.
  • For experienced developers: never "search" a stack by popping, unless you also push everything back. That is O(n) and easy to get wrong.

14. peek()

  • Signature: E peek()
  • Returns: the top element without removing it
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Look at the top item and leave it there. If the stack is empty you get an EmptyStackException, so check empty() first.

For experienced developers: peek is a synchronized read of elementAt(size - 1). It never changes the stack.

Watch out: peek() on an empty Stack throws EmptyStackException, not null.

15. search(Object)

  • Signature: int search(Object o)
  • Returns: distance from the top (top = 1), or -1 if absent
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Tells you how many pops it takes to reach an item. The item on top has the answer 1, the one below it 2, and so on.

For experienced developers: It uses lastIndexOf and converts: size() - lastIndexOf(o). If the value is present more than once, the one nearest the top is reported.

Watch out: Do not mix this up with indexOf: search is 1-based from the top, indexOf is 0-based from the bottom.

16. indexOf(Object) and lastIndexOf(Object)

  • Signature: int indexOf(Object o) / int lastIndexOf(Object o)
  • Returns: position from the bottom (0-based), or -1
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Inherited from Vector. They tell you the place counted from the bottom of the stack.

For experienced developers: Together with size() you can compute the depth from the top yourself: size() - 1 - index.

17. contains(Object)

  • Signature: boolean contains(Object o)
  • Returns: true if the stack holds an equal element
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: A yes/no question: is this item anywhere in the stack?

For experienced developers: Does not change the stack and does not depend on position. For repeated checks, keep a parallel HashSet.

18. Collections.max, min, frequency and binarySearch

  • Signature: static <T> T max(Collection<? extends T> c)
  • Returns: biggest, smallest, a count, or an index
  • Time: O(n); binarySearch O(log n) on a sorted stack

For freshers: Find the biggest or smallest item, count equal items, or (if the stack is sorted bottom to top) look up a value quickly with binarySearch.

For experienced developers: binarySearch uses indexes, which are bottom to top. It only makes sense when you have sorted the stack in ascending order.

19. stream().filter(...).findFirst() and anyMatch

  • Signature: Optional<E> findFirst()
  • Returns: an Optional or a boolean
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Find the first item that fits a rule. Remember that a stream starts from the bottom of the stack, so "first" means the oldest matching item. To find the one nearest the top, use reversed() (Java 21).

For experienced developers: stack.reversed().stream() reads from the top to the bottom, matching the order of pop.

Which finding method should I pick?

I want to know...UseCounting starts
What is on top?peek()Top
How many pops to reach x?search(x)At 1 from the top
Where is x from the bottom?indexOf(x) / lastIndexOf(x)At 0 from the bottom
Is x anywhere?contains(x)-
Biggest, smallest, how manyCollections.max / min / frequency-
First match, from bottomstream().filter(...).findFirst()Bottom
First match, from topreversed().stream()...findFirst()Top

expert.content:
Where stacks are used

LIFO order appears all over programming. Four classic jobs, each with a program:

  • Matching brackets in a compiler or editor.
  • Reversing a sequence.
  • Undo / Back history in applications and browsers.
  • Evaluating expressions (postfix notation) and the call stack of method calls, including recursion.

Example 1: checking balanced brackets

Push every opening bracket; when a closing bracket arrives, the top of the stack must be its partner.

Example 2: reversing and the browser Back button

Pushing then popping reverses the order. A Back button keeps visited pages on a stack.

Example 3: evaluating a postfix expression

In postfix notation the operator comes after its operands: 6 2 3 + * means 6 * (2 + 3). A stack evaluates it in one pass.

Example 4: recursion is a stack

Every method call is pushed onto the JVM's call stack; returning pops it. Very deep recursion overflows that stack and throws StackOverflowError. You can replace recursion by your own Stack object.

Stack versus ArrayDeque versus LinkedList as a stack

StackArrayDequeLinkedList (as Deque)
Thread-safeYes (synchronized)NoNo
SpeedSlowest (locks)FastestFast, more memory
Allows nullYesNoYes
