pop() on emptyEmptyStackExceptionNoSuchElementExceptionNoSuchElementException
peek() on emptyEmptyStackExceptionreturns nullreturns null
Iteration orderBottom to topTop to bottomTop to bottom
Exposes middle operationsYes (it is a Vector)NoYes (it is a List)
RecommendedLegacyYesOnly when you need List too

Best practices

Keep stacks correct and easy to maintain.

  • For new code use Deque<T> stack = new ArrayDeque<>().
  • Check empty() (or isEmpty()) before pop()/peek() unless an empty stack is a real bug.
  • Do not call get, add(i, e) or remove(i) on a stack; if you need them you want a List.
  • Replace deep recursion by an explicit stack when the depth can be large.
  • Declare the variable with the interface type (Deque) so you can change the class later.

Real-time examples

Stacks are hiding in everyday software: back buttons, undo, and path finding. Three small, complete programs follow.

Example 1: Browser back and forward buttons

For freshers: when you open a page it goes on the back stack; pressing Back moves the current page to the forward stack. For experienced developers: opening a new page clears the forward stack, exactly like real browsers do.

Example 2: Text editor undo

For freshers: every edit is pushed on a stack; Undo pops the last edit and removes that word. For experienced developers: real editors store small "command" objects (with undo logic) instead of text, but the stack idea is the same.

Example 3: Depth-first route search between forts

For freshers: go as deep as possible along one road, and when stuck, step back (pop) and try another road. For experienced developers: this is iterative DFS; the explicit stack replaces recursion and cannot overflow the call stack. The route is printed in a stable order because roads are stored in lists.

Sample project: Mini Browser Simulator

What we build: a text-command browser with history, using two stacks and a list of bookmarks.

  • Step 1: a Browser class holds the current page, a back stack and a forward stack.
  • Step 2: commands OPEN, BACK, FORWARD and BOOKMARK are processed from a list of text lines.
  • Step 3: empty stacks are handled politely (no exception).
  • Step 4: after every command the state is printed.
  • Step 5: a final report uses search and contains to show how deep a page is in the history.

Practice questions

Now test yourself. Each question is harder than the examples above: read the problem, write your own solution, then compare it with the one shown. Every solution was compiled and run, and its output is real.

Practice question 1: Route editor with undo and redo

Level: Medium

Problem: A route editor lets a trekker add forts to a plan and press Undo and Redo. Two stacks do the whole job: the last action done is the first one undone (LIFO).

Your task:

  1. push each action on the undo stack.
  2. pop from the undo stack and push to the redo stack when the user presses Undo.
  3. peek to show the latest step, empty() to guard against an empty stack.
  4. A second small program checks that brackets in an expression are balanced.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 2: Infix expression calculator (two stacks)

Level: Hard

Problem: Evaluate expressions such as 2 + 3 * (4 - 1) with + - * / and brackets, respecting the normal operator priority, using one stack for numbers and one for operators.

Your task:

  1. Read the expression character by character; build multi-digit numbers.
  2. ( goes on the operator stack; ) evaluates until the matching (.
  3. Before pushing an operator, evaluate every operator on top that has the same or higher priority.
  4. At the end, evaluate what is left. Test with 3 expressions.

Hints:

  • - and / are not commutative: the first number popped is the right operand.
  • After reading a number, step the index back one place so the loop does not skip a character.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 3: Reverse words and check a palindrome

Level: Easy

Problem: Using a Stack<Character>, (1) reverse the text "Raigad Fort", and (2) check whether "MADAM" and "TORNA" are palindromes (the same forwards and backwards).

Your task:

  1. Push every character, then pop them all into a StringBuilder to get the reversed text.
  2. For the palindrome, compare each character of the word with the popped character.
  3. Print true or false for each word.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 4: Next taller fort (monotonic stack)

Level: Medium

Problem: For every fort in a row, print the height of the next taller fort to its right, or -1 if there is none. Solve it in one pass with a stack of indexes, not with two nested loops.

Your task:

  1. Walk left to right; while the height at the top index is less than the current height, pop it and set its answer to the current height.
  2. Push the current index.
  3. Whatever is left in the stack has no taller fort on its right: answer -1.

Hints:

  • Each index is pushed and popped once, so the time is O(n).

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 5: Min stack: get the minimum in O(1)

Level: Medium

Problem: Build a small stack of prices that supports push, pop and min(), where min() is O(1). Use a second stack that remembers the minimum so far.

Your task:

  1. On push: push the value on the main stack; push on the min stack if it is empty or the value is smaller than or equal to its top.
  2. On pop: if the popped value equals the top of the min stack, pop the min stack as well.
  3. Run a few operations and print min after each.

Hints:

  • Use <= not <, or a duplicated minimum would be lost after one pop.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 6: Decode a nested trek code

Level: Hard

Problem: A code like 2[ab3[c]]d means: repeat "ab" followed by 3 times "c", two times, then add "d". The result is abcccabcccd. Decode such codes using two stacks (one for counts, one for the text built so far).

Your task:

  1. Read digits into a number; on [ push the number and the current text, then start a fresh text.
  2. On a letter, append it to the current text.
  3. On ] pop the count and the previous text; the current text becomes previous + current repeated count times.

Hints:

  • Think of each "[" as opening a new level and each "]" as returning to the level above.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

interviewQA: What is a Stack and which principle does it follow?
A Stack is a LIFO structure: the last element pushed is the first one popped. In Java, java.util.Stack extends Vector and offers push, pop, peek, empty and search.
What is the difference between peek() and pop()?
Both return the top element; peek() leaves it on the stack, pop() removes it. Both throw EmptyStackException on an empty Stack.
What does search() return?
The 1-based position of the element counted from the top of the stack (top = 1), the closest occurrence if there are duplicates, or -1 if absent.
Why is java.util.Stack discouraged?
It extends Vector, so it is synchronized (slow) and exposes List methods that break LIFO. ArrayDeque used through Deque is faster, has a clean end-only API and is recommended by the Javadoc.
Which exception is thrown by pop() on an empty Stack?
EmptyStackException (unchecked). A Deque throws NoSuchElementException for pop() and returns null for peek().
In which order does a for-each loop visit a Stack?
From the bottom to the top (insertion order), the reverse of the pop order. An ArrayDeque used as a stack iterates top first.
How do you check for balanced brackets?
Push each opening bracket; on a closing bracket pop and verify it is the matching opener; at the end the stack must be empty.
What is the call stack?
The JVM keeps a stack of frames for method calls: calling a method pushes a frame and returning pops it. Too deep a recursion throws StackOverflowError.
Is Stack thread-safe?
Its individual methods are synchronized (inherited from Vector), but compound actions such as peek-then-pop are not atomic.
How do you get a stack's elements top first?
Iterate with a ListIterator from the end, or use ArrayDeque, whose iterator already starts at the top.

topics.name: HashSet

beginner.content:
What is a HashSet?

A HashSet is a collection that never holds the same element twice. Add "Raigad" a second time and nothing happens. It is built for speed: asking "is this fort in the set?" takes roughly the same tiny time whether the set holds ten forts or ten million.

  • Package java.util. Implements the Set interface (a Collection with no duplicates).
  • No index: a set has no get(i). You ask whether something is in it, add it, remove it, or loop over it.
  • No guaranteed order: elements come out in an order decided by their hash codes. It can look random and can change when the set grows. If you need an order use LinkedHashSet (insertion order) or TreeSet (sorted).
  • One null is allowed.
  • Fast: add, remove and contains are O(1) on average.
  • Not thread-safe. Internally a HashSet is a HashMap whose keys are your elements.
  • Your element class must implement equals() and hashCode() properly (String, Integer and records already do).

Where HashSet sits in the Collection Framework

Iterable
(I)
← extends
Collection
(I)
← extends
Set
(I)
← implements
AbstractSet
(c)
← extends
HashSet
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. HashSet also implements Cloneable and Serializable. Its subclass LinkedHashSet adds insertion order.

Creating a HashSet: four constructors

  • new HashSet<>(): empty, capacity 16, load factor 0.75.
  • new HashSet<>(int initialCapacity): empty with room for about that many buckets.
  • new HashSet<>(int initialCapacity, float loadFactor): control both numbers.
  • new HashSet<>(Collection c): a set holding the elements of another collection (duplicates are dropped).

Your first HashSet program

  • add returns true if the element was new and false if it was already there.
  • The printed order is decided by the hash codes, not by the order of adding.

All HashSet methods at a glance

n is the number of elements, m the size of the other collection.

MethodWhat it doesTime
add(e)Adds e if not present; returns whether it was addedO(1) average
addAll(c)Adds every element of c (union)O(m)
remove(o)Removes o if present; returns whether it wasO(1) average
removeAll(c)Removes every element found in c (difference)O(m) to O(n*m)
retainAll(c)Keeps only elements found in c (intersection)O(n)
removeIf(p)Removes all elements matching a conditionO(n)
contains(o) / containsAll(c)Membership testsO(1) / O(m)
size() / isEmpty() / clear()Count, emptiness, remove allO(1) / O(1) / O(capacity)
iterator() / forEach(a)Visit every elementO(n + capacity)
stream() / toArray()Stream / array copyO(n)
clone()Shallow copyO(n)
equals(o) / hashCode() / toString()Same elements regardless of order / hash / textO(n)
Set.of(...) / Set.copyOf(c)Immutable setsO(n)

Benefits and advantages

For freshers: a HashSet is the easiest way to say "keep each thing only once" and to ask "do I already have this?" quickly.

  • No duplicates for free: you never write an "if already there" check; add does it and tells you the answer.
  • Very fast lookups: contains, add and remove take about the same tiny time for 10 or 10 million elements.
  • Set maths in one line: union (addAll), intersection (retainAll) and difference (removeAll).
  • Cleans lists: new HashSet<>(list) removes duplicates instantly.
  • Simple to use: no comparator and no ordering rules to think about.
  • Low overhead: lighter than a TreeSet, and no linked list like LinkedHashSet.

For experienced developers: O(1) average operations come from hashing into a power-of-two table; a poor hashCode is the only thing that turns this into O(log n) (treeified bins) or O(n). It is the default choice when you need only uniqueness and membership.

Disadvantages and when NOT to use it

For freshers: a HashSet is not magic. It gives up some things to be fast.

  • No order: elements come out in a hash-decided order that can change after the set grows.
  • No index: there is no get(i), so "give me the 3rd element" is impossible.
  • No sorted view or range queries: you cannot ask for "the next bigger value" or "everything between A and B".
  • Needs good equals() and hashCode(): without them duplicates sneak in or lookups fail.
  • Not thread-safe and elements must not be changed after adding.
  • Extra memory: every element is wrapped in a map entry, and the table keeps empty buckets.

For experienced developers: iteration costs O(capacity + size), so a once-huge, now-small set is slow to iterate; clear() does not shrink it. For tiny sets (under about 10 elements) a plain List can be as fast and uses less memory.

Use a HashSet whenUse something else when
You only need uniqueness and fast "is it in there?"You need sorted output or nearest-value search: TreeSet
Order does not matterYou need insertion order: LinkedHashSet
Elements are immutable (String, Integer, record)You need positions or duplicates: ArrayList
One thread uses the setSeveral threads write: ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()

intermediate.content:
Adding elements

A set decides for you whether an element is new. The return value of add tells you what happened.

1. add(E e)

  • Signature: boolean add(E e)
  • Returns: true if the element was new, false if it was already present
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: Puts the element into the set only if it is not already there. Use the return value to detect duplicates, for example to find the first repeated value in a list.

For experienced developers: It calls map.put(e, PRESENT) on the internal HashMap. A duplicate is detected with hashCode() (to find the bucket) then equals() (to compare inside the bucket). The existing element is kept; the new equal one is discarded.

2. addAll(Collection c): union

  • Signature: boolean addAll(Collection c)
  • Returns: true if the set changed
  • Time: O(m)

For freshers: Adds every element of another collection. Because a set ignores duplicates, addAll performs a union of two groups.

For experienced developers: It loops over c calling add. Pass a HashSet as the receiver and any collection as the argument; the result never contains duplicates.

Looking things up

The reason to use a HashSet: very fast membership tests.

3. contains(Object o) and containsAll(Collection c)

  • Signature: boolean contains(Object o); boolean containsAll(Collection c)
  • Returns: true or false
  • Time: O(1) / O(m)

For freshers: contains tells whether the element is in the set. It does not scan the whole set: it jumps straight to the right bucket. containsAll tests that every element of another collection is present (a "subset" test).

For experienced developers: Compare: ArrayList.contains is O(n). Turning a big list into a HashSet before many lookups is one of the most common performance fixes. Lookup cost degrades only when many elements share a bucket (bad hashCode).

4. size(), isEmpty() and clear()

  • Signature: int size(); boolean isEmpty(); void clear()
  • Returns: the count / whether empty / nothing
  • Time: O(1) / O(1) / O(capacity)

For freshers: Count the elements, test for none, or remove all of them.

For experienced developers: clear() empties the table but keeps its capacity, so the set does not shrink. Clearing a set that once held millions of elements leaves a big, empty table behind; create a new set if memory matters.

Removing elements

Remove one element, a group, the elements that match a rule, or everything outside a group.

5. remove(Object o)

  • Signature: boolean remove(Object o)
  • Returns: true if the element was present
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: Removes the element if it is there and tells you whether it was. No shifting, because a set has no positions.

For experienced developers: It deletes the entry from the bucket. As with add, the lookup uses hashCode then equals.

6. removeAll, retainAll and removeIf

  • Signature: boolean removeAll(Collection c); boolean retainAll(Collection c); boolean removeIf(Predicate filter)
  • Returns: true if the set changed
  • Time: O(n) typical

For freshers: removeAll(c) is set difference (A minus B). retainAll(c) is intersection (what both sets share). removeIf removes everything that matches a rule written as a lambda.

For experienced developers: They are inherited from AbstractSet/Collection. For removeAll, Java chooses to iterate the smaller of the two collections when the argument is a Set, which keeps it fast. The argument's contains speed matters: pass a Set, not a List.

Walking and converting

A set has no index, so you visit every element with a loop, an iterator or a stream.

7. for-each, iterator() and forEach()

  • Signature: for (E e : set) ...; Iterator iterator(); void forEach(Consumer)
  • Returns: each element once, in hash order
  • Time: O(n + capacity)

For freshers: Visit every element. The order is not insertion order and is not guaranteed. Remove while walking only through Iterator.remove() (or removeIf), otherwise you get ConcurrentModificationException.

For experienced developers: The iterator walks the bucket array, so its cost is proportional to capacity + size; a mostly empty large table is slow to iterate. The iterator is fail-fast.

8. stream(), toArray() and clone()

  • Signature: Stream stream(); Object[] toArray(); Object clone()
  • Returns: a stream / an array / a shallow copy
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Process the elements with a stream pipeline, copy them into an array, or make a shallow copy of the set.

For experienced developers: The stream is unordered (the set has no order), so results of findFirst are arbitrary. Prefer the copy constructor new HashSet<>(set) to clone().

9. equals, hashCode, toString and Set.of

  • Signature: boolean equals(Object); int hashCode(); String toString(); Set.of(...) / Set.copyOf(...)
  • Returns: comparison / hash / text / immutable sets
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Two sets are equal when they hold the same elements, whatever the order or the Set class. Set.of(...) creates an immutable set (add and remove throw UnsupportedOperationException, no nulls, no duplicates allowed at creation).

For experienced developers: Set.of rejects duplicate arguments with IllegalArgumentException, and its iteration order is randomised per JVM run (on purpose, to stop code depending on it).

Common jobs with a HashSet

Three everyday uses.

Remove duplicates from a list

Copy the list into a set. To keep the original order use LinkedHashSet instead of HashSet.
Union, intersection and difference of two groups

Fast lookups: a set instead of a list

The program counts how many blocked forts appear in a long list of visits, using a list lookup (O(n) each) and a set lookup (O(1) each). The counts are equal; only the work differs.

Master program: every HashSet method in one place

One single program that uses all the HashSet methods you learned above, step by step. Read the numbered comments from top to bottom, run it, and match each output line with its step.

Module: Sorting methods

For freshers: a HashSet never sorts itself. If you want sorted output, you make a sorted copy and leave the HashSet alone. There are four common ways, and each card below shows one tiny program.

For experienced developers: sorting is O(n log n) in every case. Pick by what you need next: a set (keep uniqueness and sorted), a list (index access) or just a one-time stream result.

10. Sorted set: new TreeSet<>(set)

  • Signature: Set<E> sorted = new TreeSet<>(set)
  • Returns: a new sorted set
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Copy the HashSet into a TreeSet. The TreeSet keeps its elements in sorted order by itself, and it is still a set (no duplicates).

For experienced developers: The copy constructor adds elements one by one (O(n log n)). If the source is already a SortedSet it is copied in linear time. Later adds also stay sorted.

11. Sorted list: stream().sorted().toList()

  • Signature: List<E> list = set.stream().sorted().toList()
  • Returns: an unmodifiable sorted list
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Turn the set into a stream, sort it, and collect it into a list. Good for printing or looping once.

For experienced developers: sorted() needs elements that are Comparable, otherwise ClassCastException. toList() (Java 16+) returns an unmodifiable list; use Collectors.toList() if you must change it.

12. Sorted list: new ArrayList + Collections.sort

  • Signature: List<E> list = new ArrayList<>(set); Collections.sort(list)
  • Returns: a sorted, changeable list
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Copy the set into an ArrayList and sort that list. You can then use get(index), which a set never allows.

For experienced developers: This is the classic pre-stream way and is still the best when you want a mutable list with index access. list.sort(null) does the same as Collections.sort(list).

13. Custom order: sorted(Comparator)

  • Signature: set.stream().sorted(Comparator<? super E>)
  • Returns: a stream in your own order
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Give your own rule when alphabetical is not what you want, for example "shortest name first, then alphabetical".

For experienced developers: Build comparators with Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...). Always add a tie-breaker; otherwise equal-ranked elements come out in the arbitrary hash order of the source set.

14. Descending order: Comparator.reverseOrder()

  • Signature: set.stream().sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder())
  • Returns: a stream, biggest first
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Biggest first (a "top list") is just a reversed comparator.

For experienced developers: Alternatives: new TreeSet<>(Comparator.reverseOrder()) then addAll, or Collections.reverse(list) after sorting.

Which sorting method to pick?

You needPickResult
Sorted AND still a setnew TreeSet<>(set)Sorted set, stays sorted when you add
Print or loop oncestream().sorted().toList()Unmodifiable list
Index access or edits after sortingnew ArrayList + Collections.sortMutable list
Own order (length, price, ...)sorted(Comparator...)Stream or list in your order
Biggest firstComparator.reverseOrder()Descending

Module: Finding (searching) methods

For freshers: "finding" in a HashSet means asking questions: is this in there? are all of these in there? what do two sets share? which elements match a rule? Each card has one tiny program.

For experienced developers: only contains uses the hash and is O(1). Everything that looks at "which elements match" (stream filters, min, max) must scan the whole set: O(n).

15. contains(Object o)

  • Signature: boolean contains(Object o)
  • Returns: true or false
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: The fastest way to find something. It jumps straight to the right bucket instead of looking at every element.

For experienced developers: Uses hashCode() then equals(). Searching for a mutated element (changed after adding) fails.

16. containsAll(Collection c)

  • Signature: boolean containsAll(Collection<?> c)
  • Returns: true only if every element is present
  • Time: O(m)

For freshers: Checks that a whole group is inside the set (is it a "subset"?). One missing element makes the answer false.

For experienced developers: Loops over the argument and calls contains on the receiver, so call it on the HashSet and pass the smaller collection.

17. retainAll(Collection c): find what two groups share

  • Signature: boolean retainAll(Collection<?> c)
  • Returns: true if the set changed
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Keeps only the elements that are also in the other collection, so what is left is the common part. Copy the set first if you still need the original.

For experienced developers: It changes the receiver. Wrap in new HashSet<>(original) first. Pass a Set as the argument, since its contains is O(1).

18. stream().filter(...): find all that match a rule

  • Signature: Stream<E> filter(Predicate<? super E>)
  • Returns: a stream of the matching elements
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: When the rule is not "equal to", for example "name is longer than 6 letters", filter the set and collect the matches.

For experienced developers: There is no index to speed this up. If you filter the same big set often by the same rule, keep a second set or a map grouped by that rule.

19. stream().anyMatch / allMatch / noneMatch

  • Signature: boolean anyMatch(Predicate); boolean allMatch(Predicate); boolean noneMatch(Predicate)
  • Returns: true or false
  • Time: O(n), stops early

For freshers: Yes/no questions about a rule: does ANY element match? do ALL? does NONE?

For experienced developers: They are short-circuiting: anyMatch stops at the first match, allMatch at the first failure. On an empty set, allMatch is true and anyMatch is false.

20. Collections.min / Collections.max

  • Signature: static <T> T min(Collection<? extends T>); static <T> T max(Collection<? extends T>)
  • Returns: the smallest / largest element
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: A HashSet cannot give you its smallest element for free, so these helpers scan the whole set and find it.

For experienced developers: If you need the min or max often, a TreeSet (first()/last() in O(log n)) is the better collection. Both throw NoSuchElementException on an empty set.

21. stream().count() with a filter

  • Signature: long count()
  • Returns: how many elements match
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Counts how many elements follow a rule. Without filter it is just size(), which is much faster.

For experienced developers: Do not write stream().count() when you mean size(): size is O(1).

Which finding method to pick?

QuestionMethodTime
Is this one value in the set?containsO(1)
Are all of these in the set?containsAllO(m)
What do two sets share?retainAll on a copyO(n)
Which elements follow a rule?stream().filter(...)O(n)
Does any / every element follow a rule?anyMatch / allMatchO(n), early stop
Smallest or largest?Collections.min / max (or use a TreeSet)O(n)
How many follow a rule?filter(...).count()O(n)

expert.content:
How HashSet works inside

A HashSet is a thin wrapper over a HashMap<E, Object>; every element is a key and every value is the same dummy object PRESENT.

  • Step 1, hash: h = e.hashCode(), then spread: h ^ (h >>> 16) so the high bits also influence the low bits.
  • Step 2, bucket: the table length is always a power of two, so the index is (n - 1) & hash, a fast "modulo".
  • Step 3, compare: inside the bucket Java compares hash codes first, then == / equals(). A match means "already present".
  • Collisions: elements that land in the same bucket form a linked list; if a bucket reaches 8 entries and the table has at least 64 buckets, the list is converted to a balanced red-black tree (O(log n) instead of O(n)).
  • Resize: when size > capacity * loadFactor (default 16 x 0.75 = 12) the table doubles and every entry is redistributed.
  • Capacity from the copy constructor: max(size / 0.75 + 1, 16), so copying avoids early resizes.
  • Because the order depends on hash codes and table size, iteration order can change after a resize.

Trap: equals() and hashCode() must agree

  • Rule: equal objects must have equal hash codes.
  • If a class overrides equals but not hashCode, two equal objects usually land in different buckets, so the set keeps both and contains fails.
  • A record (or an IDE-generated pair) gets both right.

Trap: changing an element after adding it

  • The bucket of an element is chosen from its hashCode when it is added.
  • If you later change a field that hashCode uses, the element sits in the wrong bucket: contains and remove can no longer find it.
  • Use immutable classes (records, Strings, Integers) as set elements.

Choosing a Set implementation

HashSetLinkedHashSetTreeSetCopyOnWriteArraySet
OrderNoneInsertion orderSorted (natural or Comparator)Insertion order
add / remove / containsO(1) averageO(1) averageO(log n)O(n)
InsideHashMapHashMap + linked listRed-black tree (TreeMap)Array copied on write
nullOne allowedOne allowedNot allowed (natural order)Allowed
Thread-safeNoNoNoYes
Use forDefault setPredictable iterationSorted data, range queriesFew writes, many readers

Best practices

Habits for fast and correct sets.

  • Declare with the interface: Set<String> forts = new HashSet<>();.
  • Give an expected size to avoid resizes: new HashSet<>((int) (expected / 0.75f) + 1) or HashSet.newHashSet(expected) (Java 19+).
  • Use immutable element types; always override equals and hashCode together (or use a record).
  • Do not depend on iteration order; use LinkedHashSet or TreeSet when you need one.
  • Prefer a Set over a List whenever you mostly ask "is it in there?" or must keep values unique.
  • To share between threads use ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() or Collections.synchronizedSet.

Real example: tracking unique visitors of each fort

A visitor log with repeated entries. A set per fort counts each visitor once, and the intersection finds visitors who came to both.

Real-time examples

Three small scenarios where a HashSet is the natural tool. Each is a complete program.

Example 1: unique visitors per day

For freshers: the gate scanner records a visitor id on every entry, even repeats. A set per day counts each person once.

For experienced developers: this is the in-memory version of a "distinct count". For billions of ids you would switch to a probabilistic structure such as HyperLogLog.

Example 2: removing duplicate registrations

For freshers: people sometimes register twice, once with capital letters. Clean the e-mail first (lower case), then let add tell you who is a duplicate.

For experienced developers: normalise the key before hashing (case, trim); the set only knows equals, not your business meaning of "same person".

Example 3: new versus returning visitors

For freshers: keep a set of everyone who has ever come. A new arrival is "new" when add returns true, and "returning" when it returns false.

For experienced developers: a single add call both tests and records, so there is no check-then-act race in single-threaded code; use ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() across threads.

Sample project: Trek registration desk

What we build: a console program that checks sign-ups for fort treks.

  • Step 1: a list of sign-ups (name, e-mail, fort), some of them repeated.
  • Step 2: a HashSet of keys "e-mail|fort" accepts the first sign-up and rejects repeats.
  • Step 3: a map from fort to a set of attendees gives the head count per fort.
  • Step 4: set maths finds people going to both Raigad and Torna, and the total number of different people.

Practice questions

Now test yourself. Each question is harder than the examples above: read the problem, write your own solution, then compare it with the one shown. Every solution was compiled and run, and its output is real.

Practice question 1: Visitor registration: no duplicates, and set arithmetic

Level: Medium

Problem: Two forts keep a set of registered visitor IDs. The office must reject double registration and answer questions such as "who visited both forts?"

Your task:

  1. add returns false for a duplicate: use it to detect double registration.
  2. retainAll = visited both (intersection), addAll = visited either (union), removeAll = only one fort (difference).
  3. Always copy first so the original sets stay intact.
  4. contains for an O(1) gate check.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 2: Who visited what: common, unique and first repeat

Level: Hard

Problem: Three groups recorded the forts they visited. Using only sets, answer: which forts did every group visit, which were visited by exactly one group, and what is the first fort repeated in a single group's log?

Your task:

  1. Store each group's forts in a HashSet.
  2. Intersection of all three with retainAll.
  3. Forts visited by exactly one group: count in a HashMap<String, Integer> or use removeAll cleverly.
  4. First repeated element of the log: stop when add returns false.

Hints:

  • Start the intersection from a copy of one set so the original is not destroyed.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 3: Cities in the same trips, whatever the order

Level: Easy

Problem: Two coaches kept their own logs of cities picked up. The logs are lists, may repeat a city and are in different orders. Decide whether both coaches served exactly the same cities.

Your task:

  1. Make a set from each list.
  2. Compare them with equals and print the result.
  3. For two logs that differ, print the cities that appear in only one of them (symmetric difference), sorted.

Hints:

  • Set.equals ignores order and duplicates.
  • Symmetric difference = union minus intersection.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.
codeExamples:
// Practice: same set of cities in two logs
import java.util.HashSet;  // imports the HashSet class
import java.util.List;     // imports the List class
import java.util.Set;      // imports the Set class
import java.util.TreeSet;  // imports the TreeSet class

public class SameCitiesCheck {                  // class that holds the main method
    static Set<String> onlyInOne(Set<String> a, Set<String> b) {  // method onlyInOne()
        Set<String> result = new TreeSet<>(a);  // creates a TreeSet named result copied from a
        result.addAll(b);                       // union
        Set<String> both = new HashSet<>(a);    // creates a HashSet named both copied from a
        both.retainAll(b);                      // intersection
        result.removeAll(both);                 // union minus intersection
        return result;                          // returns the result to the caller
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {  // program entry point
        Set<String> coachA = new HashSet<>(List.of("Pune", "Nashik", "Pune", "Nagpur"));  // creates a HashSet filled with the listed values
        Set<String> coachB = new HashSet<>(List.of("Nagpur", "Pune", "Nashik", "Nashik"));  // creates a HashSet filled with the listed values
        Set<String> coachC = new HashSet<>(List.of("Pune", "Nagpur", "Indore"));  // creates a HashSet filled with the listed values

        System.out.println("A and B same cities? " + coachA.equals(coachB));  // prints the comparison result
        System.out.println("A and C same cities? " + coachA.equals(coachC));  // prints the comparison result
        System.out.println("Only in A or C      : " + onlyInOne(coachA, coachC));  // prints a label followed by the value
    }
}
// OUTPUT:
// A and B same cities? true
// A and C same cities? false
// Only in A or C      : [Indore, Nashik]

expert.content:
Practice question 4: Two forts that add up to the target height

Level: Medium

Problem: Given fort heights and a target number, find every pair of different heights that add up to the target, in one pass over the data.

Your task:

  1. Walk the array once.
  2. For each height x ask a HashSet whether target - x was already seen.
  3. Print each pair found, then add x to the set.

Hints:

  • The naive double loop is O(n squared); the set makes it O(n).
  • Add the current number after checking, not before.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 5: Cities that every trip visited

Level: Medium

Problem: Several trips each visited a group of cities. Find the cities that were part of every trip, and the cities that appeared in at least one trip.

Your task:

  1. Store each trip as a Set<String> in a list.
  2. Start the "common" set as a copy of the first trip and call retainAll with each other trip.
  3. Build the "any trip" set with addAll. Print both sorted.

Hints:

  • Never start "common" as an empty set: the intersection with an empty set stays empty.
  • Copy the first trip; do not modify it.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.
codeExamples:
// Practice: intersection and union across many sets
import java.util.ArrayList;  // imports the ArrayList class
import java.util.HashSet;    // imports the HashSet class
import java.util.List;       // imports the List class
import java.util.Set;        // imports the Set class
import java.util.TreeSet;    // imports the TreeSet class

public class CommonToAllTrips {                        // class that holds the main method
    public static void main(String[] args) {           // program entry point
        List<Set<String>> trips = new ArrayList<>();   // creates an empty ArrayList named trips
        trips.add(Set.of("Pune", "Nashik", "Nagpur", "Indore"));  // adds Set.of("Pune", "Nashik", "Nagpur"... to the end of the list
        trips.add(Set.of("Pune", "Nagpur", "Surat"));  // adds Set.of("Pune", "Nagpur", "Surat") to the end of the list
        trips.add(Set.of("Nagpur", "Pune", "Indore", "Surat"));  // adds Set.of("Nagpur", "Pune", "Indore"... to the end of the list

        Set<String> common = new HashSet<>(trips.get(0));  // start with the first trip
        Set<String> any = new HashSet<>();                 // creates an empty HashSet named any
        for (Set<String> trip : trips) {                   // loops over every element of trips
            common.retainAll(trip);                        // shrink to what all trips share
            any.addAll(trip);                              // grow to everything seen
        }

        System.out.println("In every trip    : " + new TreeSet<>(common));  // prints a label followed by the value
        System.out.println("In at least one  : " + new TreeSet<>(any));  // prints a label followed by the value
    }
}
// OUTPUT:
// In every trip    : [Nagpur, Pune]
// In at least one  : [Indore, Nagpur, Nashik, Pune, Surat]

interviewQA: What is a HashSet and how does it differ from an ArrayList?
HashSet stores unique elements with no order and no index, giving O(1) average add/remove/contains. ArrayList keeps insertion order, allows duplicates and has O(n) contains.
How does HashSet detect duplicates?
It computes the element hashCode, finds the bucket, and compares candidates with equals(). A match means the element is already present and add() returns false.
Is the iteration order of a HashSet guaranteed?
No. It depends on hash codes and the table size and may change after a resize. Use LinkedHashSet for insertion order or TreeSet for sorted order.
How is HashSet implemented internally?
As a HashMap whose keys are the elements and whose values are a shared dummy object (PRESENT).
What are load factor and initial capacity?

Capacity is the number of buckets (default 16); the load factor (default 0.75) is how full the table may get before it doubles and rehashes. A lower load factor means fewer collisions but more memory.
What happens on a hash collision?
Entries in the same bucket form a linked list; with 8 or more entries in a bucket and a table of at least 64 buckets the list becomes a red-black tree, improving the worst case from O(n) to O(log n).
Why must equals() and hashCode() be overridden together?
Equal objects must produce the same hash code, or they land in different buckets and the set treats them as different elements.
Why is mutating an element after adding it dangerous?
Its bucket was chosen from the old hash code. After the change contains() and remove() look in the wrong bucket and the element appears lost.
Does HashSet allow null?
Yes, one null element. TreeSet with natural ordering does not allow null.
How do you perform union, intersection and difference with sets?
Union: addAll; intersection: retainAll; difference: removeAll (on copies, because they modify the receiver).
HashSet vs LinkedHashSet vs TreeSet?
HashSet is fastest with no order; LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order at a small cost; TreeSet keeps elements sorted with O(log n) operations and supports range queries.
Is HashSet thread-safe?
No. Use ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(), Collections.synchronizedSet(...) or CopyOnWriteArraySet depending on the access pattern.
How do you remove duplicates from a list while keeping order?
new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(list)).

topics.name: LinkedHashSet

beginner.content:
What is a LinkedHashSet?

A LinkedHashSet is a HashSet that remembers the order in which you added the elements. You still get no duplicates and fast lookups, but when you print or loop, the elements come out exactly in insertion order. Think of a visitor register: each fort is written once, in the order of the first visit.

  • Package java.util. It extends HashSet and, since Java 21, also implements SequencedSet.
  • No duplicates (the same rule as HashSet). Adding an element that is already present does not change its position.
  • Predictable order: iteration follows insertion order.
  • Fast: add, remove and contains are O(1) on average, with a small extra cost to maintain the order.
  • One null is allowed. Not thread-safe.
  • Use it when you need uniqueness and a stable order: removing duplicates from a list while keeping the order, caches, "recently seen" lists, report output.

Where LinkedHashSet sits in the Collection Framework

Collection
(I)
← extends
Set
(I)
← implements
HashSet
(c)
← extends
LinkedHashSet
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. LinkedHashSet inherits every HashSet method; it only changes how the elements are linked together inside.

Creating a LinkedHashSet

  • new LinkedHashSet<>(): empty, capacity 16, load factor 0.75.
  • new LinkedHashSet<>(int initialCapacity) and (int, float loadFactor): tune the size.
  • new LinkedHashSet<>(Collection c): a copy in the iteration order of c, duplicates dropped.

All LinkedHashSet methods at a glance

MethodWhat it doesTime
add(e) / addAll(c)Adds new elements at the end of the orderO(1) / O(m)
remove(o) / removeAll(c) / retainAll(c) / removeIf(p) / clear()Removes elements (the order of the rest stays)O(1) / O(n)
contains(o) / containsAll(c) / size() / isEmpty()Lookups and countsO(1)
iterator() / forEach(a) / stream() / toArray()Walk or convert in insertion orderO(n)
addFirst(e) / addLast(e)Adds at the front or end, moving an existing element (Java 21)O(1)
getFirst() / getLast()Reads the first / last element (Java 21)O(1)
removeFirst() / removeLast()Removes the first / last element (Java 21)O(1)
reversed()A reversed view (Java 21)O(1)
clone() / equals / hashCode / toStringCopy and compare (equality ignores order)O(n)

Benefits and advantages

For freshers: a LinkedHashSet is a HashSet that remembers the order you added things in. You get "no duplicates" and a predictable order together.

  • Predictable order: loops and toString() always show elements in insertion order.
  • Still fast: add, remove and contains are O(1) on average, like a HashSet.
  • Best way to remove duplicates but keep order: new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(list)).
  • Java 21 extras: getFirst, getLast, removeFirst, addFirst and reversed() make it easy to treat it like a queue or a history list.
  • Repeatable output: tests and printed results look the same on every run.

For experienced developers: internally a HashMap whose entries are also chained in a doubly linked list. Iteration is O(size), unlike HashSet, whose iteration is O(capacity + size). Re-adding an existing element does not change its position.

Disadvantages and when NOT to use it

For freshers: the order has a price, and it is not sorted order.

  • More memory than HashSet: every entry carries two extra links (before and after).
  • Slightly slower adds and removes because the links must be updated.
  • Insertion order is not sorted order: if you want A to Z, use a TreeSet.
  • No index: still no get(i) or indexOf.
  • Same rules as HashSet: good equals/hashCode, no changing elements after adding, not thread-safe.

For experienced developers: re-inserting to "refresh" an element needs remove then add (two operations). For a real LRU cache a LinkedHashMap with access order is a better fit.

Use a LinkedHashSet whenUse something else when
You need uniqueness AND insertion orderOrder does not matter: HashSet (less memory)
You show history, steps or a route once eachYou need sorted order or range search: TreeSet
You dedupe a list and keep the first-seen orderYou need duplicates or positions: ArrayList
You want repeatable output for testsYou need an LRU cache: LinkedHashMap (access order)

intermediate.content:
Adding, keeping the order and ignoring duplicates

LinkedHashSet behaves like HashSet, plus a stable order.

1. add(E e) and addAll(Collection c)

  • Signature: boolean add(E e); boolean addAll(Collection c)
  • Returns: true if something was added
  • Time: O(1) / O(m)

For freshers: Adds an element at the end of the order if it is new. If it is already present nothing changes, and it keeps its old position (re-adding does not move it).

For experienced developers: Internally each entry is a LinkedHashMap.Entry with before and after links in addition to the HashMap bucket link. Insertion order is not affected by re-insertion; this is different from addFirst/addLast (Java 21) which do move.

2. contains, remove and the order of the rest

  • Signature: boolean contains(Object o); boolean remove(Object o)
  • Returns: true / false
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Look up or remove an element by value, like a HashSet. After a removal the remaining elements keep their relative order.

For experienced developers: Removing unlinks the entry from both the bucket chain and the doubly linked order list, which is O(1) because it already has both neighbours.

3. removeAll, retainAll and clear

  • Signature: boolean removeAll(Collection c); boolean retainAll(Collection c); void clear()
  • Returns: true if changed / nothing
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Subtract a group, keep only a group, or remove everything. Unlike HashSet, the result keeps the insertion order of what is left, so printed results are the same every time.

For experienced developers: These are the same inherited methods as HashSet; the benefit of LinkedHashSet is the predictable output, which makes it very good for logs, reports and unit tests.

Walking and converting

Every way of visiting the elements follows the insertion order.

4. iterator, for-each, forEach, stream and toArray

  • Signature: Iterator iterator(); void forEach(Consumer); Stream stream(); Object[] toArray()
  • Returns: the elements in insertion order
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: All of them visit the elements in the order they were first added. Because the elements are also linked in a chain, iterating costs O(size), not O(capacity + size) as in HashSet.

For experienced developers: This makes LinkedHashSet faster to iterate than HashSet when the set is large but sparse. Streams over it are ordered streams.

Java 21: the first and the last element

Java 21 made LinkedHashSet a SequencedSet, which finally gives direct access to both ends.

5. getFirst, getLast, removeFirst, removeLast and reversed

  • Signature: E getFirst(); E getLast(); E removeFirst(); E removeLast(); SequencedSet reversed()
  • Returns: the element / a reversed view
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Read or remove the first or last element without writing a loop. On an empty set they throw NoSuchElementException. reversed() gives a view that walks from the last element to the first.

For experienced developers: Before Java 21 you had to iterate to the end to find the last element. reversed() is a live view, not a copy.

6. addFirst(E) and addLast(E) (Java 21)

  • Signature: void addFirst(E e); void addLast(E e)
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Add an element at the front or the end. If the element is already in the set it is moved to that position. This is the first way to re-order a LinkedHashSet without rebuilding it.

For experienced developers: This is different from add, which never moves an existing element. It makes LinkedHashSet usable as a simple "move to front" structure.

7. clone, equals, hashCode and toString

  • Signature: Object clone(); boolean equals(Object); int hashCode(); String toString()
  • Returns: copy / comparison / hash / text
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: clone makes a shallow copy that keeps the order. equals follows the Set rule: same elements means equal, and order is ignored. toString prints the elements in insertion order.

For experienced developers: Even though it is ordered, LinkedHashSet.equals does not compare the order (a List would). Two sets with the same elements in different order are equal and have the same hash code.

Master program: every LinkedHashSet method in one place

One single program that uses all the LinkedHashSet methods you learned above, step by step. Read the numbered comments from top to bottom, run it, and match each output line with its step.

Module: Sorting methods

For freshers: a LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order, which is not the same as sorted order. The cards show how to see its order, flip it, change it, and how to get a sorted result when you need one.

For experienced developers: the set has no sort() method. You always build a new collection (sort is O(n log n)); only the order of a LinkedHashSet built from a sorted stream is "frozen" as sorted until you add more.

8. Insertion order is the order

  • Signature: for (E e : linkedHashSet)
  • Returns: elements in the order they were first added
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: The order you add things is the order you get them back. Adding an element that is already there changes nothing, not even its position.

For experienced developers: This is called a stable, predictable iteration order. It is the main reason to choose LinkedHashSet over HashSet.

9. Sorted copy: new TreeSet<>(set)

  • Signature: Set<E> sorted = new TreeSet<>(set)
  • Returns: a new sorted set
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Need A to Z for one moment? Copy into a TreeSet. The LinkedHashSet itself is not touched.

For experienced developers: The copy loses insertion order (it is sorted now). Keep the original LinkedHashSet if you still need the order of arrival.

10. Sorted but still a LinkedHashSet: sorted + toCollection

  • Signature: stream().sorted().collect(Collectors.toCollection(LinkedHashSet::new))
  • Returns: a LinkedHashSet whose insertion order is sorted order
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Sort with a stream, then collect into a new LinkedHashSet. The "insertion order" of the new set is the sorted order.

For experienced developers: Useful when later code expects a LinkedHashSet or when you will add more items at the end. Later additions are not sorted in; they simply go last.

11. Newest first: reversed() (Java 21)

  • Signature: SequencedSet<E> reversed()
  • Returns: a reversed view of the set
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: Shows the elements from last added to first added. Perfect for a "recent history" list.

For experienced developers: It is a live view, not a copy: changes to the original show up in the view. Java 21 introduced the sequenced collection interfaces; before that you needed a list and Collections.reverse.

12. Change the order: remove then add

  • Signature: set.remove(e); set.add(e)
  • Returns: the element moves to the end
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Adding an element that is already inside does nothing, so to move it to the end (for example "visited again") you remove it first and add it again.

For experienced developers: This is the building block of an LRU cache. In Java 21 you can also move an element to the front with addFirst(e).

13. Sort with your own rule: ArrayList + list.sort(Comparator)

  • Signature: new ArrayList<>(set).sort(Comparator)
  • Returns: a sorted list
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Copy into a list and sort with a Comparator, for example by name length. If two names have the same length they stay in their insertion order.

For experienced developers: List sorting in Java is stable (it never swaps equal items), so a LinkedHashSet source gives a fully predictable result even without a tie-breaker.

Which sorting or ordering method to pick?

You needPickResult
Insertion order (default)just iterateOrder of first add
Latest firstreversed()Live reversed view
Alphabetical setnew TreeSet<>(set)Sorted, loses insertion order
Sorted but still a LinkedHashSetsorted().collect(toCollection(LinkedHashSet::new))Order frozen as sorted
Move one element to the endremove then addSame set, new position
Own rule with index accessnew ArrayList + sort(Comparator)Stable sorted list

Module: Finding (searching) methods

For freshers: finding in a LinkedHashSet works like a HashSet, plus extra tricks that use the order: first element, last element, "first one that matches".

For experienced developers: contains is O(1); everything that depends on position (index of an element, previous element) needs a scan or a copy to a list, O(n).

14. contains(Object o)

  • Signature: boolean contains(Object o)
  • Returns: true or false
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: Is it in the set? Answers instantly, no matter how large the set is.

For experienced developers: The linked list is not used for lookup; the hash table is.

15. containsAll(Collection c)

  • Signature: boolean containsAll(Collection<?> c)
  • Returns: true if all are present
  • Time: O(m)

For freshers: Are all the required stops in the route? One missing stop gives false. Order does not matter for this test.

For experienced developers: It only checks membership; if the order of stops must match as well, compare two lists instead.

16. getFirst() and getLast() (Java 21)

  • Signature: E getFirst(); E getLast()
  • Returns: the oldest / the newest element
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Because the set remembers order, you can ask for the first or the last element directly, which a HashSet can never do.

For experienced developers: Before Java 21 you needed an iterator for the first element and a full loop (or new ArrayList) for the last. Both throw NoSuchElementException on an empty set.

17. Position of an element: new ArrayList(set).indexOf(e)

  • Signature: int indexOf(Object o) // on a list copy
  • Returns: the position (0 based) or -1
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: A set has no index, so to find "which stop number is Nagpur?" copy the set into a list and ask the list.

For experienced developers: The copy costs O(n) each time. If you need positions often, keep an ArrayList for the order and a HashSet for uniqueness.

18. stream().filter(...).findFirst()

  • Signature: Optional<E> findFirst()
  • Returns: an Optional holding the first match in insertion order
  • Time: O(n), stops early

For freshers: Finds the earliest added element that follows a rule. With a HashSet this answer would be random; here it is dependable.

For experienced developers: Use orElse or ifPresent on the result; get() on an empty Optional throws.

19. retainAll(Collection c): common stops, order kept

  • Signature: boolean retainAll(Collection<?> c)
  • Returns: true if the set changed
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Keeps only the stops that are also in the other group, in the order of the original set.

For experienced developers: Run it on a copy. The order of the result follows the receiver, not the argument.

20. Neighbour of an element: loop with a "previous" variable

  • Signature: for (E e : set)
  • Returns: the element before another one
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: To find the stop that comes right before "Nagpur", walk the set and remember the previous element.

For experienced developers: There is no lower() as in TreeSet: "before" means insertion order, so a scan is the only way.

Which finding method to pick?

QuestionMethodTime
Is it in the set?containsO(1)
Are all of these in it?containsAllO(m)
First or last added?getFirst / getLastO(1)
Which stop number?new ArrayList(set).indexOfO(n)
First that follows a rule?stream().filter().findFirst()O(n)
What do two groups share (order kept)?retainAll on a copyO(n)
What came before X?loop with a previous variableO(n)

expert.content:
How LinkedHashSet works inside

LinkedHashSet is a HashSet whose internal map is a LinkedHashMap.

  • The constructor calls super(capacity, loadFactor, true), a package-private HashSet constructor that creates a LinkedHashMap instead of a plain HashMap.
  • Each entry carries before and after references. The map keeps head (eldest) and tail (youngest) so iteration just follows after pointers.
  • Lookups still go through the hash table, so contains/add/remove are O(1) like HashSet.
  • Memory: two extra references (8 bytes with compressed pointers) per element on top of the HashMap entry.
  • Iteration is O(size) because it ignores empty buckets (HashSet iteration is O(capacity + size)).
  • The "access order" mode (for LRU caches) exists only on LinkedHashMap, not on LinkedHashSet.

HashSet, LinkedHashSet and TreeSet side by side

HashSetLinkedHashSetTreeSet
OrderNoneInsertion orderSorted
add / remove / containsO(1)O(1)O(log n)
IterationO(capacity + n)O(n)O(n)
MemoryLowestA bit moreMost (tree nodes)
nullOneOneNo
Use forPlain uniquenessUniqueness + stable orderSorted data

Trap: you cannot sort a LinkedHashSet or index into it

  • A set has no get(i) and no sort. To sort, copy into a TreeSet or a List.
  • To get an element by position, copy to a list: new ArrayList<>(set).get(i).

Best practices

When and how to use LinkedHashSet well.

  • Choose it when you need uniqueness and a predictable order, for example to remove duplicates from a list without reordering.
  • Prefer plain HashSet when order does not matter: it uses less memory.
  • Use immutable elements and consistent equals/hashCode, as for any hash-based collection.
  • Use getFirst/getLast/reversed (Java 21) instead of iterating to find the ends.
  • For an LRU cache use LinkedHashMap with access order, not a set.

Real example: a "recently visited" list without repeats

Each visit moves a fort to the end of the list; the set never holds a fort twice, and the oldest visit is easy to drop.

Real-time examples

Three everyday jobs for a set that remembers order.

Example 1: search history with no repeats

For freshers: a search box shows your last searches, newest first, and a repeated search moves up instead of appearing twice.

For experienced developers: remove-then-add gives "most recently used" order in O(1); trimming with removeFirst bounds the memory.

Example 2: unique tags in the order the user typed them

For freshers: a user types tags with repeats. We keep each tag once, in the typed order, so the page shows exactly what the user expects.

For experienced developers: a HashSet would show tags in a random order, which makes the page jump around between runs and breaks snapshot tests.

Example 3: an itinerary where every city appears once

For freshers: a travel plan lists cities as they are booked. The final route shows each city once, numbered in order of the first booking.

For experienced developers: the first occurrence wins, which is the usual rule for deduplicating ordered input.

Sample project: Fort visit history

What we build: a small "recently viewed forts" feature like the one in a travel app.

  • Step 1: a History class with a LinkedHashSet and a size limit.
  • Step 2: visit(fort) moves a fort to the end if it was seen, and drops the oldest when the limit is passed.
  • Step 3: helper methods show the newest first, the oldest, and the newest.
  • Step 4: a main method replays a list of visits and prints the history after each one.

Practice questions

Now test yourself. Each question is harder than the examples above: read the problem, write your own solution, then compare it with the one shown. Every solution was compiled and run, and its output is real.

Practice question 1: Recently visited forts (unique, in the order of visiting)

Level: Medium

Problem: A travel app shows "Recently viewed forts": no repeats, in the order the user first looked at them, and it keeps only the newest few. LinkedHashSet removes repeats and keeps the order.

Your task:

  1. add each viewed fort: repeats are ignored.
  2. To move a repeated fort to the end, remove it and add it again.
  3. Trim to the last three using the iterator on the oldest elements.
  4. Remove duplicates from a list while keeping order.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 2: First city that appears only once

Level: Medium

Problem: A stream of city names arrives. Report the first city that occurs exactly once, in the order they first appeared. Use LinkedHashSet to keep the order while you track the repeats.

Your task:

  1. Keep one LinkedHashSet of candidates (seen once, in order) and one HashSet of repeated cities.
  2. When a city arrives: if it is new, add it to the candidates; if it was a candidate, remove it and remember it as repeated.
  3. After every city print the current first candidate (or "none").

Hints:

  • candidates.iterator().next() gives the oldest candidate in O(1).

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 3: Unique letters in the order they first appear

Level: Easy

Problem: Given a word, print its different letters in the order of their first appearance, and how many were repeats.

Your task:

  1. Loop over the characters and add each to a LinkedHashSet<Character>.
  2. Count the repeats as the number of times add returned false.
  3. Build the result text from the set.

Hints:

  • A char is boxed to Character automatically.
  • A HashSet could give the right letters but in an unpredictable order.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 4: Combine two itineraries and keep the order

Level: Medium

Problem: Plan A and plan B are lists of cities. Print the combined plan (A first, then new cities of B), the cities both plans share in plan A order, and the cities only plan B has.

Your task:

  1. Union: copy A into a LinkedHashSet and call addAll(B).
  2. Intersection: copy A and call retainAll(B).
  3. Difference: copy B and call removeAll(A).

Hints:

  • Always copy before calling retainAll or removeAll: they change the receiver.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 5: First repeated city and the loop it closes

Level: Medium

Problem: A route list visits cities. Find the first city that is visited a second time and print the loop of cities from its first visit back to it.

Your task:

  1. Walk the route adding cities to a LinkedHashSet; the first add that returns false finds the repeat.
  2. Walk the set again, collect cities starting at the repeated one.
  3. Print the loop with an arrow between cities, ending with the repeated city.

Hints:

  • The set holds cities in the order of their first visit, which is what the loop needs.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 6: A small LRU cache of fort ids with hit and miss counts

Level: Hard

Problem: Build a cache that keeps at most 3 fort names. A request is a "hit" if the fort is in the cache (and it becomes the most recent), or a "miss" if not (it is added, and the least recently used fort is evicted when full). Replay seven requests and print the result of each.

Your task:

  1. Create a class FortCache with a LinkedHashSet and a capacity.
  2. In request, use contains to decide hit or miss, refresh by remove-then-add, and evict with an iterator when the set is too big.
  3. Print each request, HIT or MISS, and the cache content; end with total hits and misses.

Hints:

  • Evict before adding the new fort, otherwise the new one may be the oldest.
  • In real code LinkedHashMap with access order and removeEldestEntry does this for you.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

interviewQA: What is a LinkedHashSet?
A HashSet that also keeps a doubly linked list through its entries, so it stores unique elements and iterates them in insertion order, with O(1) add/remove/contains.
Difference between HashSet and LinkedHashSet?
HashSet has no defined order and uses less memory; LinkedHashSet iterates in insertion order and has two extra references per entry. Both are O(1) for add, remove and contains.
How is LinkedHashSet implemented?
It extends HashSet and constructs a LinkedHashMap as the backing map; each entry has before/after links, and the map keeps head and tail.
What happens if you add an element that already exists?
The set is unchanged and the element keeps its original position (plain add never moves it). With Java 21 addFirst/addLast do move an existing element.
Does equals() on a LinkedHashSet consider order?
No. Two sets with the same elements are equal regardless of order.
How do you remove duplicates from a list and keep the order?
new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(list)).
Why is iteration over LinkedHashSet faster than HashSet for sparse tables?
LinkedHashSet follows the chain of entries (O(size)), while HashSet iterates over all buckets (O(capacity + size)).
What did Java 21 add to LinkedHashSet?
The SequencedSet methods: getFirst, getLast, addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast and reversed.
Does LinkedHashSet allow null?
Yes, one null element, like HashSet.
Is LinkedHashSet thread-safe?
No. Wrap with Collections.synchronizedSet or use a concurrent structure.

topics.name: TreeSet

beginner.content:
What is a TreeSet?

A TreeSet is a set that keeps its elements sorted at all times. Add forts in any order and they come out alphabetically; add numbers and they come out from small to large. It also never holds duplicates, and it can answer questions such as "which fort comes right after Raigad?" or "give me all forts between P and S".

  • Package java.util. Implements NavigableSet (which extends SortedSet, which extends Set).
  • Sorted order: by the elements' natural order (Comparable) or by a Comparator you supply.
  • No duplicates: "duplicate" means compareTo / compare returns 0, not equals().
  • Slower than HashSet: add, remove and contains are O(log n) because it is a balanced tree.
  • No null with natural ordering (it cannot compare null). Not thread-safe.
  • Elements must be mutually comparable, otherwise ClassCastException.
  • Use it when you need sorted output or range and neighbour queries.

Where TreeSet sits in the Collection Framework

Collection
(I)
← extends
Set
(I)
← extends
SortedSet
(I)
← extends
NavigableSet
(I)
← implements
TreeSet
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. TreeSet extends AbstractSet and is built on a TreeMap.

Creating a TreeSet: four constructors

  • new TreeSet<>(): natural ordering of the elements.
  • new TreeSet<>(Comparator c): your own ordering.
  • new TreeSet<>(Collection c): copy with natural ordering, duplicates dropped.
  • new TreeSet<>(SortedSet s): copy that keeps the ordering of s.

All TreeSet methods at a glance

n is the number of elements.

MethodWhat it doesTime
add(e) / addAll(c)Adds in sorted positionO(log n)
remove(o) / removeIf(p) / clear()Removes elementsO(log n) / O(n)
contains(o) / size() / isEmpty()Lookup / countO(log n) / O(1)
first() / last()Smallest / largest element (throws if empty)O(log n)
pollFirst() / pollLast()Remove and return smallest / largest (null if empty)O(log n)
lower(e) / floor(e)Greatest element < e / ≤ eO(log n)
higher(e) / ceiling(e)Smallest element > e / ≥ eO(log n)
headSet(to) / tailSet(from) / subSet(a, b)Range viewsO(log n)
descendingSet() / descendingIterator()Reverse order view / iteratorO(1)
iterator() / forEach(a) / stream()Walk in sorted orderO(n)
comparator()The Comparator in use (null for natural order)O(1)
clone() / equals / toStringCopy and compareO(n)
reversed() / getFirst() / getLast()Java 21 sequenced methodsO(1) / O(log n)

Benefits and advantages

For freshers: a TreeSet is a set that keeps itself sorted. You add in any order, and when you loop you always get smallest to biggest.

  • Always sorted: no separate sort step; every add puts the element in the right place.
  • No duplicates, just like every set.
  • Smallest and largest instantly: first() and last().
  • "Nearest value" search: floor, ceiling, lower, higher find the closest smaller or bigger element.
  • Range views: headSet, tailSet, subSet give everything below, above or between values.
  • Your own order: pass a Comparator (newest first, by score, ignoring case, ...).

For experienced developers: backed by a red-black tree (TreeMap); every operation is O(log n) worst case, never degraded by bad hash codes. It implements NavigableSet, so it can replace many "sort then binary search" code paths.

Disadvantages and when NOT to use it

For freshers: being sorted is not free.

  • Slower than HashSet: O(log n) instead of O(1) for add, remove and contains.
  • Elements must be comparable: they implement Comparable or you give a Comparator, or you get ClassCastException.
  • No null with natural ordering.
  • "Same" means compareTo is 0, not equals: a Comparator that ignores a field silently treats different objects as duplicates.
  • More memory: each element lives in a tree node with left, right and parent links.
  • No index and not thread-safe (use ConcurrentSkipListSet for threads).

For experienced developers: iterating in order is O(n) and cache-unfriendly compared with an array. If data is loaded once and then only read, a sorted ArrayList plus Collections.binarySearch is smaller and faster.

Use a TreeSet whenUse something else when
You need sorted output at all timesYou only need uniqueness and speed: HashSet
You search by nearest value or rangeYou need insertion order: LinkedHashSet
You often need the smallest or largestData is loaded once, then only read: sorted ArrayList + binary search
Elements have a clear ordering ruleElements have no natural order and equals matters

intermediate.content:
Adding and the sorted order

Whatever order you add in, the elements are kept sorted.

1. add(E e) and addAll(Collection c)

  • Signature: boolean add(E e); boolean addAll(Collection c)
  • Returns: true if the element was new
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Inserts the element at the position that keeps the set sorted. If an element that compares as equal (compareTo returns 0) is already present, nothing is added.

For experienced developers: The tree walks from the root comparing with compareTo (or the comparator), so the cost is the height of the tree: O(log n). Because uniqueness is decided by the comparison, a comparator that ignores a field also treats elements that differ in that field as duplicates (see the trap below).

2. remove, contains, size, isEmpty and clear

  • Signature: boolean remove(Object o); boolean contains(Object o); int size(); boolean isEmpty(); void clear()
  • Returns: true / false / count
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Remove and look up by value, count the elements, or remove all. The set stays sorted after every change.

For experienced developers: Lookups use the same comparison as add, so they need a comparable argument; contains(null) throws NullPointerException with natural ordering.

The ends: first, last, pollFirst and pollLast

Because the set is sorted, the smallest and the largest elements are always easy to reach.

3. first() and last()

  • Signature: E first(); E last()
  • Returns: the smallest / the largest element
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Return the smallest and the largest element without removing them. On an empty set they throw NoSuchElementException.

For experienced developers: In Java 21, getFirst() and getLast() are the equivalent sequenced-collection names. Both walk down the left-most or right-most branch of the tree.

4. pollFirst() and pollLast()

  • Signature: E pollFirst(); E pollLast()
  • Returns: the removed element, or null if empty
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Remove and return the smallest or the largest element. Use them to treat a TreeSet like a priority queue that has no duplicates: repeat pollFirst until it returns null.

For experienced developers: Safe for empty sets (they return null), unlike removeFirst in Java 21 which throws. Because a TreeSet cannot contain null, a null result is unambiguous here.

Neighbours: lower, floor, ceiling and higher

The reason people choose a TreeSet over a HashSet. Given a value, find the closest elements even if the value itself is not in the set.

5. lower, floor, ceiling and higher

  • Signature: E lower(E e); E floor(E e); E ceiling(E e); E higher(E e)
  • Returns: the neighbour, or null if there is none
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Four "nearest element" questions: lower(e) = the greatest element strictly below e; floor(e) = the greatest element below or equal; ceiling(e) = the smallest element above or equal; higher(e) = the smallest element strictly above. Memory trick: floor and lower look down; ceiling and higher look up; floor/ceiling may return e itself.

For experienced developers: Each is one root-to-leaf walk. They are what make TreeSet useful for "find the next time slot", "nearest price", "which range does this value fall in". e does not have to be in the set.

Range views: headSet, tailSet and subSet

Take a part of the set by value. The result is a live view of the same data.

6. headSet, tailSet and subSet

  • Signature: SortedSet headSet(E to); NavigableSet headSet(E to, boolean inclusive); tailSet(from[, inclusive]); subSet(from, to) / subSet(from, fromInc, to, toInc)
  • Returns: a view of that range
  • Time: O(log n) to create

For freshers: headSet(to) = everything before to; tailSet(from) = everything from from onwards; subSet(from, to) = from (included) up to to (excluded). The longer forms let you choose whether each end is included.

For experienced developers: These are views, not copies: changing the view changes the set and vice versa, and adding an element outside the range to the view throws IllegalArgumentException. Wrap in new TreeSet<>(view) for an independent copy.

Reverse order and iteration

Walk the set from the end, or look at it upside down.

7. descendingSet(), descendingIterator() and reversed()

  • Signature: NavigableSet descendingSet(); Iterator descendingIterator(); NavigableSet reversed()
  • Returns: a reversed view / iterator
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: descendingSet() shows the same elements from largest to smallest, as a live view. descendingIterator() walks them that way. In Java 21 reversed() does the same as descendingSet().

For experienced developers: Views are free (no copying). Because it is a NavigableSet itself, you can chain operations, for example set.descendingSet().headSet(x).

8. iterator, forEach, stream and comparator()

  • Signature: Iterator iterator(); void forEach(Consumer); Stream stream(); Comparator comparator()
  • Returns: elements in sorted order / the ordering in use
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Iteration, forEach and streams all visit the elements in sorted order. comparator() returns the Comparator that defines the order, or null when natural ordering is used.

For experienced developers: Streams from a TreeSet are SORTED and DISTINCT, so stream().sorted() is free and distinct() is redundant. The iterator is fail-fast.

Master program: every TreeSet method in one place

One single program that uses all the TreeSet methods you learned above, step by step. Read the numbered comments from top to bottom, run it, and match each output line with its step.

Module: Sorting methods

For freshers: a TreeSet is the sorting tool. You choose the rule: natural order (A to Z, small to big) or your own Comparator. The cards show each way, with a tiny program.

For experienced developers: the order is decided once, at construction, and cannot be changed later. Inserting is O(log n), so building a TreeSet of n elements is O(n log n), the same as one sort.

9. Natural order: no extra code

  • Signature: new TreeSet<>()
  • Returns: elements ordered by compareTo
  • Time: O(log n) per add

For freshers: Numbers sort small to big and Strings sort alphabetically (capital letters before small letters). Just add the elements.

For experienced developers: The element type must implement Comparable. Your own class needs a compareTo method.

10. Reverse order: Comparator.reverseOrder()

  • Signature: new TreeSet<>(Comparator.reverseOrder())
  • Returns: elements biggest first
  • Time: O(log n) per add

For freshers: Hand the TreeSet a rule when you create it. reverseOrder() flips the natural order.

For experienced developers: The comparator is part of the set for its whole life, and it decides what a duplicate is. Pass it in the constructor, you cannot add it later.

11. Several rules: Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...)

  • Signature: new TreeSet<>(Comparator)
  • Returns: objects ordered by more than one field
  • Time: O(log n) per add

For freshers: Sort forts by height (tallest first) and, when heights are equal, by name. Always finish with a field that makes every element different, otherwise equal-ranked elements are lost as "duplicates".

For experienced developers: A record is ideal as the element: immutable, with equals and hashCode for free.

12. Ignore letter case: String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER

  • Signature: new TreeSet<>(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER)
  • Returns: strings sorted ignoring case
  • Time: O(log n) per add

For freshers: "raigad" and "Raigad" are different Strings, but with this comparator they are the same element, so the second one is ignored.

For experienced developers: This shows the rule: a TreeSet decides "duplicate" with the comparator, not with equals. That can be a feature (case-insensitive sets) or a bug (a comparator that ignores a field).

13. Reverse view: descendingSet()

  • Signature: NavigableSet<E> descendingSet()
  • Returns: a live reversed view
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: Need the same set from biggest to smallest, without building a new one? Ask for the descending view.

For experienced developers: It is a view, so changes through either set show in the other. reversed() (Java 21) gives the same thing.

14. Sorted list with positions: new ArrayList<>(treeSet)

  • Signature: List<E> list = new ArrayList<>(set)
  • Returns: a sorted list you can index
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: The set has no get(i). Copy it into a list, which keeps the sorted order, and then ask for the 1st, 2nd or 3rd smallest.

For experienced developers: The copy is O(n) and does not need to sort again. Do it once and reuse the list rather than copying inside a loop.

Which sorting approach to pick?

You needPickNote
Small to big or A to Znew TreeSet<>()Elements must be Comparable
Biggest firstComparator.reverseOrder()Set at creation
Sort objects by fieldsComparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...)End with a unique field
Case-insensitive stringsString.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER"Raigad" equals "raigad" here
Both directionsdescendingSet()View, no copy
Position accessnew ArrayList<>(set)Copy once

Module: Finding (searching) methods
