For freshers: a TreeSet can find things a HashSet cannot: "the smallest", "the closest smaller one", "everything between 1300 and 1400". Each card has one tiny program.

For experienced developers: the navigation methods are O(log n) walks down the tree. The views from headSet/tailSet/subSet are O(1) to create, but calling size() on them is O(k) for k elements.

15. contains(Object o)

  • Signature: boolean contains(Object o)
  • Returns: true or false
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Is the value in the set? It walks down the tree, going left or right at each step, so even a million elements need about 20 steps.

For experienced developers: Uses the comparator (compareTo), not hashCode. With a case-insensitive comparator, contains("RAIGAD") is true for "raigad".

16. first() and last(): the smallest and the biggest

  • Signature: E first(); E last()
  • Returns: the lowest / the highest element
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: No scanning needed: the smallest is at the far left of the tree and the biggest at the far right.

For experienced developers: Both throw NoSuchElementException on an empty set. pollFirst/pollLast also remove and return null when empty.

17. lower(e) and floor(e): the nearest value below

  • Signature: E lower(E e); E floor(E e)
  • Returns: the greatest element below (lower) or at-or-below (floor), or null
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: lower means "strictly smaller", floor means "smaller or equal". Handy for "what is the last slot before 10:30?".

For experienced developers: Both return null when nothing qualifies, so check before unboxing an Integer to int (a NullPointerException otherwise).

18. higher(e) and ceiling(e): the nearest value above

  • Signature: E higher(E e); E ceiling(E e)
  • Returns: the least element above (higher) or at-or-above (ceiling), or null
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: higher means "strictly bigger", ceiling means "bigger or equal". Great for "the next free slot at or after 10:30".

For experienced developers: Together, floor and ceiling give the two neighbours of any value, which is the basis of "closest element" and "overlap check" algorithms.

19. headSet and tailSet: everything below or above

  • Signature: SortedSet<E> headSet(E to); SortedSet<E> tailSet(E from)
  • Returns: a live view of the elements below / from a value
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: headSet(x) is everything before x (x not included). tailSet(x) is x and everything after. Add true/false as a second argument to include or exclude the border.

For experienced developers: These are views over the same tree. Adding a value outside the range through the view throws IllegalArgumentException.

20. subSet: a range between two values

  • Signature: NavigableSet<E> subSet(E from, boolean fromInc, E to, boolean toInc)
  • Returns: a live view of the range
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: Everything between two values, for example all forts between 1300 and 1400 metres. The two booleans say whether the border values are included.

For experienced developers: The short form subSet(from, to) is "from included, to excluded". If from is greater than to you get IllegalArgumentException.

21. stream().filter(...).findFirst()

  • Signature: Optional<E> findFirst()
  • Returns: the smallest element that follows a rule
  • Time: O(n), stops early

For freshers: For a rule that is not about the order (for example "an even number"), filter the stream. Because the TreeSet is sorted, findFirst gives the smallest match.

For experienced developers: If the rule is about the value itself (at least X), use ceiling(X) instead: it is O(log n), the stream is O(n).

22. retainAll(Collection c): values both groups share

  • Signature: boolean retainAll(Collection<?> c)
  • Returns: true if the set changed
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Keep only the values that also appear in the other group. The result stays sorted.

For experienced developers: It changes the receiver, so work on a copy: new TreeSet<>(original).

Which finding method to pick?

QuestionMethodTime
Is this value in the set?containsO(log n)
Smallest or biggest?first / lastO(log n)
Nearest below (strict / or equal)?lower / floorO(log n)
Nearest above (strict / or equal)?higher / ceilingO(log n)
Everything below / above a value?headSet / tailSetO(1) view
Everything between two values?subSetO(1) view
Smallest that follows a rule?stream().filter().findFirst()O(n)
What do two groups share?retainAll on a copyO(n log n)

expert.content:
How TreeSet works inside

A TreeSet is a thin wrapper over a TreeMap<E, Object> (the values are the shared PRESENT object). The TreeMap is a red-black tree.

  • A binary search tree keeps smaller elements in the left subtree and larger ones in the right subtree, so a lookup discards half of the remaining elements at each step.
  • A plain BST can degrade into a list when you add sorted data. The red-black rules (each node red or black, no two red nodes in a row, equal black height on every path) are restored by rotations and recolouring after each insert or delete, so the height never exceeds about 2 log2(n+1).
  • That guarantees O(log n) for add, remove, contains, floor, ceiling, first and last. One million elements need about 20 comparisons.
  • Every node stores key, value, left, right, parent and a colour flag: roughly 40 bytes per element, more than HashSet.
  • Order is defined only by compareTo / compare. equals() and hashCode() are never used.
  • Iteration walks the tree in order via successor links: O(1) amortised per step.

Natural ordering: elements must be Comparable

  • Strings, Integers, Doubles, Dates and enums are already Comparable.
  • For your own class, implement Comparable<T> (one natural order) or pass a Comparator (any order).
  • Adding a class that is not comparable throws ClassCastException on the first add.

Trap: the comparator decides what a "duplicate" is

  • A TreeSet treats two elements as the same when the comparison returns 0.
  • If your comparator looks only at the length of a name, "Torna" and "Lohag" (both length 5) are "equal", and the second is silently not added.
  • Always add a tie-breaker (thenComparing) so the comparator is consistent with equals unless you really want to merge such elements.

Real use: finding the nearest slot with ceiling and floor

A tour operator has fixed departure hours. For a requested hour, ceiling gives the next departure and floor the previous one: an O(log n) query a HashSet cannot answer.

TreeSet versus HashSet versus LinkedHashSet versus ConcurrentSkipListSet

TreeSetHashSetLinkedHashSetConcurrentSkipListSet
OrderSortedNoneInsertionSorted
add / remove / containsO(log n)O(1)O(1)O(log n)
Neighbour / range queriesYesNoNoYes
nullNoOneOneNo
Thread-safeNoNoNoYes (lock-free)
Uniqueness decided bycompareTo / Comparatorequals / hashCodeequals / hashCodecompareTo / Comparator

Best practices

Use TreeSet when order matters, and use it carefully.

  • Choose TreeSet only when you need sorted iteration or neighbour/range queries; otherwise HashSet is faster.
  • Keep the comparator consistent with equals and never throw from it; always add a tie-breaker.
  • Use immutable elements, or at least never change a field that takes part in the comparison after adding (the element would sit in the wrong place in the tree).
  • Do not add null; guard inputs.
  • Declare as NavigableSet / SortedSet when you use their methods, or Set when you do not.
  • For concurrent use choose ConcurrentSkipListSet.

Real-time examples

Three situations where a sorted set is the right answer.

Example 1: a leaderboard

For freshers: teams score points, and the board must always show the best team first. A TreeSet with a "highest points first" comparator keeps the order for you.

For experienced developers: to change a score, remove the old object and add the new one; changing a field of an element already inside breaks the tree order.

Example 2: discount slabs with floor()

For freshers: "Orders from 0 get 0%, from 1000 get 5%, from 5000 get 10%." Find the highest slab that is not above the order amount. That is exactly floor.

For experienced developers: this is a small step function stored as a sorted set of boundaries. With a TreeMap you would use floorEntry to get the value too.

Example 3: events inside a time window

For freshers: an event hall stores start times (in hours). Show the events between 10 and 14 without looking at every event.

For experienced developers: subSet locates both ends in O(log n) and then iterates only the matching elements, so the cost depends on the answer size, not on the total.

Sample project: Fort ranking board

What we build: a console program that keeps forts ranked by height and answers questions about the ranking.

  • Step 1: a Fort record and a comparator "tallest first, then name".
  • Step 2: add forts to a TreeSet; they sort themselves.
  • Step 3: print the ranking, the top 3, and the rank of one fort (headSet(fort).size() + 1).
  • Step 4: neighbours of a fort with lower and higher.
  • Step 5: update a fort height by remove then add, and print the new ranking.

Practice questions

Now test yourself. Each question is harder than the examples above: read the problem, write your own solution, then compare it with the one shown. Every solution was compiled and run, and its output is real.

Practice question 1: Trek slot finder (next free slot, sorted directory, ranges)

Level: Medium

Problem: A trek company keeps the booked start times (in minutes from midnight) of a fort in a TreeSet, and also a sorted directory of fort names. Sorted sets answer "what is the nearest slot?" in O(log n).

Your task:

  1. ceiling / floor / higher / lower find the nearest booked time.
  2. subSet / headSet / tailSet list the bookings in a time range.
  3. first / last / pollFirst process the earliest booking.
  4. A Comparator keeps a fort directory in case-insensitive order.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 2: Slot booking that rejects overlaps

Level: Hard

Problem: A guide accepts trek bookings as time ranges (start hour, end hour). A new booking must be rejected if it overlaps an existing one. Ranges that only touch (one ends at 10, the next starts at 10) are allowed.

Your task:

  1. Store bookings in a TreeSet ordered by start time.
  2. For a new range, look at floor (the booking starting at or before it) and ceiling (the next one starting at or after it).
  3. Reject if the previous booking ends after the new start, or the next one starts before the new end.
  4. Try 6 requests and print accepted/rejected for each.

Hints:

  • The comparator uses only start, so two slots with the same start count as the same: this is what you want here.
  • Touching slots are fine, so compare with > and <, not >=.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 3: Highest three and lowest three forts

Level: Easy

Problem: From a set of fort heights, print the three tallest (tallest first) and the three lowest (lowest first).

Your task:

  1. Put the heights into a TreeSet.
  2. Lowest three: stream the set and limit(3).
  3. Tallest three: do the same on descendingSet().

Hints:

  • No sorting code is needed: the TreeSet is already sorted.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 4: The fort closest to a target height

Level: Medium

Problem: For each target height find the fort height in the set that is closest to it. If two are equally close, choose the lower one.

Your task:

  1. Ask floor(target) and ceiling(target).
  2. Handle the case where one of them is null.
  3. Otherwise pick the one with the smaller difference.

Hints:

  • floor and ceiling return null at the ends: check before subtracting.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 5: How many forts fall in each height band

Level: Medium

Problem: Count the forts in the bands "below 1100", "1100 to 1399" and "1400 and above", using range views of one TreeSet.

Your task:

  1. Create a sorted set of heights.
  2. Use headSet, subSet and tailSet with the right inclusive flags.
  3. Print the sizes and check that the three counts add up to the total.

Hints:

  • The boundary 1100 belongs to exactly one band: decide which and use inclusive flags to match.
  • size() of a view walks the elements: fine for small sets, avoid in hot loops.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 6: Nearby almost-duplicate numbers

Level: Hard

Problem: Given an array of numbers and two limits k and t, decide whether there are two different positions i and j with |i - j| <= k and |nums[i] - nums[j]| <= t. Solve it in O(n log k) with a TreeSet.

Your task:

  1. Keep a TreeSet of the last k numbers (the sliding window).
  2. For each number ask ceiling(num - t): if it exists and is at most num + t, the answer is true.
  3. Add the number, and remove the one that leaves the window. Test three inputs.

Hints:

  • A window that holds the last k numbers gives distance in index for free.
  • The check is one O(log k) call per number instead of scanning the window.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

interviewQA: What is a TreeSet and when would you use it?
A TreeSet is a sorted NavigableSet backed by a red-black tree (a TreeMap). Use it when you need unique elements in sorted order or neighbour/range queries (floor, ceiling, headSet, tailSet).
Time complexity of TreeSet operations?
add, remove, contains, first, last, floor, ceiling, higher and lower are O(log n); iteration is O(n) in sorted order.
How does TreeSet decide whether two elements are duplicates?
By compareTo (natural ordering) or the Comparator returning 0, not by equals() or hashCode().
Can a TreeSet contain null?
Not with natural ordering: comparing null throws NullPointerException. A custom comparator could accept null, but that is rare and discouraged.
What happens if the elements are not Comparable?
ClassCastException is thrown on the first add unless you supply a Comparator.
Difference between floor, lower, ceiling and higher?
lower: greatest strictly less; floor: greatest less than or equal; ceiling: smallest greater than or equal; higher: smallest strictly greater. Each returns null if no such element exists.
What are headSet, tailSet and subSet?
Live range views: headSet(to) is the elements before to, tailSet(from) from from onwards, subSet(from, to) from from (inclusive) to to (exclusive). The long forms allow choosing inclusivity.
HashSet vs TreeSet?
HashSet: unordered, O(1), one null, equals/hashCode. TreeSet: sorted, O(log n), no null, compareTo/Comparator, supports navigation and ranges.
How is TreeSet implemented?
It wraps a TreeMap, a self-balancing red-black tree where each element is a key and the value is a dummy object.
Why is a comparator that is inconsistent with equals dangerous in a TreeSet?
Elements the comparator considers equal are treated as duplicates and the later ones are silently dropped, even if equals() says they differ.
Is TreeSet thread-safe?
No. Use ConcurrentSkipListSet or Collections.synchronizedSortedSet.
How do you get a descending view?
descendingSet() (or reversed() in Java 21) returns a live reversed view; descendingIterator() returns a reverse iterator.

topics.name: HashMap

beginner.content:
What is a HashMap?

A HashMap stores pairs: a key and the value that belongs to it. You give the map a key and it gives back the value almost instantly, like looking up a city in a telephone-code table: key "Pune", value 20. Each key appears once; each key maps to one value.

  • Package java.util. Implements Map<K, V>. It is not a Collection (it has its own interface).
  • Unique keys: putting an existing key again replaces the value. Values may repeat.
  • Fast: get, put, remove and containsKey are O(1) on average.
  • No order: iteration order depends on hash codes and can change when the map grows. Use LinkedHashMap or TreeMap for an order.
  • One null key and any number of null values are allowed.
  • Not thread-safe. For threads use ConcurrentHashMap.
  • Key classes must have correct equals() and hashCode() (String, Integer and records already do).

Where HashMap sits in the Collection Framework

Map
(I)
← implements
AbstractMap
(c)
← extends
HashMap
(c)
← extended by
LinkedHashMap
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. HashMap also implements Cloneable and Serializable. Its subclass LinkedHashMap adds a predictable order.

Creating a HashMap: four constructors

  • new HashMap<>(): empty, capacity 16, load factor 0.75.
  • new HashMap<>(int initialCapacity) and (int, float loadFactor): tune the table size.
  • new HashMap<>(Map m): a copy of another map.
  • Declare the variable as Map<K, V>, not HashMap.

Your first HashMap program

  • put(key, value) adds a pair; get(key) returns the value or null if the key is missing.
  • Printing a map shows {key=value, key=value}.
  • Putting the same key again replaces the value and returns the old one.

All HashMap methods at a glance

n is the number of entries.

MethodWhat it doesTime
put(k, v) / putAll(m) / putIfAbsent(k, v)Adds or replaces / adds a whole map / adds only if the key is missingO(1)
get(k) / getOrDefault(k, d)Reads a value (null / default when missing)O(1)
containsKey(k) / containsValue(v)Tests for a key / for a valueO(1) / O(n)
remove(k) / remove(k, v)Removes by key / only if it has that valueO(1)
replace(k, v) / replaceAll(f)Replaces one value / transforms every valueO(1) / O(n)
compute(k, f) / computeIfAbsent(k, f) / computeIfPresent(k, f)Calculates the new value for a keyO(1)
merge(k, v, f)Inserts v, or combines the old value and v with fO(1)
keySet() / values() / entrySet()Live views of the keys / values / pairsO(1) to create
forEach(f)Runs an action for every pairO(n + capacity)
size() / isEmpty() / clear()Count, emptiness, remove allO(1) / O(1) / O(capacity)
clone() / equals / hashCode / toStringCopy and compareO(n)
Map.of(...) / Map.entry(k, v) / Map.copyOf(m)Immutable maps and entriesO(n)

Benefits and advantages

For freshers: a HashMap is the first tool to reach for when you need to "look something up by name". Why it is popular:

  • Very fast lookup. Finding the value for a key takes about the same time whether the map holds 10 or 10 million pairs.
  • Natural shape for real data. City to area code, roll number to marks, word to count: all are key-value pairs.
  • No duplicate keys. You never check "is this key already there?" by hand; merge, putIfAbsent and computeIfAbsent do it for you.
  • Great for counting and grouping. One line, map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum), counts anything.
  • Flexible. Any object can be a key or a value; one null key and many null values are allowed.
  • One API for all maps. The same Map methods work for every map class, so what you learn here transfers.
  • For experienced developers: O(1) average get/put/remove; buckets with 8 or more colliding entries become red-black trees (when the table is at least 64 slots), so the worst case is O(log n), not O(n). Resizing doubles the table and is amortised O(1) per insert.

Disadvantages and when NOT to use it

For freshers: a HashMap is not the answer to everything. Know its weak spots:

  • No order. If you print or loop over it, the order looks random and may change after the map grows.
  • Cannot be sorted in place. A map has no sort(); you must copy it into a TreeMap or LinkedHashMap.
  • Searching by value is slow. containsValue checks every entry (O(n)).
  • Not thread-safe. Two threads writing at once can lose data. Use ConcurrentHashMap.
  • Needs good keys. A key class without correct equals and hashCode, or a key you change after inserting it, makes entries unreachable.
  • Uses more memory than an array or list: every pair is a small Node object plus the table.
  • For experienced developers: keys with a poor hashCode collide and degrade lookups; iteration costs O(n + capacity), so a huge, mostly empty map is slow to loop over; autoboxing of int keys and values adds garbage; changing the map while iterating throws ConcurrentModificationException.

Quick guide:

Use a HashMap whenUse something else when
You look values up by key and order does not matterYou need a sorted view: use TreeMap
You count, group or cache thingsYou need insertion order or an LRU cache: use LinkedHashMap
One thread uses the map (or it is read-only after loading)Many threads write: use ConcurrentHashMap
Keys are Strings, Integers, enums or recordsKeys are small enums only: EnumMap is faster and ordered
You have a key-value relationshipYou only need unique items with no value: use HashSet

intermediate.content:
Putting pairs in

Four ways to add: replace freely, add a whole map, add only when missing, or compute.

1. put(K key, V value)

  • Signature: V put(K key, V value)
  • Returns: the previous value for the key, or null if there was none
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: Stores the pair. If the key is new the pair is added and null is returned. If the key exists, its value is replaced and the old value is returned.

For experienced developers: The key's hashCode selects a bucket; the key is then compared with equals inside the bucket. On a replace the original key object is kept, only the value changes. A null return is ambiguous when null values are allowed (use containsKey to tell).

2. putAll(Map m)

  • Signature: void putAll(Map m)
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: O(m)

For freshers: Copies every pair of another map into this one. Keys that already exist get their value replaced.

For experienced developers: It pre-sizes the table for the incoming entries and then does one put per entry. Use it to merge two maps: the argument "wins" on conflicts.

3. putIfAbsent(K key, V value)

  • Signature: V putIfAbsent(K key, V value)
  • Returns: the existing value, or null if the pair was added
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Adds the pair only if the key has no value yet. If the key is already there nothing changes and you get the existing value back. It is the safe way to write "set a default".

For experienced developers: It is one atomic call instead of if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) (two lookups, and a race in concurrent code). A key mapped to null counts as "no value" and is filled.

Reading values

Read by key. A missing key gives null, unless you ask for a default.

4. get(Object key) and getOrDefault(Object key, V defaultValue)

  • Signature: V get(Object key); V getOrDefault(Object key, V defaultValue)
  • Returns: the value, or null / the default if the key is missing
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: get returns the value stored for the key, or null when the key is absent. getOrDefault lets you give a value to use instead of null, which avoids a NullPointerException when you unbox the result.

For experienced developers: A null from get can mean "no key" or "the value is null". Use containsKey to tell them apart. int hours = map.get("x") throws NullPointerException when the key is missing because of the unboxing; getOrDefault("x", 0) does not.

5. containsKey(Object key) and containsValue(Object value)

  • Signature: boolean containsKey(Object key); boolean containsValue(Object value)
  • Returns: true or false
  • Time: O(1) / O(n)

For freshers: containsKey asks "is this key in the map?" and is very fast. containsValue asks "does any key have this value?" and has to scan every entry, so it is slow on big maps.

For experienced developers: If you need fast "by value" lookups, keep a second map from value to key, or use a bidirectional map from a library. containsKey also tells you whether get returned null because of a missing key or a null value.

6. size(), isEmpty() and clear()

  • Signature: int size(); boolean isEmpty(); void clear()
  • Returns: the count / emptiness / nothing
  • Time: O(1) / O(1) / O(capacity)

For freshers: Count the pairs, test for none, or remove every pair.

For experienced developers: clear() removes the entries but keeps the table size, so a map that once held millions of entries stays big in memory. Create a new map if you want to release it.

Removing and replacing

Remove by key, remove conditionally, and replace without adding new keys.

7. remove(Object key) and remove(Object key, Object value)

  • Signature: V remove(Object key); boolean remove(Object key, Object value)
  • Returns: the removed value (or null) / true if removed
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: remove(key) deletes the pair and returns the value that was stored. remove(key, value) deletes it only if the key currently has exactly that value.

For experienced developers: The two-argument form is a compare-and-remove, useful for "remove this entry only if nobody changed it".

8. replace(K, V) and replaceAll(BiFunction)

  • Signature: V replace(K key, V value); boolean replace(K key, V oldValue, V newValue); void replaceAll(BiFunction function)
  • Returns: the old value / whether replaced / nothing
  • Time: O(1) / O(n)

For freshers: replace(key, value) changes the value only if the key exists (unlike put, it never adds a new key). replaceAll(function) recalculates every value from its key and old value.

For experienced developers: replaceAll is a clean way to transform all values in place, for example "add 1 to every count" or "make all values upper case".

Calculating values: compute, computeIfAbsent, computeIfPresent and merge

These four methods (Java 8) replace the old "get, check, put" pattern. They do the lookup once.

9. computeIfAbsent(K, Function)

  • Signature: V computeIfAbsent(K key, Function mappingFunction)
  • Returns: the existing or newly computed value
  • Time: O(1) + function

For freshers: If the key has no value, call the function to create one, store it and return it. If the key already has a value, return it and do not call the function. The classic use is a map of lists: map.computeIfAbsent(city, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(fort).

For experienced developers: The function must not modify the map (it can throw ConcurrentModificationException). Returning null from the function means "do not store anything".

10. computeIfPresent(K, BiFunction)

  • Signature: V computeIfPresent(K key, BiFunction remappingFunction)
  • Returns: the new value, or null if removed / absent
  • Time: O(1) + function

For freshers: If the key exists (with a non-null value), call the function with the key and the old value and store the result. If the function returns null the entry is removed. If the key is missing nothing happens.

For experienced developers: Perfect for "update if it exists" and for "decrement, and delete when it reaches zero".

11. compute(K, BiFunction)

  • Signature: V compute(K key, BiFunction remappingFunction)
  • Returns: the new value (or null if the entry was removed)
  • Time: O(1) + function

For freshers: Calls the function whether or not the key exists. The function receives the key and the old value (or null) and returns the new value. A null result removes the entry. Use it for a counter: map.compute(word, (k, v) -> v == null ? 1 : v + 1).

For experienced developers: Compared with merge, compute sees the key and can treat "absent" and "present" differently in one expression.

12. merge(K, V, BiFunction)

  • Signature: V merge(K key, V value, BiFunction remappingFunction)
  • Returns: the new value in the map
  • Time: O(1) + function

For freshers: The shortest way to count or to combine values. If the key is absent, it stores the given value. If the key is present, it stores function(oldValue, givenValue). A null result removes the entry. Counting words: map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum).

For experienced developers: The function takes the two values (not the key), so method references such as Integer::sum, String::concat or Math::max fit perfectly. Neither the value nor the function may be null.

Walking through a map

A map offers three views: the keys, the values and the pairs. Choose the one that gives you what you need in a single loop.

13. keySet(), values() and entrySet()

  • Signature: Set keySet(); Collection values(); Set> entrySet()
  • Returns: live views
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: keySet() is the set of keys, values() the collection of values and entrySet() the set of key-value pairs (Map.Entry). They are views: removing from a view removes from the map. Loop over entrySet() when you need both key and value; looping over keySet() and calling get does an extra lookup for every key.

For experienced developers: Views do not support add. The iteration order is the map's order (for HashMap: arbitrary). Removing during iteration must go through the iterator, removeIf on the view, or Map.removeIf-style calls on entrySet().

14. forEach(BiConsumer)

  • Signature: void forEach(BiConsumer action)
  • Returns: nothing (void)
  • Time: O(n + capacity)

For freshers: Runs an action for every pair, written as a lambda with two parameters: map.forEach((key, value) -> ...). It is the shortest loop when you only need to read.

For experienced developers: Cannot break out of it. It is fail-fast: changing the map inside the lambda throws ConcurrentModificationException at the end of the loop.

15. Iterating safely: removing while looping

  • Signature: entrySet().iterator() with remove(), entrySet().removeIf(...), keySet().removeIf(...)
  • Returns: removes pairs without an exception
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Removing from a map inside a for-each loop throws ConcurrentModificationException. Use an Iterator, or the one-line entrySet().removeIf(...).

For experienced developers: This is the same fail-fast rule as for lists. HashMap checks a modification counter on each step.

Copies, equality and immutable maps

Finish with the helper methods.

16. clone, equals, hashCode and toString

  • Signature: Object clone(); boolean equals(Object); int hashCode(); String toString()
  • Returns: a shallow copy / comparison / hash / text
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Two maps are equal when they have the same keys with equal values, whatever the Map class and the order. clone() makes a shallow copy (keys and values are shared).

For experienced developers: Prefer new HashMap<>(map) to clone(). The map's hash code is the sum of the hash codes of its entries, so it is order-independent.

17. Map.of, Map.entry, Map.ofEntries and Map.copyOf

  • Signature: Map.of(k1, v1, ...); Map.entry(k, v); Map.ofEntries(...); Map.copyOf(map)
  • Returns: an immutable map / entry
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Create small immutable maps quickly. Map.of takes up to 10 key-value pairs; Map.ofEntries(Map.entry(...), ...) takes any number; Map.copyOf makes an immutable copy. They reject null and duplicate keys, and any change throws UnsupportedOperationException.

For experienced developers: Their iteration order is deliberately randomised per JVM run. Wrap with new HashMap<>(Map.of(...)) when you need a modifiable map, as in the other examples of this page.

Master program: every HashMap method in one place

One single program that uses all the HashMap methods you learned above, step by step. Read the numbered comments from top to bottom, run it, and match each output line with its step.

Module: Sorting methods

For freshers: a HashMap cannot be sorted itself, because it keeps no order. To "sort a map" you build a new map or list that has the order you want. For experienced developers: every approach below is O(n log n); pick by what you need afterwards (a sorted map, a ranked list, or just the top few).

18. Sort by key: copy into a TreeMap

  • Signature: new TreeMap<>(Map m)
  • Returns: a new TreeMap sorted by key
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: The simplest way to sort by key. A TreeMap keeps its keys in order (A to Z for Strings, small to large for numbers), so copying the map into one sorts it.

For experienced developers: The original HashMap is not changed. Keys must be Comparable, or pass a Comparator to the TreeMap constructor.

19. Sort by value: stream + comparingByValue

  • Signature: entrySet().stream().sorted(Map.Entry.comparingByValue())
  • Returns: a sorted Stream of entries
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: To sort by value, stream the entries, sort them with Map.Entry.comparingByValue() and put them into a LinkedHashMap, which remembers the order you insert.

For experienced developers: A plain HashMap would forget the order again, so the target must be a LinkedHashMap. Values must be Comparable.

20. Sort by value descending: Collectors.toMap into LinkedHashMap

  • Signature: Collectors.toMap(k, v, merge, LinkedHashMap::new)
  • Returns: a LinkedHashMap in the sorted order
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: For "highest first" give comparingByValue a reverse order. The four-argument toMap collects the sorted stream straight into a LinkedHashMap.

For experienced developers: The third argument (merge function) is required for the four-argument form; it is never called here because keys are already unique. Without LinkedHashMap::new the result would be a HashMap and the order would be lost.

21. Sort with ties: List of entries + thenComparing

  • Signature: list.sort(comparingByValue().reversed().thenComparing(comparingByKey()))
  • Returns: nothing; the list is sorted in place
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: When two values are equal, say which comes first. Copy the entries into a List (lists can be sorted) and chain thenComparing for the tie-break, here "same visitors: A to Z".

For experienced developers: A list of entries is the best shape when you only want to read a ranking. Use Map.entry(k, v) if you need entry copies that do not depend on the map.

22. Top N: sorted + limit

  • Signature: stream().sorted(...).limit(n)
  • Returns: a Stream with only the first n entries
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Often you do not need the whole sorted map, only the "top 3". Sort, then limit(3) keeps just the first three.

For experienced developers: For a very large map and a small n, a bounded PriorityQueue of size n does the same in O(m log n) time. For normal sizes the stream is clearer.

Which sorting approach to pick?

You wantUseResult
Keys A to Z, as a mapnew TreeMap<>(map)sorted map (stays sorted as you add)
Sorted by value, as a mapstream().sorted(comparingByValue()).collect(toMap(..., LinkedHashMap::new))ordered LinkedHashMap (fixed snapshot)
A ranking with tie-breaksList of entries + sort(...thenComparing...)sorted list
Only the best fewsorted(...).limit(n)first n entries

Module: Finding (searching) methods

For freshers: a HashMap is built for finding by key; that is instant. Finding by value or by a condition means looking at the entries one by one. For experienced developers: key lookups are O(1); anything that scans values, finds a maximum or filters is O(n). If you search by value often, keep a second (reverse) map.

23. get and getOrDefault: find a value by key

  • Signature: V get(Object key) / V getOrDefault(Object key, V defaultValue)
  • Returns: the value, or null / the default if the key is missing
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: get returns the value for a key or null. getOrDefault returns a value you choose instead of null, which avoids NullPointerException when you unbox.

For experienced developers: get returning null can mean "missing" or "mapped to null"; getOrDefault returns null too when the key is mapped to null.

24. containsKey: does this key exist?

  • Signature: boolean containsKey(Object key)
  • Returns: true if the key is present
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Answers yes or no. Use it when you only care whether a key exists, not what its value is.

For experienced developers: It is as cheap as get. To "check then use" prefer a single get (and test for null) so the key is hashed once.

25. containsValue: does this value exist?

  • Signature: boolean containsValue(Object value)
  • Returns: true if at least one key has this value
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Checks whether any entry has the given value. It has to look at the entries one by one, so it is slower than containsKey.

For experienced developers: It walks every bucket using equals. For frequent value lookups, maintain a reverse Map<V, K> or a HashSet of values.

26. Find the key for a value

  • Signature: for (Map.Entry e : map.entrySet()) if (value.equals(e.getValue()))
  • Returns: the first matching key, or null
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: A map goes from key to value, not back. To find the key of a value, loop over the entries and compare. Stop as soon as you find it.

For experienced developers: Several keys can share a value; a HashMap gives no guarantee which one you meet first. To get all of them, collect with a stream filter (see the next card).

27. Stream filter: find all matches

  • Signature: entrySet().stream().filter(...).map(...).toList()
  • Returns: a List of the matching keys or entries
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: To find every entry that meets a rule, filter the stream. Here: all forts higher than 1350 m. Sort the result if you print it, because a HashMap order is not fixed.

For experienced developers: Use anyMatch / allMatch / noneMatch for yes/no questions (they stop early) and count() for how many.

28. Max and min entry

  • Signature: Collections.max(map.entrySet(), Map.Entry.comparingByValue())
  • Returns: the entry with the largest (or smallest) value
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: To find the highest or lowest value and who owns it, use Collections.max / Collections.min on the entries, or the stream version stream().min(...) which returns an Optional.

For experienced developers: No sorting is needed, so this is O(n), cheaper than sorting. Collections.max throws on an empty map; the stream form returns an empty Optional. On equal values, either entry may win.

Which finding method to pick?

QuestionMethodTime
What is the value for this key?get / getOrDefaultO(1)
Is this key present?containsKeyO(1)
Is this value present?containsValue (or values().stream().anyMatch)O(n)
Which key has this value?loop over entrySet(), or keep a reverse mapO(n)
All entries matching a rulestream().filter(...)O(n)
Highest or lowest value and its keyCollections.max/min or stream().max/minO(n)

expert.content:
How HashMap works inside

Everything in the tables above follows from a few ideas.

  • Storage: an array of buckets, Node<K,V>[] table, whose length is always a power of two (default 16). Each Node holds hash, key, value and next.
  • Hash: h = key.hashCode(), then h ^ (h >>> 16) to mix the high bits into the low bits. A null key always hashes to 0 (bucket 0).
  • Index: index = (n - 1) & hash, which is a fast way of writing hash % n for a power-of-two n.
  • put: if the bucket is empty the node goes in. Otherwise Java compares each node: same hash and (same reference or equals) means "same key, replace value"; if no node matches, the new node is appended to the bucket's chain.
  • Treeify: when a chain reaches 8 nodes and the table has at least 64 buckets, the chain becomes a red-black tree (O(log n) lookup in a crowded bucket). With fewer buckets, the table is resized instead. A tree shrinks back to a list at 6 nodes.
  • Resize: when size > threshold (capacity x loadFactor = 12 for the default), the table doubles and nodes are redistributed. Because the size doubles, each node either stays at its index or moves by exactly the old capacity.
  • Lazy: the table is created on the first put. new HashMap<>(n) rounds n up to a power of two (tableSizeFor).
  • Iteration cost is O(capacity + size) because it scans all buckets.
  • Not thread-safe: concurrent resizes can lose entries (and in old JDKs loop forever). Use ConcurrentHashMap.

Time complexity summary

OperationAverageWorst caseNote
get, put, remove, containsKeyO(1)O(log n) (O(n) before Java 8)Worst case when many keys share one bucket
containsValueO(n)O(n)Scans every entry
Iteration over keys / values / entriesO(capacity + n)O(capacity + n)Scans all buckets
ResizeO(n)O(n)Happens rarely; amortised O(1) per put

Trap: keys need equals() and hashCode(); never mutate a key

  • A key without hashCode/equals is compared by identity, so a "new equal" key does not find the value.
  • If you change a field used by hashCode after the key is in the map, the entry sits in the wrong bucket and can no longer be found.
  • Immutable keys (String, Integer, enums, records) avoid both problems.

Real example 1: word frequency

The most common HashMap job: count how often each item appears, then show the result sorted.

Real example 2: a lookup cache

Store the result of a slow calculation so the second request for the same key is instant. computeIfAbsent runs the calculation only once per key.

HashMap versus other Map classes

HashMapLinkedHashMapTreeMapHashtableConcurrentHashMap
OrderNoneInsertion (or access)Sorted by keyNoneNone
get / putO(1)O(1)O(log n)O(1)O(1)
null key / valueOne / manyOne / manyNo / yesNo / NoNo / No
Thread-safeNoNoNoYes (whole-table lock)Yes (fine-grained)
Use forDefault mapPredictable order, LRU cachesSorted keys, range queriesLegacyShared between threads

Best practices

Habits for correct and fast maps.

  • Declare as Map<K, V>.
  • Use immutable keys and always override equals and hashCode together (or use a record).
  • Use getOrDefault, merge, computeIfAbsent and putIfAbsent instead of "get, check, put".
  • Iterate with entrySet() (or forEach) when you need both key and value.
  • Pre-size big maps: HashMap.newHashMap(expected) (Java 19+) or new HashMap<>((int) (expected / 0.75f) + 1).
  • Do not rely on iteration order; choose LinkedHashMap or TreeMap when you need one.
  • Use ConcurrentHashMap for shared maps, not HashMap and not Hashtable.
  • Do not use a mutable collection as a key.

Real-time examples

Three small, realistic jobs where a HashMap is the right tool. Each program is complete: copy it, run it, change the data.

Scenario 1: Vote counter

For freshers: every vote is a name; the map keeps one counter per candidate. merge(name, 1, Integer::sum) means "start at 1, or add 1 to what is there". For experienced developers: this is the standard frequency-count idiom, O(1) per vote. We print through a TreeMap so the order is stable.

Scenario 2: Student marks lookup

For freshers: the roll number is the key and the student record is the value, so a result desk can find any student at once. Always handle the "roll number not found" case. For experienced developers: computeIfPresent updates a value only when the key exists and does the lookup once; a record makes a good immutable value.

Scenario 3: Price cache

For freshers: asking a slow database for the same fort fee again and again wastes time. Keep answers in a map: look in the map first, and only call the slow method when the key is missing. For experienced developers: this is a read-through cache. With a HashMap, do not call computeIfAbsent recursively on the same map (it can throw ConcurrentModificationException); a plain get-then-put is safe here. For threads use ConcurrentHashMap.

Sample project: Fort Visitor Register

What we build: a console program that reads a visit log and uses three HashMaps (fees, ticket counts, visitor names) to print a report per fort.

Steps:

  • Step 1: create the log of visits (fort, visitor, tickets).
  • Step 2: keep the entry fee of each fort in a Map<String, Integer>.
  • Step 3: count tickets per fort with merge.
  • Step 4: group visitor names per fort with computeIfAbsent.
  • Step 5: compute revenue = tickets x fee, and find the busiest fort.
  • Step 6: print the report in A to Z order and test a fort that has no fee.

Read the step comments in the program, run it, then extend it with your own idea.

Practice questions

Now test yourself. Each question is harder than the examples above: read the problem, write your own solution, then compare it with the one shown. Every solution was compiled and run, and its output is real.

Practice question 1: Trek kit inventory (stock, counting, grouping)

Level: Medium

Problem: A shop keeps the stock of trek gear in a HashMap. It counts what each customer buys, flags low stock and groups items by category: the three jobs HashMap does best.

Your task:

  1. put / get / getOrDefault manage the stock.
  2. merge counts sales; computeIfAbsent groups items by category.
  3. entrySet loop to report low stock; removeIf to drop sold-out items.
  4. TreeMap copy only to print in a stable order.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 2: Top cities and the pair of forts that reach a target height

Level: Hard

Problem: Two classic problems solved with a HashMap. (1) From a visit log, print the 3 most visited cities, breaking ties alphabetically. (2) Given fort heights, find two different forts whose heights add up to 2777 m in a single pass.

Your task:

  1. Count visits with merge, then sort the entries by count (descending) then name, and take 3.
  2. For the pair: for each fort, look up target - height in a map of heights seen so far; if present, you found the pair; otherwise store this fort.

Hints:

  • Use comparingByValue().reversed().thenComparing(comparingByKey()) for count-desc then name.
  • The "seen so far" map is what makes the pair search O(n) instead of O(n²).

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 3: Area-code directory (add, update, search, remove)

Level: Easy

Problem: Build a tiny telephone directory with a HashMap and use the main methods once each.

Your task:

  1. Add Pune=20, Mumbai=22, Nagpur=712 with put.
  2. Update Nagpur to 7122 and print the old value that put returns.
  3. Look up Pune and an unknown city using getOrDefault.
  4. Remove Mumbai and print the directory in A to Z order.

Hints:

  • put on an existing key returns the previous value.
  • Wrap the map in new TreeMap<>(map) to print it in a fixed order.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 4: Busiest district (group, count, tie-break)

Level: Medium

Problem: Each fort belongs to a district. Given a visit log of fort names, find the district with the most visits. If two districts tie, the one that comes first alphabetically wins.

Your task:

  1. Store fort to district in a HashMap.
  2. For every visit, look up the district and count it with merge.
  3. Choose the winner with a comparator: count descending, then name ascending.

Hints:

  • Pune and Kolhapur-style ties are settled by thenComparing(Map.Entry.comparingByKey()).

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 5: Counting climbing routes with a memo map

Level: Medium

Problem: A trekker climbs a fort one or two steps at a time. The number of ways to reach step n is ways(n-1) + ways(n-2). A plain recursion repeats the same work millions of times. Use a HashMap as a memo to make it fast.

Your task:

  1. Write a recursive ways(int n, Map<Integer, Long> memo).
  2. Return 1 for n = 1 and 2 for n = 2.
  3. Before computing, look in the memo; after computing, store the answer.
  4. Print ways(40) and the number of values saved in the memo.

Hints:

  • Use get-then-put rather than computeIfAbsent in a recursive call on a HashMap.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 6: Day-ranges that add up to a target (prefix sums)

Level: Hard

Problem: A trek log lists the height gained each day (it can be negative on a descent). Count how many continuous day ranges gain exactly 7 m in total, and find the length of the longest such range, in one pass.

Your task:

  1. Keep a running sum. For each day, the number of earlier prefix sums equal to sum - target is the number of ranges ending today.
  2. Store prefix sums in a HashMap<Integer, Integer> (sum to how many times seen). Start with {0 = 1}.
  3. For the longest range keep a second map: prefix sum to the first index where it appeared.

Hints:

  • A range from day a+1 to day b has sum prefix[b] - prefix[a].
  • putIfAbsent keeps the first index, which gives the longest range.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.
codeExamples:
// Practice: subarray sum with a HashMap of prefix sums
import java.util.*;  // imports every class of java.util

public class HmPrefixSums {                      // class that holds the main method
    public static void main(String[] args) {     // program entry point
        int[] gain = {3, 4, 7, 2, -3, 1, 4, 2};  // stores the value in gain
        int target = 7;                          // declares int target with value 7

        Map<Integer, Integer> seenCount = new HashMap<>();   // prefix sum -> how many times
        Map<Integer, Integer> firstIndex = new HashMap<>();  // prefix sum -> first index
        seenCount.put(0, 1);                                 // maps key 0 to value 1
        firstIndex.put(0, -1);                               // maps key 0 to value -1

        int sum = 0, ranges = 0, longest = 0;                   // declares int sum with value 0, ranges = 0, long...
        for (int i = 0; i < gain.length; i++) {                 // loops through all the indexes
            sum += gain[i];                                     // updates sum
            ranges += seenCount.getOrDefault(sum - target, 0);  // ranges that end at day i
            Integer start = firstIndex.get(sum - target);       // stores the result: reads the value stored for key sum - target
            if (start != null) {                                // checks for null
                longest = Math.max(longest, i - start);         // assigns a new value to longest
            }
            seenCount.merge(sum, 1, Integer::sum);              // combines the old and new value for the key
            firstIndex.putIfAbsent(sum, i);                     // keep the earliest index only
        }
        System.out.println("Ranges that add up to " + target + ": " + ranges);  // prints a label followed by the value
        System.out.println("Longest range (days): " + longest);  // prints a label followed by the value
    }
}
// OUTPUT:
// Ranges that add up to 7: 4
// Longest range (days): 4

interviewQA: How does HashMap work internally?

It keeps an array of buckets (power-of-two size). The key hash is spread (h ^ h>>>16), the bucket index is (n-1)&hash, and entries in the same bucket form a linked list that becomes a red-black tree when it reaches 8 nodes (table >= 64). When size exceeds capacity x load factor the table doubles.
What is the default capacity and load factor?
16 buckets and 0.75, so the first resize happens when the 13th entry is added.
What happens when two keys have the same hash code?
They go to the same bucket; equals() decides whether they are the same key (replace value) or different keys (both stored in the chain/tree).
What does put() return?
The previous value for the key, or null if the key was new (or its value was null).
Why must equals() and hashCode() be overridden together for keys?
HashMap finds the bucket with hashCode and the entry with equals. If equal keys can have different hash codes, lookups look in the wrong bucket and fail.
Can HashMap have null keys or values?
One null key (stored in bucket 0) and any number of null values. Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap allow neither.
HashMap vs Hashtable?
HashMap is unsynchronized, allows one null key and null values, and is faster; Hashtable is a legacy synchronized class that allows no nulls. Use ConcurrentHashMap for thread safety.
HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap?
HashMap: no order, O(1). LinkedHashMap: insertion or access order, O(1). TreeMap: sorted by key, O(log n), supports navigation.
What is the difference between getOrDefault and putIfAbsent?
getOrDefault only reads and returns the default without storing it; putIfAbsent stores the value when the key has none.
How do you count occurrences with a HashMap?
map.merge(item, 1, Integer::sum) (or compute with a null check).
How do you iterate a HashMap?
entrySet() with for-each (best when you need keys and values), keySet(), values(), or forEach((k, v) -> ...).
Why does HashMap throw ConcurrentModificationException?
Its iterators are fail-fast: they compare modCount with the value seen at creation, so structural changes during iteration (other than through the iterator) are detected.
How can HashMap lose data in multi-threaded code?
Concurrent puts and resizes can overwrite each other or corrupt the table. Use ConcurrentHashMap or external synchronization.
What is treeification?
When a bucket holds 8 or more nodes and the table has at least 64 buckets, the linked list is replaced by a red-black tree to keep worst-case lookups at O(log n).
Which is faster for a mostly-read lookup of a million entries: HashMap or TreeMap?
HashMap (O(1) average versus O(log n)), unless you need sorted order or range queries.

topics.name: LinkedHashMap

beginner.content:
What is a LinkedHashMap?

A LinkedHashMap is a HashMap that remembers the order of its entries. Everything you know about HashMap still applies (unique keys, O(1) lookups, one null key), but when you print or loop over it, the pairs come out in a predictable order: the order in which the keys were first added.

  • Package java.util. It extends HashMap and (Java 21) implements SequencedMap.
  • Insertion order (default): iteration follows the order of first insertion. Putting an existing key again does not move it.
  • Access order (optional): with the constructor flag accessOrder = true the most recently read or written entry moves to the end. This is the basis of an LRU cache.
  • Fast: get, put and remove are O(1) on average, with a small extra cost to keep the links.
  • One null key and null values are allowed. Not thread-safe.
  • Use it for: reports and JSON output in a stable order, "last seen" lists, LRU caches.

Where LinkedHashMap sits in the Collection Framework

Map
(I)
← extends
SequencedMap
(I)
← implemented by
HashMap
(c)
← extends
LinkedHashMap
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. In Java 21 SequencedMap was added between Map and LinkedHashMap/TreeMap.

Creating a LinkedHashMap

  • new LinkedHashMap<>(): empty, insertion order.
  • new LinkedHashMap<>(int initialCapacity) and (int, float loadFactor): tune the table.
  • new LinkedHashMap<>(int, float, boolean accessOrder): true means access order.
  • new LinkedHashMap<>(Map m): a copy in the iteration order of m.

All LinkedHashMap methods at a glance

MethodWhat it doesTime
put, putAll, putIfAbsent, get, getOrDefault, containsKey, containsValue, remove, replace, replaceAllExactly as in HashMapO(1) (containsValue O(n))
compute, computeIfAbsent, computeIfPresent, mergeExactly as in HashMapO(1)
keySet(), values(), entrySet(), forEach()Views and loops, in insertion (or access) orderO(n)
removeEldestEntry(e)Hook called after each insertion; return true to remove the eldest entryO(1)
firstEntry() / lastEntry()The first / last entry (Java 21)O(1)
pollFirstEntry() / pollLastEntry()Remove and return the first / last entry (Java 21)O(1)
putFirst(k, v) / putLast(k, v)Put at the front / back, moving an existing key (Java 21)O(1)
sequencedKeySet() / sequencedValues() / sequencedEntrySet() / reversed()Ordered views, reversed view (Java 21)O(1)
clone, equals, hashCode, toStringCopy and compare (equals ignores order)O(n)

Benefits and advantages

For freshers: a LinkedHashMap is a HashMap that remembers the order in which you added things. Why use it:

  • Predictable order. Printing or looping gives the pairs in the order you inserted them, every time.
  • Still fast. get, put and containsKey are O(1), just like HashMap.
  • Easy sorted results. Sort entries with a stream, collect into a LinkedHashMap, and the sorted order sticks.
  • Built-in LRU cache. With access order on, the entry you used last moves to the end, and removeEldestEntry drops the oldest one.
  • Stable output. Reports, JSON-like printing and tests give the same text on every run.
  • Java 21 bonus. It is a SequencedMap: firstEntry(), lastEntry(), putFirst(), reversed() work directly.
  • For experienced developers: it is a HashMap whose entries are also linked in a doubly linked list, so iteration is O(n) (not O(n + capacity)) and often faster than HashMap for sparse tables. Cost: two extra references per entry.

Disadvantages and when NOT to use it

For freshers: the order is free to read, but it is not free to keep. Know the limits:

  • Not sorted. The order is insertion order, not A to Z or small to large. Use TreeMap for a real sort.
  • More memory than HashMap. Every entry carries two extra links (before and after).
  • Slightly slower writes than HashMap, because the links must be updated too.
  • Not thread-safe. Wrap with Collections.synchronizedMap if threads share it.
  • Re-putting a key does not move it in the default mode; the old position stays. Remove it first if you want it at the end.
  • For experienced developers: in access-order mode even get changes the structure, so reading while iterating throws ConcurrentModificationException, and reads are no longer safe to do concurrently without locking.

Quick guide:

Use a LinkedHashMap whenUse something else when
You need the pairs in the order they arrivedOrder does not matter and memory is tight: HashMap
You build a report or a sorted snapshot and print itThe map must stay sorted as you add: TreeMap
You want a small LRU cache or bounded historyYou need a big concurrent cache: a cache library or ConcurrentHashMap
You group things and keep first-seen orderYou need range queries (floor, ceiling): TreeMap

intermediate.content:
Insertion order in action

All the HashMap methods work; the new thing is the order of every view and loop.

1. put, get, remove and the order of pairs

  • Signature: V put(K, V); V get(Object); V remove(Object)
  • Returns: as HashMap
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: New keys are added at the end of the order. Putting a key that already exists replaces its value but keeps its position. Removing a key just closes the gap.

For experienced developers: Each entry is a LinkedHashMap.Entry with before and after links in addition to the bucket link, so adding, removing and reordering are all O(1) pointer changes.

2. keySet(), values(), entrySet() and forEach()

  • Signature: Set keySet(); Collection values(); Set> entrySet(); void forEach(BiConsumer)
  • Returns: views in insertion order
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Every view and every loop visits the pairs in insertion order, so printed results are the same on every run: ideal for reports, logs and tests.

For experienced developers: Iteration costs O(size), not O(capacity + size), because it follows the entry chain and skips empty buckets.

3. computeIfAbsent, merge and the other compute methods

  • Signature: compute / computeIfAbsent / computeIfPresent / merge
  • Returns: as HashMap
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: They behave exactly as in HashMap. A new key created by one of them is added at the end of the order.

For experienced developers: When you build a grouped or counted result that you later print, LinkedHashMap gives you the groups in the order they were first seen.

Access order and the LRU cache

The special power of LinkedHashMap.

4. Access order: new LinkedHashMap(capacity, loadFactor, true)

  • Signature: LinkedHashMap(int initialCapacity, float loadFactor, boolean accessOrder)
  • Returns: a map ordered by last access
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: With accessOrder = true, every get or put of a key moves that entry to the end. So the first entry is always the least recently used one and the last entry is the most recently used.

For experienced developers: In access-order mode even get is a structural modification (it re-links the entry), so iterating while calling get throws ConcurrentModificationException. containsKey, containsValue and the views do not count as access.

5. removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry eldest)

  • Signature: protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry eldest)
  • Returns: true to remove the eldest entry after an insertion
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: LinkedHashMap calls this method after every put. By default it returns false. Override it to return true when the map is too big and the oldest entry is removed automatically. Together with access order this builds an LRU (least recently used) cache in a few lines.

For experienced developers: The method may also modify the map itself, but the usual pattern is just return size() > MAX. Wrap the class with Collections.synchronizedMap for thread safety (or use Caffeine for a production cache).

Java 21: first and last entries

The new SequencedMap methods.

6. firstEntry, lastEntry, pollFirstEntry and pollLastEntry

  • Signature: Map.Entry firstEntry(); lastEntry(); pollFirstEntry(); pollLastEntry()
  • Returns: the entry, or null if the map is empty
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Read or remove the first or last pair directly. The poll versions remove and return it. The returned entries are snapshots (immutable).

For experienced developers: Before Java 21 you had to iterate to the end to find the last entry. With pollFirstEntry in a loop a LinkedHashMap can act as an ordered work queue with key lookups.

7. putFirst, putLast and reversed

  • Signature: V putFirst(K, V); V putLast(K, V); SequencedMap reversed()
  • Returns: the previous value / a reversed view
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: putFirst and putLast add a pair at the front or the back; if the key already exists it is moved there. reversed() is a live view that walks from the last entry to the first.

For experienced developers: This finally allows reordering a LinkedHashMap without removing and re-adding. sequencedKeySet(), sequencedValues() and sequencedEntrySet() give the same ordered views with getFirst, getLast and reversed.

8. clone, equals and toString

  • Signature: Object clone(); boolean equals(Object); String toString()
  • Returns: a shallow copy / comparison / text
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: A LinkedHashMap is equal to any other Map with the same pairs; the order is ignored by equals. toString prints the pairs in order.

For experienced developers: Copy with new LinkedHashMap<>(map) to keep the order of the source map.

Master program: every LinkedHashMap method in one place

One single program that uses all the LinkedHashMap methods you learned above, step by step. Read the numbered comments from top to bottom, run it, and match each output line with its step.

Module: Sorting methods

For freshers: a LinkedHashMap cannot sort itself either, but it is the best home for sorted data: whatever order you insert is the order you get back. For experienced developers: sorting is always "produce a sorted sequence, then insert in that order"; the cost is the O(n log n) sort. Access order and reversed() cover the other orderings.

9. Sort by key: TreeMap, then LinkedHashMap

  • Signature: new LinkedHashMap<>(new TreeMap<>(map))
  • Returns: a LinkedHashMap whose order is the sorted key order
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Copy the pairs into a TreeMap (sorts the keys), then copy that into a LinkedHashMap. The result is a fixed, key-sorted snapshot.

For experienced developers: If you only need to print, the TreeMap alone is enough. The extra copy is useful when later code must add new keys after the sorted ones without re-sorting.

10. Sort by value: stream into a new LinkedHashMap

  • Signature: entrySet().stream().sorted(comparingByValue()).collect(toMap(..., LinkedHashMap::new))
  • Returns: a new LinkedHashMap sorted by value
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Stream the entries, sort them by value and collect into a LinkedHashMap. The sorted order is kept because that map remembers insertion order.

For experienced developers: The four-argument Collectors.toMap needs a merge function; (a, b) -> a is fine because keys are unique. The original map is untouched.

11. reversed(): the map in the opposite order (Java 21)

  • Signature: SequencedMap reversed()
  • Returns: a live reverse-order view of the same map
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: Want the newest first? reversed() gives the same pairs from last to first. It is a view, not a copy, so it costs almost nothing.

For experienced developers: Because it is a view, changes show through in both directions. Copy it with new LinkedHashMap<>(map.reversed()) if you need a separate map. This replaces the old trick of copying keys into a list and calling Collections.reverse.

12. Access order: move the used entry to the end

  • Signature: new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true)
  • Returns: a map ordered by last use, not by first insert
  • Time: O(1) per access

For freshers: Pass true as the third constructor argument and every get or put of a key moves that entry to the end. The first entry is then the one used longest ago.

For experienced developers: This is the engine of an LRU cache: add removeEldestEntry to drop the first entry when the map is too big. Remember that get now modifies the map.

13. Move an entry to the front or the end by hand

  • Signature: putFirst(k, v) / putLast(k, v)
  • Returns: the previous value or null
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: In Java 21 you can place a pair exactly where you want: putFirst puts it at the start, putLast at the end. If the key already exists it is moved there.

For experienced developers: Before Java 21 you had to remove then put to move a key to the end, and there was no way to insert at the front. Both new methods are O(1) because of the linked list.

Which ordering approach to pick?

You wantUseNote
Keys A to Z, kept as a snapshotnew LinkedHashMap<>(new TreeMap<>(map))new keys are appended, not sorted in
Sorted by valuestream + sorted + toMap(..., LinkedHashMap::new)copy; original unchanged
Newest firstmap.reversed()view, O(1)
Order by last use (LRU)constructor with accessOrder = trueget reorders
Put one entry first or lastputFirst / putLastJava 21

Module: Finding (searching) methods

For freshers: everything that finds in a HashMap works here, and because the order is fixed, "find the first" and "find the last" have a clear answer. For experienced developers: key lookups are O(1); first/last are O(1) thanks to the linked list; scans by value or condition are O(n) but deterministic.

14. get, getOrDefault and containsKey

  • Signature: V get(Object key) / boolean containsKey(Object key)
  • Returns: the value (or null), or true/false
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: The same as in HashMap: look up by key. getOrDefault gives your own value when the key is missing.

For experienced developers: In an access-order map each of these calls also moves the entry to the end. If you must peek without changing the order, use containsKey first only when order does not matter, or use a normal (insertion-order) map.

15. firstEntry and lastEntry: the oldest and the newest (Java 21)

  • Signature: Map.Entry firstEntry() / lastEntry()
  • Returns: the first / last entry, or null if empty
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Find the entry that was added first or last without looping. Great for "what is the oldest item?" or "what was added most recently?".

For experienced developers: The returned entry is a snapshot: it does not change if the map changes later. Before Java 21 you needed map.entrySet().iterator().next() for the first and a full loop for the last.

16. pollFirstEntry and pollLastEntry: find and remove

  • Signature: Map.Entry pollFirstEntry() / pollLastEntry()
  • Returns: the removed entry, or null if empty
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Like firstEntry, but it also removes the entry. Use it to treat the map as a queue: take the oldest one and process it.

For experienced developers: Useful for bounded histories and FIFO caches. Calling it in a loop until the map is empty drains the map in insertion order.

17. Find the key for a value (first match)

  • Signature: for (Map.Entry e : map.entrySet())
  • Returns: the first key (in map order) that has the value
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Loop over the entries and stop at the first match. Unlike HashMap, "first" has a clear meaning here: the earliest inserted key that has this value.

For experienced developers: If many keys share the value, you get the earliest one every time, so results are repeatable. For many value lookups build a reverse map.

18. Stream filter and findFirst

  • Signature: entrySet().stream().filter(...).findFirst()
  • Returns: an Optional of the first matching entry
  • Time: O(n), stops early

For freshers: Describe what you are looking for with a rule and take the first match. Because the order is fixed, findFirst always returns the same entry.

For experienced developers: The stream stops as soon as it finds a match. Optional forces you to handle "not found" (orElse, ifPresent).

19. Find by position (nth entry)

  • Signature: new ArrayList<>(map.keySet()).get(index)
  • Returns: the key at that position
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: A map has no index, but the order is fixed, so "the 2nd stop" has a meaning. Copy the keys into a list and use get(index).

For experienced developers: Copying is O(n); for one-off lookups skip the copy and use stream().skip(i).findFirst(). If you need positions often, a List is the better structure.

Which finding method to pick?

QuestionMethodTime
Value for a key / does a key existget, getOrDefault, containsKeyO(1)
Oldest / newest entryfirstEntry / lastEntryO(1)
Take the oldest outpollFirstEntryO(1)
First key with a valueloop over entrySet()O(n)
First entry matching a rulestream().filter(...).findFirst()O(n)
The nth entrycopy keys to a List, then get(i)O(n)

expert.content:
How LinkedHashMap works inside

It adds one doubly linked list on top of HashMap's buckets.

  • Entries are LinkedHashMap.Entry<K,V>: a HashMap node plus before and after references. The map keeps head (eldest) and tail (youngest).
  • HashMap exposes three hooks that LinkedHashMap overrides: afterNodeInsertion (calls removeEldestEntry), afterNodeAccess (moves the entry to the tail in access-order mode) and afterNodeRemoval (unlinks the entry).
  • Lookups still use the hash table, so get, put and remove stay O(1).
  • Iteration follows after links: O(size), independent of capacity.
  • Memory: two extra references (8 bytes with compressed pointers) per entry compared with HashMap.
  • In access-order mode get relinks the entry, so it changes modCount and is not safe for concurrent readers.

HashMap, LinkedHashMap and TreeMap side by side

HashMapLinkedHashMapTreeMap
OrderNoneInsertion or access orderSorted by key
get / put / removeO(1)O(1)O(log n)
IterationO(capacity + n)O(n)O(n)
MemoryLowestSlightly moreMost
null keyOneOneNo
LRU cacheNoYesNo

Trap: get() changes the order in access-order mode

  • A read relinks the entry, so reading while iterating the same map throws ConcurrentModificationException.
  • Iterate over a copy of the keys (or entries) when you need to read inside the loop.

Real example: ordered JSON-style report

Fields must appear in the order they were defined, so a LinkedHashMap is the natural container for a record that will be written out.

Best practices

When LinkedHashMap is the right tool.

  • Use it when the order of iteration matters (output, serialization, tests) and you still want O(1) lookups.
  • For caches use access order plus removeEldestEntry, but wrap it for threads (Collections.synchronizedMap) or use a library cache.
  • Do not read the map inside a loop over the same map in access-order mode.
  • Use plain HashMap when order does not matter: it needs less memory.
  • Use immutable keys with consistent equals/hashCode, as for any hash map.
  • In Java 21 prefer firstEntry, lastEntry, putFirst, putLast and reversed() to hand-written iteration.

Real-time examples

Three small jobs where the order of the pairs matters, so a LinkedHashMap is the right tool.

Scenario 1: Menu that prints in the order it was defined

For freshers: a console menu must show options as 1, 2, 3 in the order you wrote them. A HashMap could shuffle them; a LinkedHashMap cannot. For experienced developers: use it for configuration, column definitions and anything where order is part of the data.

Scenario 2: City visits in first-seen order

For freshers: a trip log lists cities again and again. We want each city once, with its count, in the order the trip first reached it. For experienced developers: merge on a LinkedHashMap keeps the original position of a key when its value is updated, which is exactly "first appearance order".

Scenario 3: Last 3 searches (bounded history)

For freshers: a search box remembers only the last three searches. When a fourth arrives, the oldest is dropped. For experienced developers: overriding removeEldestEntry turns the map into a size-limited FIFO. It is called after every put; return true to remove the eldest entry.

Sample project: Fort Tour Itinerary Planner

What we build: a console planner that keeps tour stops in order with a LinkedHashMap, lets you insert, move and reverse stops, and prints a timeline.

Steps:

  • Step 1: add stops in visiting order (stop name to hours spent).
  • Step 2: insert an early stop at the front with putFirst.
  • Step 3: move one stop to the end with putLast.
  • Step 4: print a timeline with the clock time each stop starts (start at 8:00).
  • Step 5: find the longest stop and the total hours.
  • Step 6: print the return journey with reversed().

Read the step comments in the program, run it, then extend it with your own idea.

Practice questions

Now test yourself. Each question is harder than the examples above: read the problem, write your own solution, then compare it with the one shown. Every solution was compiled and run, and its output is real.

Practice question 1: Fort page cache (LRU: least recently used is thrown out)

Level: Medium

Problem: A website keeps the last 3 fort pages in memory. When a fourth page is loaded, the page nobody has used for the longest time is removed. An access-ordered LinkedHashMap does this with one overridden method.

Your task:

  1. Create the map with accessOrder = true, so every get moves the entry to the end.
  2. Override removeEldestEntry to remove the oldest when size exceeds 3.
  3. Show hits, misses and the cache contents after each request.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 2: Bookings grouped by district, in the order they arrived

Level: Medium

Problem: A report must list districts in the order they first received a booking, and inside each district the forts in booking order. Print the report and the district with the most bookings.

Your task:

  1. Use LinkedHashMap<String, List<String>> and computeIfAbsent.
  2. Print each district with its numbered forts.
  3. Find the district with the most bookings (first one wins a tie).

Hints:

  • Use > (not >=) when comparing sizes so the earlier district wins a tie.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 3: Unique cities in arrival order

Level: Easy

Problem: A booking list contains repeated city names. Print every city once, in the order it first appeared, with the number of bookings.

Your task:

  1. Create a LinkedHashMap<String, Integer>.
  2. Use merge for each city.
  3. Print one line per city.

Hints:

  • merge keeps the position of a key that already exists.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 4: Recently viewed forts, newest first

Level: Medium

Problem: A page shows the last forts a user opened, newest first, with no repeats. Opening a fort that is already in the list moves it to the top. Keep at most 4.

Your task:

  1. Use a LinkedHashMap and putLast for every view (it moves a repeat to the end).
  2. If the size goes above 4, remove the first entry with pollFirstEntry.
  3. Print the result with reversed() so the newest comes first.

Hints:

  • A repeated putLast moves the key; it does not add a second entry.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 5: Merge two ordered itineraries

Level: Medium

Problem: Two guides each keep a LinkedHashMap of stop to hours. Merge them: stops of guide A first (in A order), then the new stops of guide B (in B order). For a stop in both, keep the larger number of hours.

Your task:

  1. Copy A into the result.
  2. For every entry of B, use merge(stop, hours, Math::max).
  3. Print the result and prove that A's order was kept.

Hints:

  • Math::max works as the merge function for two Integer values.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 6: Leaderboard with ranks and shared places

Level: Hard

Problem: Given scores per trekker, print a leaderboard sorted by score (high first, then name). Trekkers with the same score share a rank, and the next rank skips (1, 2, 2, 4).

Your task:

  1. Sort the entries into a LinkedHashMap (score descending, name ascending).
  2. Walk through it, keep the rank of the previous score, and update it only when the score changes.
  3. Print rank, name and score.

Hints:

  • Rank = position of the first trekker with that score.
  • e.getValue() != lastScore compares ints after unboxing, which is fine here.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

interviewQA: What is a LinkedHashMap and how does it differ from HashMap?

It is a HashMap that also keeps a doubly linked list through its entries, so iteration follows insertion order (or access order) instead of hash order. Operations stay O(1) with slightly more memory per entry.
How do you create an LRU cache in Java?
Extend LinkedHashMap, call super(capacity, 0.75f, true) for access order, and override removeEldestEntry to return size() > capacity.
What is access order?
A mode enabled by the third constructor argument: each get or put moves the entry to the end, so the first entry is the least recently used.
What does removeEldestEntry do?
It is called after each insertion with the eldest entry; returning true removes it. The default returns false.
Does re-inserting an existing key change its position?
Not in insertion-order mode. In access-order mode it moves to the end. In Java 21, putFirst/putLast move it explicitly.
Is LinkedHashMap thread-safe?
No. In access-order mode even get() modifies the structure. Use Collections.synchronizedMap or a concurrent cache.
Why is iteration over LinkedHashMap faster than HashMap for sparse tables?
It follows the entry chain (O(size)) instead of scanning all buckets (O(capacity + size)).
What did Java 21 add to LinkedHashMap?
SequencedMap methods: firstEntry, lastEntry, pollFirstEntry, pollLastEntry, putFirst, putLast, reversed and sequenced views of keys, values and entries.
Does equals() of a LinkedHashMap consider order?
No. Two maps with the same pairs are equal regardless of order.
When would you choose TreeMap over LinkedHashMap?
When you need entries sorted by key or navigation methods (floorKey, headMap, ...). LinkedHashMap orders by insertion/access, not by key.

topics.name: TreeMap

beginner.content:
