What is a TreeMap?

A TreeMap is a map whose keys are always kept sorted. Put the pairs in any order and they come out ordered by key: forts A to Z, numbers small to large. On top of the ordinary map methods it can answer neighbour and range questions: "which key comes just after 500?" or "give me all entries between P and S".

  • Package java.util. Implements NavigableMap (which extends SortedMap, which extends Map).
  • Sorted by key: by the keys' natural order (Comparable) or by a Comparator you supply.
  • Unique keys: two keys are "the same" when compareTo / compare returns 0 (not when equals says so).
  • O(log n) for get, put, remove and containsKey: slower than HashMap but ordered.
  • No null key with natural ordering; null values are allowed.
  • Not thread-safe. Use ConcurrentSkipListMap for concurrent sorted maps.
  • Use it for: sorted output, range queries, "nearest" lookups, rate tables and time lines.

Where TreeMap sits in the Collection Framework

Map
(I)
← extends
SortedMap
(I)
← extends
NavigableMap
(I)
← implements
AbstractMap
(c)
← extends
TreeMap
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. TreeMap also implements Cloneable and Serializable. It is the engine behind TreeSet.

Creating a TreeMap: four constructors

  • new TreeMap<>(): natural ordering of the keys.
  • new TreeMap<>(Comparator c): your own key ordering.
  • new TreeMap<>(Map m): copy with natural ordering.
  • new TreeMap<>(SortedMap m): copy that keeps the ordering of m.

All TreeMap methods at a glance

n is the number of entries.

MethodWhat it doesTime
put, get, remove, containsKey, getOrDefault, putIfAbsent, replace, merge, compute...The ordinary Map methodsO(log n)
containsValue(v)Scans all entriesO(n)
firstKey() / lastKey()Smallest / largest key (throws if empty)O(log n)
firstEntry() / lastEntry()Smallest / largest entry (null if empty)O(log n)
pollFirstEntry() / pollLastEntry()Remove and return smallest / largest entryO(log n)
lowerKey / floorKey / ceilingKey / higherKeyNeighbour key below or above a valueO(log n)
lowerEntry / floorEntry / ceilingEntry / higherEntryThe same, returning the whole entryO(log n)
headMap(to) / tailMap(from) / subMap(a, b)Range viewsO(log n)
descendingMap() / descendingKeySet() / navigableKeySet()Reverse / key set viewsO(1)
keySet() / values() / entrySet() / forEach()Views and loops in key orderO(n)
comparator()The ordering in use (null = natural)O(1)
clone / equals / toStringCopy and compareO(n)

Benefits and advantages

For freshers: a TreeMap is a map that keeps its keys sorted all the time, so you never sort it yourself. Why use it:

  • Always sorted. Keys come out A to Z (or small to large) every time you print or loop, with no extra code.
  • "Nearest" questions are easy. floorKey, ceilingKey, lowerKey, higherKey answer "the closest key at or below / above this one".
  • Range slices. headMap, tailMap and subMap give "everything before / after / between" in one call.
  • Smallest and biggest at once. firstKey and lastKey need no loop.
  • Custom order. Give it a Comparator for reverse order, case-insensitive order, or order by length.
  • Predictable speed. Every operation is O(log n), never worse, even for many similar keys.
  • For experienced developers: it is a red-black tree implementing NavigableMap. There is no hashing, so keys need no hashCode; equality is decided by the comparator (compare == 0). The sub-maps and descending map are live views, not copies.

Disadvantages and when NOT to use it

For freshers: sorting has a price. Know when a TreeMap is the wrong choice:

  • Slower than HashMap. O(log n) instead of O(1) for get and put. For a million keys that is about 20 steps instead of 1.
  • Keys must be comparable. They need to implement Comparable, or you must supply a Comparator; otherwise you get a ClassCastException.
  • No null keys with natural ordering (a NullPointerException). Null values are allowed.
  • Sorted by key only. It cannot keep the pairs sorted by value.
  • Not thread-safe. Use ConcurrentSkipListMap for a sorted map shared by threads.
  • For experienced developers: an inconsistent comparator (one that does not agree with equals) silently treats different keys as the same key and drops entries; tree nodes use more memory than hash nodes and have poor cache locality; changing a key object after inserting it breaks the ordering.

Quick guide:

Use a TreeMap whenUse something else when
You need keys always sortedOrder does not matter: HashMap is faster
You ask "next / previous / between" questionsYou only need insertion order: LinkedHashMap
You build ranges, slabs, schedules or leaderboards by keyMany threads share it: ConcurrentSkipListMap
You print a report sorted by name or dateYou must sort by value: stream + LinkedHashMap

intermediate.content:
Putting and reading: the sorted map

All the usual Map methods work, and every view is in key order.

1. put, get, remove and containsKey

  • Signature: V put(K, V); V get(Object); V remove(Object); boolean containsKey(Object)
  • Returns: as Map
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Same meaning as in HashMap, but the map keeps itself sorted. A new key is inserted at its sorted place; an existing key just has its value replaced.

For experienced developers: Each call walks from the root comparing the key, so the cost is the tree height. Passing a key that is not comparable throws ClassCastException; passing null throws NullPointerException (natural ordering).

2. merge, computeIfAbsent and the other compute methods

  • Signature: compute / computeIfAbsent / computeIfPresent / merge / putIfAbsent / getOrDefault
  • Returns: as HashMap
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: They behave exactly as in HashMap. Combine them with a TreeMap to get sorted counts and groups.

For experienced developers: A TreeMap is often the finishing step of a data pipeline: collect into a HashMap for speed, then copy into a TreeMap to print in order.

3. keySet(), values(), entrySet() and forEach()

  • Signature: Set keySet(); Collection values(); Set> entrySet(); void forEach(BiConsumer)
  • Returns: views in ascending key order
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Every view and loop is in ascending key order. They are live views: removing from a view removes from the map.

For experienced developers: navigableKeySet() returns the keys as a NavigableSet and descendingKeySet() in reverse. Entries from entrySet() support setValue, but entries returned by firstEntry() and friends are immutable snapshots.

The ends of the map

Smallest and largest key, with or without removing them.

4. firstKey, lastKey, firstEntry and lastEntry

  • Signature: K firstKey(); K lastKey(); Map.Entry firstEntry(); Map.Entry lastEntry()
  • Returns: the key / the entry
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: firstKey() and lastKey() return the smallest and the largest key and throw NoSuchElementException when the map is empty. firstEntry() and lastEntry() return the whole pair (or null when empty).

For experienced developers: The entry versions are safer for possibly-empty maps and give the value in the same call. The returned entries are snapshots: calling setValue on them throws UnsupportedOperationException.

5. pollFirstEntry() and pollLastEntry()

  • Signature: Map.Entry pollFirstEntry(); Map.Entry pollLastEntry()
  • Returns: the removed entry, or null if empty
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Remove and return the entry with the smallest or the largest key. Repeat pollFirstEntry until it returns null to process entries in key order while consuming them (a sorted queue with lookups).

For experienced developers: Handy for event schedulers: key = time, value = task; pollFirstEntry always gives the next task due.

Neighbours: lowerKey, floorKey, ceilingKey and higherKey

Find the closest key to a value, even if the value is not a key. Each has an Entry twin: lowerEntry, floorEntry, ceilingEntry, higherEntry.

6. lowerKey, floorKey, ceilingKey, higherKey (and the Entry versions)

  • Signature: K lowerKey(K); K floorKey(K); K ceilingKey(K); K higherKey(K); Map.Entry lowerEntry(K) ...
  • Returns: the neighbouring key / entry, or null
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: lowerKey(k) = greatest key strictly below k; floorKey(k) = greatest key below or equal; ceilingKey(k) = smallest key above or equal; higherKey(k) = smallest key strictly above. If there is no such key the result is null.

For experienced developers: The Entry versions return the key and its value in one call, which is what you usually want. This is the standard way to implement price slabs, tax brackets, grade boundaries and time-line lookups.

Range views: headMap, tailMap and subMap

Take a part of the map by key. The result is a live view.

7. headMap, tailMap and subMap

  • Signature: SortedMap headMap(K toKey); NavigableMap headMap(K toKey, boolean inclusive); tailMap(K fromKey[, boolean]); subMap(from, to) / subMap(from, fromInc, to, toInc)
  • Returns: a view of that key range
  • Time: O(log n) to create

For freshers: headMap(to) = entries with keys before to; tailMap(from) = keys from from onwards; subMap(from, to) = from (included) to to (excluded). The long forms let you choose whether each end is included.

For experienced developers: Views are not copies: changing the view changes the map and the other way round. Putting a key outside the view's range throws IllegalArgumentException. Copy with new TreeMap<>(view) for an independent map.

Reverse order

See the map upside down without copying it.

8. descendingMap(), descendingKeySet(), navigableKeySet() and reversed()

  • Signature: NavigableMap descendingMap(); NavigableSet descendingKeySet(); NavigableSet navigableKeySet(); NavigableMap reversed()
  • Returns: live reversed / key-set views
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: descendingMap() shows the same entries from the largest key to the smallest. descendingKeySet() does the same for the keys only. In Java 21 reversed() is the same as descendingMap().

For experienced developers: All are views: they update when the map changes, and removing through them changes the map. They can be chained: map.descendingMap().headMap(x).

9. comparator(), clone, equals and toString

  • Signature: Comparator comparator(); Object clone(); boolean equals(Object); String toString()
  • Returns: the ordering / a shallow copy / comparison / text
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: comparator() returns the ordering in use (null for natural ordering). A TreeMap is equal to any Map with the same pairs, whatever the order or class.

For experienced developers: A clone copies the structure and keeps the comparator. Because equals on maps uses equals of the keys, a TreeMap with an unusual comparator can be "not equal" to a HashMap that looks identical.

Master program: every TreeMap method in one place

One single program that uses all the TreeMap methods you learned above, step by step. Read the numbered comments from top to bottom, run it, and match each output line with its step.

Module: Sorting methods

For freshers: the TreeMap does the sorting for you, by key. Your job is only to choose the order: natural, reversed, or your own rule. For experienced developers: insertion costs O(log n) each, so building a TreeMap of n keys is O(n log n); once built, reading in order is O(n) with no extra sort.

10. Natural order: new TreeMap<>()

  • Signature: new TreeMap<>()
  • Returns: a map sorted by the keys' natural order
  • Time: O(log n) per put

For freshers: Put keys in any order; they come out sorted. Strings go A to Z (capital letters before small ones), numbers go small to large.

For experienced developers: Natural order uses compareTo of the key class, so String, Integer, LocalDate and enums work out of the box.

11. Custom order: pass a Comparator

  • Signature: new TreeMap<>(Comparator c)
  • Returns: a map sorted by your rule
  • Time: O(log n) per put

For freshers: To change the order, give the constructor a Comparator. Comparator.reverseOrder() flips it; String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER ignores capital letters.

For experienced developers: The comparator also defines which keys are "equal": with case-insensitive order, "raigad" and "Raigad" are the same key, and the second put replaces the value but keeps the first spelling.

12. descendingMap and descendingKeySet

  • Signature: NavigableMap descendingMap()
  • Returns: a live view of the map in reverse key order
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: Need the biggest key first? descendingMap() shows the same pairs from last to first, without building a new map.

For experienced developers: It is a view: changes to either map show in the other. descendingKeySet() does the same for just the keys. Iterating is still O(n).

13. Sort by value: stream into a LinkedHashMap

  • Signature: entrySet().stream().sorted(comparingByValue())
  • Returns: a LinkedHashMap in value order
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: A TreeMap sorts only by key. To order the pairs by value, stream the entries, sort them, and collect into a LinkedHashMap.

For experienced developers: A comparator that looks up the value inside a TreeMap (for example (a, b) -> map.get(a) - map.get(b)) is a classic bug: it breaks get and drops keys with equal values. Use the stream approach.

14. Re-sort with another order: copy with a new Comparator

  • Signature: TreeMap other = new TreeMap<>(newComparator); other.putAll(map)
  • Returns: a new map in the new order
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: The order of a TreeMap is fixed when it is created. To get another order, make a second TreeMap with a different comparator and copy the pairs in with putAll.

For experienced developers: Here the order is "shortest name first, then A to Z". A comparator must be consistent: always return 0 only for keys you consider equal, so use thenComparing as a tie-break or keys will be lost.

Which ordering approach to pick?

You wantUseNote
Keys sorted naturallynew TreeMap<>()always sorted, even after later puts
Reverse, case-insensitive or custom key ordernew TreeMap<>(comparator)comparator also decides key equality
The same map, biggest firstdescendingMap()live view
Pairs ordered by valuestream + sorted + LinkedHashMapa snapshot; TreeMap cannot do it

Module: Finding (searching) methods

For freshers: a TreeMap can answer questions a HashMap cannot: "what is the next key after this?", "what is the closest key below?", "give me everything between A and B". For experienced developers: all key-based navigation is O(log n); value scans stay O(n). The range methods return views that cost O(log n) to create and let you read or even clear a whole range.

15. get, containsKey and containsValue

  • Signature: V get(Object key) / boolean containsKey(Object key) / boolean containsValue(Object value)
  • Returns: the value, or true/false
  • Time: O(log n) by key, O(n) by value

For freshers: Look up by key as usual. Finding by key walks down the tree; finding by value must check the entries one by one.

For experienced developers: A TreeMap compares keys with the comparator, not equals, so get finds keys the comparator treats as equal. The key must be comparable with the stored keys or a ClassCastException follows.

16. firstKey, lastKey, firstEntry, lastEntry

  • Signature: K firstKey() / K lastKey() / Map.Entry firstEntry() / lastEntry()
  • Returns: the smallest / biggest key or entry
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: The smallest and the biggest key are always at the ends. These methods return them with no loop.

For experienced developers: firstKey and lastKey throw NoSuchElementException on an empty map, while firstEntry and lastEntry return null. The entries are read-only snapshots.

17. floorKey, ceilingKey, lowerKey, higherKey

  • Signature: K floorKey(K k) / ceilingKey(K k) / lowerKey(K k) / higherKey(K k)
  • Returns: the closest key, or null if there is none
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Find the nearest key to a target. floor = biggest key at or below it, ceiling = smallest key at or above it, lower = strictly below, higher = strictly above.

For experienced developers: Each has an ...Entry twin (floorEntry, ...) that returns the pair, saving a second lookup. They are the reason to choose a TreeMap for slabs, grades and schedules.

18. headMap, tailMap, subMap: find a range

  • Signature: SortedMap headMap(K to) / tailMap(K from) / NavigableMap subMap(K from, boolean, K to, boolean)
  • Returns: a live view of the keys in the range
  • Time: O(log n) to create

For freshers: Get "everything below", "everything from here up" or "everything between two keys". headMap excludes the end key by default; pass true to include it.

For experienced developers: The result is a view: clearing it removes those entries from the original, and putting a key outside its range throws IllegalArgumentException.

19. Find all matches by value or rule

  • Signature: entrySet().stream().filter(...)
  • Returns: the matching entries, in key order
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Searching by value or by a condition scans every entry. In a TreeMap the matches come out already in key order, so no extra sort is needed.

For experienced developers: Collections.max(map.entrySet(), comparingByValue()) finds the entry with the biggest value in O(n). If you search by value often, build a second TreeMap keyed by that value.

Which finding method to pick?

QuestionMethodTime
Value for a key, does a key existget, containsKeyO(log n)
Smallest / biggest keyfirstKey / lastKey (or the Entry versions)O(log n)
Closest key at or below / abovefloorKey / ceilingKeyO(log n)
Closest key strictly below / abovelowerKey / higherKeyO(log n)
All keys before / after / betweenheadMap / tailMap / subMapO(log n) + size of result
Entries matching a rule on the valuestream().filter(...)O(n)

expert.content:
How TreeMap works inside

TreeMap is a red-black tree: a binary search tree that rebalances itself.

  • Every node (TreeMap.Entry) stores key, value, left, right, parent and a colour flag (red or black).
  • The binary-search-tree rule: all keys in the left subtree are smaller, all keys in the right subtree are larger. A lookup therefore discards half of the remaining keys at every step.
  • The red-black rules (root is black; a red node has black children; every path from a node to its leaves has the same number of black nodes) are repaired after each insert/delete by rotations and recolouring. The height stays at most about 2 log2(n + 1).
  • So get, put, remove, floorKey, ceilingKey, firstKey ... are all O(log n): about 20 comparisons for a million entries.
  • Ordering comes only from compareTo or the Comparator. hashCode is never used; equals is not used to find keys.
  • Iteration walks the tree in order using successor links: O(1) amortised per step, O(n) overall.
  • Memory: about 40 bytes of overhead per entry (more than HashMap).

Trap: the comparator decides which keys are "the same"

  • If the comparator returns 0 for two different keys, the second put replaces the value of the first key and no new entry is created.
  • Add tie-breakers with thenComparing so that only truly equal keys compare as 0.

Real example 1: tax / price slabs with floorEntry

A table of slabs keyed by the lower bound. floorEntry(amount) finds the slab that contains any amount in one O(log n) call.

Real example 2: an event timeline with subMap

Keep events keyed by hour; subMap returns everything in a time window.

TreeMap versus HashMap versus LinkedHashMap versus ConcurrentSkipListMap

TreeMapHashMapLinkedHashMapConcurrentSkipListMap
OrderSorted by keyNoneInsertion / accessSorted by key
get / put / removeO(log n)O(1)O(1)O(log n)
Range / neighbour queriesYesNoNoYes
null keyNoOneOneNo
Thread-safeNoNoNoYes (lock-free)
Key identity decided bycompareTo / Comparatorequals / hashCodeequals / hashCodecompareTo / Comparator

Best practices

Use TreeMap for what only it can do.

  • Choose TreeMap when you need sorted keys, "nearest key" lookups or range queries; otherwise HashMap is faster.
  • Keep the comparator consistent with equals and add tie-breakers (thenComparing).
  • Never modify a key in a way that changes its ordering after inserting it.
  • Do not use null keys. Check inputs.
  • Prefer the *Entry navigation methods to the *Key ones when you also need the value.
  • For a concurrent sorted map use ConcurrentSkipListMap; for a one-off sorted print, copy a HashMap into a TreeMap.

Real-time examples

Three jobs where sorted keys and "nearest key" questions make a TreeMap the natural choice.

Scenario 1: Phone directory with prefix search

For freshers: names are kept A to Z automatically, and a search box can list every name that starts with "Am". For experienced developers: subMap(prefix, prefix + Character.MAX_VALUE) is a prefix search in O(log n + k), where k is the number of matches. A HashMap would need a full scan.

Scenario 2: Marks to grade

For freshers: a grade does not belong to one mark but to a range of marks. Store only where each grade starts; floorEntry finds the grade whose start is at or below the mark. For experienced developers: this replaces a long chain of if / else if with data, so changing the slabs needs no code change. The same pattern fits tax slabs and shipping charges.

Scenario 3: The fort closest to a height

For freshers: a hiker asks "which fort is nearest to 1200 m?". The answer is either the closest fort below or the closest above; compare the two. For experienced developers: two O(log n) lookups (floorEntry, ceilingEntry) beat scanning all forts. Always check for null: one side may not exist.

Sample project: Fort Height Explorer

What we build: a console tool that stores forts in a TreeMap keyed by height and answers sorted, nearest and range questions.

Steps:

  • Step 1: load forts into a TreeMap<Integer, String> (height to name).
  • Step 2: print the list from tallest to shortest with descendingMap.
  • Step 3: print the shortest and the tallest with firstEntry and lastEntry.
  • Step 4: list the forts between two heights with subMap.
  • Step 5: report the next taller and next shorter fort than a chosen one with higherEntry and lowerEntry.
  • Step 6: remove every fort below 900 m with headMap(900).clear() and print what remains.

Read the step comments in the program, run it, then extend it with your own idea.

Practice questions

Now test yourself. Each question is harder than the examples above: read the problem, write your own solution, then compare it with the one shown. Every solution was compiled and run, and its output is real.

Practice question 1: Bus timetable (next departure, previous bus, a window of time)

Level: Medium

Problem: A bus stand keeps departures in a TreeMap keyed by the time of day. Passengers ask "when is the next bus after 10:30?", and the board shows everything leaving in the next two hours.

Your task:

  1. put departures in any order: the map keeps them sorted.
  2. ceilingEntry / higherEntry / floorEntry answer the nearest-time questions.
  3. subMap gives the departure board for a time window.
  4. pollFirstEntry removes the bus that has just left.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 2: Progressive entry-fee calculator

Level: Hard

Problem: Group fees per person are charged by slabs: the first 10 people pay 100 each, the next 15 (people 11 to 25) pay 80 each, everyone after that pays 60. Compute the total for any group size using a TreeMap of slab starts.

Your task:

  1. Store the slab start (1, 11, 26) as key and the fee as value.
  2. For a group of N, walk the slabs in order and charge each slab for the people that fall inside it.
  3. Print the total for groups of 5, 10, 18, 25 and 40, and which slab each ends in (use floorEntry).

Hints:

  • higherKey(start) tells you where the next slab begins, so the end of this slab is next - 1.
  • Check by hand: 18 people = 10 x 100 + 8 x 80 = 1640.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 3: Sorted word frequency (ignore capital letters)

Level: Easy

Problem: Count how often each word appears in a sentence, ignoring upper and lower case, and print the words A to Z with their counts.

Your task:

  1. Create a TreeMap with String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER.
  2. Split the sentence by spaces and use merge.
  3. Print the map.

Hints:

  • The first spelling that is stored stays as the key.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 4: Name autocomplete

Level: Medium

Problem: Given a sorted contact book, return the names that start with a typed prefix, and the first name that comes alphabetically after all of them.

Your task:

  1. Store names in a TreeMap<String, String>.
  2. Use subMap(prefix, prefix + Character.MAX_VALUE) for matches.
  3. Use higherKey on the last match to find the next name.

Hints:

  • Keys are compared as Strings, so "Pan..." names sit next to each other.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 5: Fort lookup by height with tie-break

Level: Medium

Problem: For a list of target heights, print the nearest fort. If a target is exactly in the middle of two forts, choose the taller one. A target equal to a fort height returns that fort.

Your task:

  1. Use floorEntry and ceilingEntry.
  2. Handle a missing neighbour.
  3. Compare the two distances.

Hints:

  • If the gaps are equal, return the upper entry.

Practice question 6: How many guides are busy at the same time? (sweep line)

Level: Hard

Problem: Tour bookings are time ranges [start, end) in hours. Find the largest number of bookings that overlap, and the first hour where that happens.

Your task:

  1. Make a TreeMap<Integer, Integer> of time to change: +1 at every start, -1 at every end (use merge).
  2. Walk the map in key order, keep a running total, and track the maximum and the hour it first appears.

Hints:

  • Several events can fall on the same hour; merge adds them into one number, so ends and starts at the same time cancel.

interviewQA: What is a TreeMap and how is it implemented?
A sorted NavigableMap implemented as a red-black tree: a self-balancing binary search tree that keeps keys ordered and guarantees O(log n) get, put, remove and navigation.
Time complexity of TreeMap operations?
get, put, remove, containsKey, floorKey, ceilingKey, firstKey, lastKey: O(log n). Iteration is O(n) in key order; containsValue is O(n).
How does TreeMap decide whether two keys are equal?
With compareTo or the Comparator returning 0; equals() and hashCode() are not used.
Can TreeMap have null keys or values?
No null keys with natural ordering (NullPointerException); null values are allowed.
What happens when keys are not Comparable?
ClassCastException when you put the first key, unless you pass a Comparator.
Explain floorKey, ceilingKey, lowerKey and higherKey.

lowerKey: greatest key strictly less; floorKey: greatest key <=; ceilingKey: smallest key >=; higherKey: smallest key strictly greater. They return null if no such key exists. The *Entry versions return the entry.
What do headMap, tailMap and subMap return?
Live range views: headMap(to) keys before to, tailMap(from) keys from from onwards, subMap(from, to) from inclusive to exclusive; overloads allow inclusivity flags.
HashMap vs TreeMap?
HashMap: unordered, O(1), one null key, equals/hashCode. TreeMap: sorted by key, O(log n), no null keys, compareTo/Comparator, navigation and range views.
How do you sort a HashMap by key and by value?
By key: new TreeMap<>(hashMap). By value: put the entries in a list and sort it with Map.Entry.comparingByValue(), or stream entrySet().sorted(...) into a LinkedHashMap.
Is TreeMap thread-safe?
No. Use ConcurrentSkipListMap or Collections.synchronizedSortedMap.
What is a consistent-with-equals comparator and why does it matter?
It returns 0 only when equals() is true. Otherwise a TreeMap treats keys that equals() says are different as the same key and replaces values.
How do you get entries in descending key order?
descendingMap() (or reversed() in Java 21), or construct the TreeMap with Comparator.reverseOrder().

topics.name: Hashtable

beginner.content:
What is a Hashtable?

Hashtable is the original (Java 1.0) key-value store. It works like a HashMap but every method is synchronized, and it refuses null keys and values. Today it is a legacy class: you will meet it in old code and interviews, but new code should use HashMap (single thread) or ConcurrentHashMap (many threads).

  • Package java.util. Extends the old Dictionary class and implements Map.
  • Thread-safe: each method locks the whole table, so only one thread works at a time.
  • No null key and no null value: put(null, x) and put(k, null) throw NullPointerException.
  • No guaranteed order, and it iterates in a different order from HashMap.
  • Default capacity 11, load factor 0.75, grows to 2 * old + 1.
  • Index = (hash & 0x7FFFFFFF) % table.length. Buckets are plain linked lists (no tree conversion).
  • Legacy extras: keys(), elements() (Enumeration) and contains().

Where Hashtable sits in the Collection Framework

Map
(I)
Dictionary
(c)
← extends Dictionary, implements Map
Hashtable
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. Properties extends Hashtable and is used for configuration files.

Creating a Hashtable: four constructors

  • new Hashtable<>(): capacity 11, load factor 0.75.
  • new Hashtable<>(int capacity): chosen start size.
  • new Hashtable<>(int capacity, float loadFactor): both chosen.
  • new Hashtable<>(Map m): copy of another map.

All Hashtable methods at a glance

Every method is synchronized.

MethodWhat it doesTime
put(k, v)Add or replace a pair (no nulls)O(1) average
get(k)Value for a key, or null if absentO(1) average
remove(k)Delete a key and return its valueO(1) average
containsKey(k)Is the key present?O(1) average
containsValue(v) / contains(v)Is the value present? (the same thing)O(n)
size() / isEmpty() / clear()Count, emptiness check, delete allO(1) / O(n)
putIfAbsent, getOrDefault, replace, merge, compute...Java 8 Map methods (atomic here)O(1) average
keys() / elements()Legacy Enumeration of keys / valuesO(1) to create
keySet() / values() / entrySet()Live views for loopsO(n)
putAll(map) / clone()Copy pairs / shallow copyO(n)
equals / hashCode / toStringCompare and printO(n)

Benefits and advantages

For freshers: a Hashtable is the old, built-in "safe for threads" cousin of HashMap. You will meet it in older code and in Properties files. Why it can still be useful:

  • Thread-safe out of the box. Every method is synchronized, so two threads cannot corrupt the table by writing at the same moment.
  • Simple to reason about. One lock, one rule: only one thread uses the table at a time.
  • No hidden nulls. Null keys and null values are rejected, so get returning null always means "key not found".
  • Fast lookup. Like HashMap, get and put are O(1) on average.
  • Base of Properties. java.util.Properties, used for configuration files, extends Hashtable.
  • Works with old APIs. Code written before Java 2 uses Dictionary and Enumeration; Hashtable fits it.
  • For experienced developers: single-method calls are atomic (put, get, and the Java 8 overrides merge, putIfAbsent, compute are synchronized), and its iterators are fail-fast. It is a perfectly correct choice for a small, low-contention shared table.

Disadvantages and when NOT to use it

For freshers: Hashtable is mostly kept for old code. For new code there are better tools:

  • Slow under load. One lock for the whole table: while one thread works, all other threads wait, even for plain reads.
  • No nulls. put(null, x) or put(x, null) throws NullPointerException.
  • Legacy design. It has old methods (keys(), elements(), contains()) that return Enumeration, and it extends the obsolete Dictionary class.
  • Not truly safe for "check then act". Each call is atomic, but if (!t.containsKey(k)) t.put(k, v) is two calls, and another thread can sneak in between.
  • No order and no sorting; iteration order looks odd (from the end of the table).
  • For experienced developers: prefer ConcurrentHashMap (lock striping, lock-free reads, atomic compute family) for shared maps and HashMap for single-threaded code. Hashtable's whole-table lock also makes iteration while writing from another thread throw ConcurrentModificationException.

Quick guide:

Use a Hashtable whenUse something else when
You maintain old code or work with PropertiesYou write new code: HashMap or ConcurrentHashMap
A small table is shared by a few threads, rarelyMany threads read and write often: ConcurrentHashMap
You want null keys and values rejectedYou need null values: HashMap
Simple "one lock for everything" safety is enoughYou need sorted keys: TreeMap (or ConcurrentSkipListMap for threads)

intermediate.content:
Adding and reading

The basic methods, with the null rules that set Hashtable apart.

1. put(K key, V value)

  • Signature: V put(K key, V value)
  • Returns: the old value, or null for a new key
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: Stores the pair. Putting an existing key replaces its value and returns the old one. Neither the key nor the value may be null.

For experienced developers: It locks the whole table. The key must implement hashCode and equals correctly. A null key fails at key.hashCode(); a null value is explicitly rejected.

2. get(Object key), getOrDefault and containsKey

  • Signature: V get(Object key); V getOrDefault(Object key, V default); boolean containsKey(Object key)
  • Returns: the value / default / boolean
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: get returns the value for a key or null when it is absent. Because values can never be null, null always means "no such key": a small advantage over HashMap.

For experienced developers: getOrDefault avoids the null check. get(null) throws NullPointerException.

3. remove(Object key), size(), isEmpty() and clear()

  • Signature: V remove(Object key); boolean remove(Object key, Object value); int size(); boolean isEmpty(); void clear()
  • Returns: old value / boolean / count
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: remove(key) deletes a pair and returns the old value (or null). The two-argument form deletes only when the value also matches. clear() empties the table.

For experienced developers: After clear() the internal array keeps its size; only the entries go.

4. containsValue(Object) and contains(Object)

  • Signature: boolean containsValue(Object value); boolean contains(Object value)
  • Returns: boolean
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Both ask "does any pair have this value?". contains is the legacy name and does exactly the same as containsValue.

For experienced developers: It scans every bucket, so it is slow on big tables. Beware: contains checks values, not keys, which surprises people used to Collection.contains.

Java 8 methods

The same atomic helpers as HashMap, and in Hashtable each one is also synchronized.

5. putIfAbsent, replace, merge and computeIfAbsent

  • Signature: V putIfAbsent(K, V); V replace(K, V); V merge(K, V, BiFunction); V computeIfAbsent(K, Function)
  • Returns: the previous / new value
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: putIfAbsent adds only a missing key; replace changes only an existing key; merge combines the old and new value (word counts, totals); computeIfAbsent builds a value only when the key is absent.

For experienced developers: In a Hashtable each of these runs under the table lock, so the check-and-act sequence is atomic. That is a real benefit, but ConcurrentHashMap gives the same safety with far less blocking.

Looping

Three ways: the modern views, forEach, and the legacy Enumeration.

6. keySet(), values(), entrySet() and forEach()

  • Signature: Set keySet(); Collection values(); Set> entrySet(); void forEach(BiConsumer)
  • Returns: live views
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Loop over the keys, the values, or the pairs. The views are live: removing through them removes from the table.

For experienced developers: The order is not insertion order and not the same as a HashMap's. These iterators are fail-fast (as in HashMap), so changing the table inside a for-each throws ConcurrentModificationException.

7. keys() and elements() (legacy Enumeration)

  • Signature: Enumeration keys(); Enumeration elements()
  • Returns: an Enumeration
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: The Java 1.0 way to loop. An Enumeration has just hasMoreElements() and nextElement(). You will see it in old code.

For experienced developers: Unlike an Iterator, an Enumeration has no remove() and is not fail-fast. Prefer keySet() and entrySet() in new code.

8. putAll(Map), clone, equals and toString

  • Signature: void putAll(Map); Object clone(); boolean equals(Object); String toString()
  • Returns: copy / comparison / text
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: putAll copies all pairs from another map, clone makes a shallow copy, equals compares the pairs, toString prints {k=v, ...}.

For experienced developers: A clone copies the table but shares the key and value objects. Two maps are equal when they hold the same pairs, whatever their class.

Master program: every Hashtable method in one place

One single program that uses all the Hashtable methods you learned above, step by step. Read the numbered comments from top to bottom, run it, and match each output line with its step.

Module: Sorting methods

For freshers: a Hashtable has no order and no sort method. To see its data sorted, copy it into something that can be sorted. For experienced developers: copying through entrySet() or new TreeMap<>(table) is safe because those methods hold the table lock while they copy; the sorting itself then runs on your private copy with no locking.

9. Sort by key: copy into a TreeMap

  • Signature: new TreeMap<>(Map m)
  • Returns: a new TreeMap sorted by key
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: The easiest sort: build a TreeMap from the Hashtable. The TreeMap keeps the keys A to Z.

For experienced developers: The Hashtable itself is unchanged. Because the copy is private, other threads can keep using the Hashtable while you print or process the sorted copy.

10. Sorted key list: Collections.list + sort

  • Signature: Collections.list(Enumeration) / Collections.sort(List)
  • Returns: a sorted List of the keys
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: The old keys() method gives an Enumeration. Collections.list turns it into a normal list that you can sort. Then look up each value with get.

For experienced developers: In modern code you can write new ArrayList<>(table.keySet()) instead. Use Collections.list(table.keys()) when you are given an Enumeration from a legacy API.

11. Sort by value: stream into a LinkedHashMap

  • Signature: entrySet().stream().sorted(comparingByValue()).collect(toMap(..., LinkedHashMap::new))
  • Returns: a new LinkedHashMap in value order
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: To order the pairs by value (for example the busiest fort first), stream the entries, sort, and collect into a LinkedHashMap, which remembers the order.

For experienced developers: The stream works on a snapshot taken from entrySet(). The result is a plain LinkedHashMap: it is no longer thread-safe, which is fine for printing a report.

12. Sorted values: ArrayList of values + sort

  • Signature: new ArrayList<>(table.values()); list.sort(...)
  • Returns: a sorted List of the values
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: If you only need the values in order (not the keys), copy values() into a list and sort the list.

For experienced developers: Duplicates stay in the list, so the same value can appear many times. Use Comparator.reverseOrder() for biggest first.

Which sorting approach to pick?

You wantUseResult
Pairs sorted by keynew TreeMap<>(table)sorted map copy
Only the keys, sortedCollections.list(table.keys()) + sortsorted list
Pairs sorted by valuestream + sorted + LinkedHashMapordered map copy
Only the values, sortednew ArrayList<>(table.values()) + sortsorted list

Module: Finding (searching) methods

For freshers: finding by key is instant. Hashtable also has old-style search methods (contains, keys, elements) that you will see in legacy code. For experienced developers: every call takes the table lock, so a long scan blocks other threads; copy to a list first when the scan is heavy.

13. get, getOrDefault and containsKey (no null keys)

  • Signature: V get(Object key) / boolean containsKey(Object key)
  • Returns: the value (or null), or true/false
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: Look up by key. A missing key gives null. A Hashtable never stores null, so null always means "not found". Asking for a null key itself throws NullPointerException.

For experienced developers: Unlike HashMap, even the lookup methods throw on a null key because hashCode() is called on it. Methods are synchronized, so lookups from different threads wait for each other.

14. contains and containsValue: find a value

  • Signature: boolean contains(Object value) / boolean containsValue(Object value)
  • Returns: true if some key has this value
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: contains(value) is the old method that looks for a value (not a key!). containsValue does exactly the same and is the name used by every other Map.

For experienced developers: The names confuse beginners: contains checks values, containsKey checks keys. In new code always write containsValue. Both scan the whole table.

15. keys() and elements(): search with an Enumeration

  • Signature: Enumeration keys() / Enumeration elements()
  • Returns: an Enumeration over the keys / values
  • Time: O(n) to walk

For freshers: The old way to walk a Hashtable. Loop with hasMoreElements() and nextElement() and test each item.

For experienced developers: An Enumeration has no remove, and it is not fail-fast the way an Iterator is. Prefer keySet().iterator() or a stream in new code.

16. Find the key for a value

  • Signature: for (Map.Entry e : table.entrySet())
  • Returns: a matching key, or null
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: A Hashtable goes from key to value only. To go backwards, loop over the entries and compare values.

For experienced developers: If several keys share the value, the one you reach first depends on the internal table, so do not rely on it. Collect all matches and sort them if you need a stable answer.

17. Stream filter and max/min entry

  • Signature: entrySet().stream().filter(...) / Collections.max(entrySet, comparingByValue())
  • Returns: matching entries / the entry with the biggest value
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Describe the search as a rule and let the stream do the loop. Collections.max finds the entry with the largest value.

For experienced developers: entrySet() of a Hashtable is a synchronized view; streaming over it while another thread writes can throw ConcurrentModificationException. Copy first (new ArrayList<>(table.entrySet())) if writers are active.

Which finding method to pick?

QuestionMethodTime
Value for a key / is the key thereget, getOrDefault, containsKeyO(1)
Is a value therecontainsValue (avoid the old contains)O(n)
Walk and test every key or valuekeys() / elements() (legacy) or keySet() / values()O(n)
Which keys have this valueloop over entrySet()O(n)
Entries matching a rule, or the biggeststream().filter, Collections.maxO(n)

expert.content:
How Hashtable works inside

The structure is the one HashMap started from.

  • An array of Entry nodes; each bucket is a singly linked list (never converted to a tree, unlike HashMap since Java 8).
  • Bucket index = (key.hashCode() & 0x7FFFFFFF) % table.length. The modulo works on any size, so the default is the prime-ish number 11, not a power of two.
  • Rehash when count >= threshold (capacity x 0.75): new length = old * 2 + 1, and every entry is re-linked.
  • New entries are inserted at the head of the bucket list.
  • Locking: every public method is synchronized on the table itself. Reads block writes and other reads, so a busy table becomes a bottleneck.
  • Because hashCode() is called on the key without a null check, a null key throws NPE.

Trap: a synchronized table is not a synchronized program

  • Each method is atomic, but a check-then-act sequence made of two methods is not: another thread can slip in between containsKey and put.
  • Use the atomic methods (putIfAbsent, merge, computeIfAbsent) or hold your own lock around the whole sequence.

Real example: loading configuration with Properties

Properties extends Hashtable and holds String to String settings, with a default value for missing keys.

Hashtable versus HashMap versus ConcurrentHashMap versus synchronizedMap

HashtableHashMapConcurrentHashMapCollections.synchronizedMap
Thread-safeYes (whole-table lock)NoYes (fine-grained / lock-free reads)Yes (one lock)
null keyNoOneNoDepends on the wrapped map
null valueNoYesNoDepends on the wrapped map
Speed (many threads)SlowFastest (single thread)FastSlow
Bucket structureLinked listList then treeList then treeAs wrapped
Default capacity111616As wrapped
StatusLegacyCurrentCurrentCurrent

Best practices

Know Hashtable, but do not choose it for new code.

  • Single thread: HashMap. Many threads: ConcurrentHashMap.
  • Keep Hashtable only when an old API forces it (for example Properties or an older library).
  • Never rely on a particular iteration order.
  • Do not combine containsKey and put to "add if missing": use putIfAbsent.
  • Do not modify a table while looping over it (fail-fast).

Real-time examples

Three jobs where a small, thread-safe, no-nulls table is a reasonable fit, especially in older code bases.

Scenario 1: Login session store

For freshers: after login, the server gives each user a token and keeps token to user name in a table. Each web request looks the token up. A Hashtable is safe if several request threads use it. For experienced developers: because nulls are rejected, get(token) == null reliably means "not logged in". For a busy server use ConcurrentHashMap with expiry.

Scenario 2: Application settings with Properties

For freshers: Properties is a Hashtable whose keys and values are Strings. It is the standard way to hold settings such as a title or a port. getProperty lets you give a default. For experienced developers: Properties extends Hashtable<Object, Object>, so you can call put with non-String values by mistake; always use setProperty and getProperty.

Scenario 3: Thread-safe visit counter

For freshers: four counter threads each add 1000 visits to the same table. Because every Hashtable method is synchronized and merge is a single call, no visit is lost. For experienced developers: a plain HashMap in this test can lose updates or even corrupt itself, and the total would change from run to run. Here the total is always 4000 per fort.

Sample project: Thread-safe Trek Seat Booking

What we build: four booking-desk threads fight for the last seats of three forts. A shared Hashtable holds the seats left, and a lock makes "check the seats, then reduce them" one atomic step.

Steps:

  • Step 1: create the seat table (fort to seats left).
  • Step 2: write a booking method that checks and reduces seats inside synchronized (seats); this is the "check then act" fix.
  • Step 3: create four desk threads; each tries 15 bookings for every fort.
  • Step 4: count booked and rejected requests with AtomicInteger.
  • Step 5: start the threads, wait with join, and print the totals: no seat is sold twice.

Read the step comments in the program, run it, then extend it with your own idea.

Practice questions

Now test yourself. Each question is harder than the examples above: read the problem, write your own solution, then compare it with the one shown. Every solution was compiled and run, and its output is real.

Practice question 1: Visitor counters shared by threads (atomic merge, legacy Enumeration)

Level: Medium

Problem: Old code that must be thread-safe still uses Hashtable. Here three threads count visitors per fort in one shared table (using the atomic merge), and the same table is then read with the legacy Enumeration API.

Your task:

  1. merge is atomic, so three threads never lose a count.
  2. keys() and elements() read the table the old way.
  3. A null key or value is rejected: the program shows the exception.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 2: Merge and invert legacy inventories

Level: Medium

Problem: Two old systems each keep a Hashtable of trek-gear stock. Merge them (adding the counts of items that appear in both), then build the inverse table: for each count, which items have it.

Your task:

  1. Merge with merge(key, count, Integer::sum).
  2. Invert: a Hashtable<Integer, List<String>>, count to item names (sorted).
  3. Print the merged table and the inverse in key order.

Hints:

  • A Hashtable has no order, so copy it into a TreeMap only when you print.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 3: Safe lookup helper for a table that rejects nulls

Level: Easy

Problem: A helper must never crash, whatever the caller passes. Write fee(Hashtable, String fort) that returns the fee, or -1 if the fort is missing or the name is null.

Your task:

  1. Return -1 at once for a null name (a Hashtable throws NullPointerException for it).
  2. Otherwise use getOrDefault.
  3. Test with a known fort, an unknown fort and null.

Hints:

  • Both a null key and a null value throw NullPointerException in a Hashtable.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 4: Hashtable or HashMap? Compare how they behave

Level: Medium

Problem: Run the same four operations on a Hashtable and a HashMap and print what each does: put a null key, put a null value, call get for a missing key, and remove during a for-each loop.

Your task:

  1. Write a small helper that runs an action and prints "ok" or the name of the exception.
  2. Call it for each operation and each map.
  3. Read the table of results and decide which map you would choose for a shared settings table.

Hints:

  • The for-each loop uses an iterator that checks for changes; removing through the map (not the iterator) is detected.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 5: Atomic withdrawal: why check-then-act needs a lock

Level: Medium

Problem: A fort has 100 tickets in a Hashtable. Ten threads each try to take 20 tickets one at a time. Make sure exactly 100 are sold and the stock never goes below zero.

Your task:

  1. Write a sell() method that does get and put inside synchronized (stock).
  2. Start 10 threads, join them, then print sold and left.
  3. Explain in a comment why the lock is needed even though each Hashtable call is synchronized.

Hints:

  • synchronized (stock) uses the same lock that the Hashtable methods use, so no thread can slip in between your get and put.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 6: Predict the enumeration order of a Hashtable

Level: Hard

Problem: A Hashtable stores a key at index (hashCode & 0x7FFFFFFF) % capacity (default capacity 11), puts a new entry at the front of a bucket's chain, and keys() walks the buckets from the last index to the first. Predict the order for six Integer keys with your own code, then check it against the real table.

Your task:

  1. Build the six buckets by hand with a list of LinkedLists, inserting each key at the front of its bucket.
  2. Produce the predicted order by reading buckets 10 down to 0.
  3. Compare it with Collections.list(table.keys()) and print whether they match.
  4. Also compute when the table first grows: threshold = capacity x 0.75, and the new capacity is old * 2 + 1.

Hints:

  • An Integer's hash code is the number itself.
  • Keys 3, 14 and 25 all land in bucket 3 because 14 % 11 = 3 and 25 % 11 = 3.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

interviewQA: What is a Hashtable?
A legacy (Java 1.0) synchronized hash-based Map. It allows no null keys or values and has no guaranteed order.
Difference between HashMap and Hashtable?

Hashtable is synchronized (slow), forbids null keys and values, is legacy and extends Dictionary; HashMap is not synchronized, allows one null key and many null values, is faster and uses tree bins for long collision chains.
Why does Hashtable not allow null?
A null key fails on key.hashCode(); a null value is rejected so that get() returning null can only mean "key absent", which is safe to use in multi-threaded code.
Is Hashtable thread-safe? Is that enough?
Each method is, but compound actions such as containsKey then put are not atomic. Use putIfAbsent / merge / computeIfAbsent or external locking.
What is the default capacity and growth of Hashtable?
Capacity 11, load factor 0.75, new capacity = old * 2 + 1.
How is the bucket index computed?
(hashCode & 0x7FFFFFFF) % table.length. HashMap instead spreads the hash and uses (n - 1) & hash on a power-of-two table.
Hashtable vs ConcurrentHashMap?
ConcurrentHashMap locks only parts of the table (CAS and per-bin locks), reads are non-blocking and it scales; Hashtable locks the whole table for every call.
What is the difference between Enumeration and Iterator?
Enumeration is the legacy read-only cursor without remove() and without fail-fast behaviour; Iterator can remove and is fail-fast.
What is Properties?
A subclass of Hashtable for String to String settings, with getProperty(key, default), and load/store for .properties files.
Is Hashtable ordered?
No. Use LinkedHashMap for insertion order or TreeMap for sorted order.
How do you make a HashMap thread-safe?
Use ConcurrentHashMap (preferred) or wrap with Collections.synchronizedMap.

topics.name: Comparable Interface

beginner.content:
What is Comparable?

Comparable gives a class its natural order: the one default way two objects of that class are compared. It has a single method, compareTo. Once a class implements it, Collections.sort, Arrays.sort, TreeSet, TreeMap, PriorityQueue and stream().sorted() all know how to order it.

  • Package java.lang (no import needed). The interface is Comparable<T>.
  • One method: int compareTo(T other), implemented inside the class being sorted.
  • Return negative if this object comes first, zero if equal in order, positive if this comes later.
  • String, Integer, Long, Double, Character, LocalDate, BigDecimal and enums are already Comparable.
  • There can be only one natural order per class. For other orders use Comparator.

Where Comparable sits

Comparable<T>
(I)
← implements
String / Integer / LocalDate ...
(c)
← implements
Your class (Fort)
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. It is not part of the Collection hierarchy but sorted collections depend on it.

The contract in one picture

compareTo returnsMeaningExample
Negativethis comes before other"Raigad".compareTo("Torna") is negative
Zerosame position in the order"Torna".compareTo("Torna") is 0
Positivethis comes after other"Torna".compareTo("Raigad") is positive

Benefits and advantages

For freshers: Comparable teaches Java how to put your own objects in order, once, so you never repeat it.

  • Write once, sort everywhere: after compareTo exists, Collections.sort, Arrays.sort, TreeSet, TreeMap, PriorityQueue and stream().sorted() all work with no extra argument.
  • Short calls: Collections.sort(list) reads better than passing a comparator each time.
  • Natural meaning: the order lives next to the data, so any reader finds "what is the default order of a Fort?" in one place.
  • Binary search and range queries (binarySearch, floor, ceiling) just work on sorted data.
  • Built into the JDK: String, Integer, LocalDate and enums already have it.

For experienced developers: the natural order is part of the type contract. TreeMap, PriorityQueue and the sort algorithms (TimSort, dual-pivot quicksort) call compareTo directly with no lambda indirection, and a consistent order lets you rely on set semantics.

Disadvantages and when NOT to use it

  • Only one order per class. Need name today and salary tomorrow? Comparable cannot do both.
  • You must edit the class. You cannot add it to String, to a library class or to a record from another team.
  • Hidden coupling: if someone changes compareTo, every TreeSet, sorted list and binary search that relied on it changes silently.
  • Easy to get wrong: subtraction overflow, ignoring tie-breakers, or being inconsistent with equals.
  • It is a poor fit when the "right" order depends on the screen, the user or the report. Use a Comparator there.

For experienced developers: a wrong or mutable-field compareTo is worse than none, because a TreeSet silently loses elements and sort can throw "Comparison method violates its general contract".

When to use which: Comparable or Comparator

SituationPickWhy
One obvious default order (id, name, date)ComparableZero extra arguments at every call site
Several orders (name, salary, city)ComparatorAny number of orders, kept outside the class
Class belongs to a libraryComparatorYou cannot edit the source
Used as a TreeMap / TreeSet keyEitherComparable is shorter; Comparator allows a different order per collection
Order depends on user choice at run timeComparatorChoose or build it on demand

intermediate.content:
Making your own class Comparable

Implement Comparable<YourClass> and write compareTo.

1. compareTo(T other)

  • Signature: int compareTo(T other)
  • Returns: negative, zero or positive int
  • Time: depends on your code

For freshers: Compare the field you want to sort by. Use the helper methods Integer.compare, Double.compare, String.compareTo instead of subtracting.

For experienced developers: Never write return this.x - other.x: the subtraction can overflow for large or negative values and give the wrong sign. Integer.compare(this.x, other.x) is always correct.

2. Sorting with the natural order

  • Signature: Collections.sort(list); Arrays.sort(array); list.sort(null); stream.sorted()
  • Returns: sorted in place / a sorted stream
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Every sorting tool uses compareTo when you do not give a Comparator. If the class is not Comparable you get a ClassCastException at run time.

For experienced developers: list.sort(null) means "use the natural order". The sort is stable for objects: equal elements keep their relative order.

3. Sorted collections: TreeSet, TreeMap, PriorityQueue

  • Signature: new TreeSet<>(); new TreeMap<>(); new PriorityQueue<>()
  • Returns: sorted containers
  • Time: O(log n) per add

For freshers: These containers keep elements ordered as you add them, using compareTo. A TreeSet of Comparable forts therefore prints in order and rejects duplicates.

For experienced developers: Here compareTo also decides duplicates: a TreeSet treats two objects as the same when compareTo returns 0, even if equals says they differ.

Choosing the field

The natural order is your decision: name, number, date. Pick the one that is most obviously "the" order.

4. Comparing by a number: descending and ascending

  • Signature: Integer.compare(a, b); Double.compare(a, b); Long.compare(a, b)
  • Returns: negative, zero or positive
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: For ascending order write Integer.compare(this.x, other.x). For descending swap the arguments: Integer.compare(other.x, this.x).

For experienced developers: A natural order should be obvious. If readers could argue about whether "natural" means height or name, keep the natural order simple and use a Comparator for the rest.

5. Comparing by two fields (tie-breaker)

  • Signature: if (first != 0) return first; return second
  • Returns: negative, zero or positive
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: When the first field is equal, compare a second one. This keeps the order total and avoids accidental duplicates in a TreeSet.

For experienced developers: Write the tie-break by hand as below, or build it with Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...) and call it from compareTo.

Module: Sorting methods

For freshers: "sorting" means putting items in order. Because your class is Comparable, each tool below knows how to do it without being told. For experienced developers: all of them end in compareTo; object sorts use stable TimSort (O(n log n)), tree containers cost O(log n) per insert, and a heap gives O(log n) offer / poll.

6. compareTo(T other): the engine behind every sort

  • Signature: int compareTo(T other)
  • Returns: negative, zero or positive
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: It answers one question: "should I come before, with, or after the other object?" Everything else is built on that answer.

For experienced developers: Use Integer.compare for numbers. For descending order swap the two operands.

7. Collections.sort(List<T>)

  • Signature: static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> void sort(List<T> list)
  • Returns: void (list sorted in place)
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: The classic way to sort a list of Comparable objects. The list itself is changed.

For experienced developers: It copies to an array, runs TimSort and writes back. The element type must be Comparable or the call does not compile.

8. List.sort(null)

  • Signature: default void sort(Comparator<? super E> c)
  • Returns: void (list sorted in place)
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: The instance version of the same sort. Passing null means "use the natural order".

For experienced developers: ArrayList overrides it to sort its internal array directly (no copy). Prefer it over Collections.sort in new code.

9. Arrays.sort(T[])

  • Signature: static void sort(Object[] a); static void sort(Object[] a, int from, int to)
  • Returns: void (array sorted in place)
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Sorts an array of objects by compareTo. You can sort only a range with the from / to version.

For experienced developers: For object arrays it is stable TimSort. For primitive arrays (int[]) it is dual-pivot quicksort and the question of stability does not arise.

10. stream().sorted()

  • Signature: Stream<T> sorted()
  • Returns: a new sorted stream
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Sorts without changing the original list: you get a new sorted result. Add .toList() to collect it.

For experienced developers: It is a stateful intermediate operation: it must see all elements before emitting the first. Elements must be Comparable, otherwise a ClassCastException is thrown at run time.

11. TreeSet and TreeMap (always sorted)

  • Signature: new TreeSet<>(); new TreeMap<>()
  • Returns: a container kept sorted
  • Time: O(log n) per add / put

For freshers: You do not call sort at all: every element goes into its correct place when added, and printing shows the order.

For experienced developers: Backed by a red-black tree. compareTo == 0 means "same element", so equal-ordered objects are merged.

12. PriorityQueue (sorted by removal)

  • Signature: new PriorityQueue<>(); poll(); peek()
  • Returns: smallest element first
  • Time: O(log n) offer / poll

For freshers: A queue that always hands out the smallest element first. Great for "next task" and "top N".

For experienced developers: It is a binary heap in an array. Printing the queue is not in sorted order; only poll() is. It is a min-heap by compareTo.

Sorting methods: which one to pick

NeedUseChanges original?Cost
Sort a list oncelist.sort(null) / Collections.sortYesO(n log n)
Sort an arrayArrays.sort(array)YesO(n log n)
Sorted copy, keep originalstream().sorted().toList()NoO(n log n)
Always sorted, many insertsTreeSet / TreeMapn/aO(log n) per add
Only the next smallest, repeatedlyPriorityQueuen/aO(log n) per poll

Module: Finding (searching) methods

For freshers: once objects have an order, you can find the biggest, the smallest, or one exact item quickly. For experienced developers: binary search needs a list already sorted by the same order (O(log n) on an ArrayList, O(n) walking on a LinkedList); max/min are a single O(n) pass; tree containers answer nearest-neighbour questions in O(log n).

13. Collections.binarySearch(list, key)

  • Signature: static int binarySearch(List<? extends Comparable<? super T>> list, T key)
  • Returns: index if found; otherwise -(insertion point) - 1
  • Time: O(log n) on ArrayList

For freshers: Finds an item by halving the search area each step. The list must already be sorted. A negative result means "not found".

For experienced developers: On a sorted list with duplicates, which index you get is unspecified. The negative result tells you where to insert: -(result) - 1.

14. Arrays.binarySearch(array, key)

  • Signature: static int binarySearch(Object[] a, Object key)
  • Returns: index if found; otherwise -(insertion point) - 1
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: The same idea for arrays. Sort the array first with Arrays.sort.

For experienced developers: Searching an unsorted array gives undefined results, not an exception, so always sort first or keep the array sorted.

15. Collections.max(c) and Collections.min(c)

  • Signature: static T max(Collection<? extends T> c); static T min(Collection<? extends T> c)
  • Returns: the largest / smallest element
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Walk the whole collection once and return the biggest (or smallest) by compareTo. No sorting needed.

For experienced developers: Throws NoSuchElementException on an empty collection. For a single pass it is cheaper than sorting.

16. stream().max(...) and min(...)

  • Signature: Optional<T> max(Comparator<? super T> c); min(...)
  • Returns: an Optional (empty if no elements)
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Streams need to be told the order, so pass Comparator.naturalOrder() (which uses compareTo). The answer arrives inside an Optional.

For experienced developers: The Optional avoids the exception of Collections.max on empty input. Use orElse or ifPresent.

17. sorted().findFirst()

  • Signature: Optional<T> findFirst()
  • Returns: first element of the sorted stream
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Sort, then take the first one: a way to find "the smallest that matches a rule". Add a filter before it.

For experienced developers: For just one smallest element min is O(n) and better; use sorted + findFirst only when you also need more of the order.

18. TreeSet: first, last, floor, ceiling

  • Signature: first(); last(); floor(e); ceiling(e); lower(e); higher(e)
  • Returns: an element or null
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: floor = biggest element at or below the value, ceiling = smallest at or above it. Handy for "nearest" questions.

For experienced developers: lower / higher are the strict versions. They return null (not an exception) when nothing qualifies, unlike first() on an empty set.

19. TreeMap: floorKey, ceilingEntry, firstEntry

  • Signature: floorKey(k); ceilingEntry(k); firstEntry(); lastEntry()
  • Returns: a key / entry or null
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: Same nearest-key idea for maps. Useful for slabs and ranges such as "which tax band does this salary fall in?".

For experienced developers: Combine with headMap / tailMap / subMap for range views that need no copying.

Finding methods: which one to pick

QuestionUseNeeds sorted input?Cost
Biggest or smallestCollections.max / min, stream.max / minNoO(n)
Is X present, and where?binarySearchYesO(log n)
Nearest value at or below / aboveTreeSet.floor / ceilingKept sortedO(log n)
Band or range lookupTreeMap.floorEntryKept sortedO(log n)
Smallest that passes a rulefilter + minNoO(n)

expert.content:
Rules of a correct compareTo

Sorting algorithms assume these rules. Breaking them gives wrong order or IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract.

  • Antisymmetry: sign(a.compareTo(b)) == -sign(b.compareTo(a)).
  • Transitivity: if a < b and b < c then a < c.
  • Consistency: if a.compareTo(b) == 0 then a and b compare the same way against every other object.
  • Consistent with equals (strongly recommended): a.compareTo(b) == 0 exactly when a.equals(b). Otherwise TreeSet / TreeMap and HashSet / HashMap disagree about duplicates.
  • compareTo(null) should throw NullPointerException.
  • Never compare floating-point with - or by casting; use Double.compare (it also orders NaN and -0.0 correctly).

Trap: inconsistent with equals

A class that sorts by one field but defines equals on another behaves differently in a TreeSet and a HashSet.
Trap: subtraction overflows

Real example: a sorted fort register

A record can implement Comparable too, so a few lines give a fully ordered value type.

Comparable versus Comparator

ComparableComparator
Packagejava.langjava.util
MethodcompareTo(T other) (one object)compare(T a, T b) (two objects)
Where writtenInside the class being sortedOutside, in its own class / lambda
How many ordersOne (the natural order)As many as you like
Can sort classes you cannot editNoYes
Used by defaultsort(), TreeSet, TreeMap, PriorityQueueOnly when you pass it in

Best practices

Keep the natural order simple and correct.

  • Implement Comparable only when one order is clearly "the" order (name, id, date).
  • Always use Integer.compare / Double.compare, never subtraction.
  • Keep compareTo consistent with equals and hashCode.
  • Compare the same fields in equals and compareTo; add a tie-breaker field if needed.
  • Use Comparator for any extra orders and for classes you cannot modify.
  • Do not use mutable fields in compareTo for objects stored in a TreeSet or TreeMap.

Real-time examples

Three small, realistic programs. Each class is Comparable, so every tool in the lesson works on it without extra arguments.

Example 1: Employees by salary, then name

For freshers: the highest salary comes first; when two salaries are equal, the name decides. For experienced developers: the tie-breaker keeps the order total, so a TreeSet will not drop two employees with the same salary.

Example 2: Product catalogue by price

A shop lists products cheapest first. We find the cheapest, the dearest, and the best product that fits a budget with floor.

Example 3: Student rank list

Rank 1 is the highest marks. Students with equal marks share a rank, so we compare marks only when giving a rank but use name to keep the order stable.

Sample project: Fort Register

What we build: a console register of forts whose natural order is district A to Z, tallest first, then name.

  • Step 1: define a Fort record that implements Comparable.
  • Step 2: load the data and sort it with Collections.sort.
  • Step 3: keep it in a TreeSet and ask for neighbours with floor / ceiling.
  • Step 4: find the exact fort with binarySearch on the sorted list.
  • Step 5: use a PriorityQueue to print the first three forts in order, and Collections.max for the last.

Practice questions

Now test yourself. Each question is harder than the examples above: read the problem, write your own solution, then compare it with the one shown. Every solution was compiled and run, and its output is real.

Practice question 1: Fort register: natural order drives sort, TreeSet and binary search

Level: Medium

Problem: A register class declares one natural order (by fort name). The same compareTo then makes sorting, a sorted set, min / max and binarySearch work with no extra code.

Your task:

  1. Implement Comparable<Fort> once.
  2. Collections.sort, max / min and binarySearch reuse it.
  3. A TreeSet stores the forts sorted and rejects the same name twice.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 2: Fort ranking with a full natural order

Level: Hard

Problem: Define the natural order of a Fort: district A to Z, then height highest first, then name. Use it for sorting, for removing duplicates with a TreeSet and for finding the top 3 with a PriorityQueue.

Your task:

  1. Implement Comparable<Fort> with the three-level rule (use Integer.compare).
  2. Sort a list with Collections.sort.
  3. Put the list in a TreeSet: forts that compare as equal (same district, height and name) must collapse into one.
  4. Use a PriorityQueue (a min-heap on the same order) and print the first 3 polled.

Hints:

  • Swap the two arguments of Integer.compare to get "highest first".
  • A record gives you equals that agrees with compareTo here, because all three fields are compared.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 3: City distance list with binary search

Level: Easy

Problem: A trip planner stores cities with their distance from Pune. The natural order is distance, nearest first.

Your task:

  1. Create record City(String name, int km) implements Comparable<City> using Integer.compare.
  2. Sort a list of five cities with list.sort(null) and print it.
  3. Use Collections.binarySearch with a probe new City("?", 450) to find the city that is 450 km away.
  4. Print the farthest city with Collections.max.

Hints:

  • The probe only needs the field that compareTo uses.
  • A negative binarySearch result means "not found".

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 4: Version numbers: 1.10 is bigger than 1.9

Level: Medium

Problem: Plain string comparison says "1.9" is bigger than "1.10". Build a Version class that compares numerically part by part.

Your task:

  1. Create class Version implements Comparable<Version> that parses a text such as "1.10.2" into an int[].
  2. In compareTo compare part by part; a missing part counts as 0 (so 1.2 equals 1.2.0).
  3. Sort five versions and print them. Also show that "1.9" sorts after "1.10" as plain strings.
  4. Print the newest version using Collections.max.

Hints:

  • Loop to the longer length and treat a missing index as 0.

Practice question 5: compareTo consistent with equals

Level: Medium

Problem: Two products are "the same" when their code is the same. Make compareTo, equals and hashCode agree, then prove it with a TreeSet and a HashSet.

Your task:

  1. Create a Product class with code and name; compareTo, equals and hashCode must all use only code.
  2. Add three products, two of them with the same code, to both a TreeSet and a HashSet.
  3. Print both sizes (they must match).
  4. Call compareTo(null) inside try/catch and print which exception is thrown.

Your task:

  2. Add six tasks to a PriorityQueue and poll them all, printing the run order.
