interviewQA: What is the Comparable interface?
A java.lang interface with one method, compareTo, that defines the natural ordering of a class; sorted collections and sort methods use it by default.
What does compareTo return?
Negative if this is less than the argument, zero if equal in order, positive if greater.
Comparable vs Comparator?
Comparable is implemented inside the class (one natural order, compareTo(T)); Comparator is a separate object (many orders, compare(T, T)) and works on classes you cannot edit.
What happens if a class is not Comparable and you put it in a TreeSet?
ClassCastException at run time when the first element is added (unless a Comparator was supplied).
Why not use subtraction in compareTo?
It can overflow and return the wrong sign. Use Integer.compare / Double.compare.
What does "consistent with equals" mean?
compareTo returns 0 exactly when equals returns true. If not, TreeSet/TreeMap and HashSet/HashMap treat duplicates differently.
Which built-in classes are Comparable?
String, the wrapper classes (Integer, Long, Double, Character...), BigInteger, BigDecimal, LocalDate/LocalDateTime, enums (by ordinal) and more.
How do you sort in descending order using Comparable?
Swap the operands in compareTo, or leave the natural order and sort with Collections.reverseOrder() / a reversed Comparator.
Can a class have more than one natural order?
No: compareTo gives exactly one. Use Comparators for other orders.
Is Collections.sort stable?
Yes for objects (it uses TimSort): equal elements keep their original relative order.

topics.name: Comparator Interface

beginner.content:
What is a Comparator?

A Comparator is a small object that says how to order two objects, kept outside the class. Use it when a class has no natural order, when you cannot edit the class, or when you need several different orders (by name, by height, by trek time...).

  • Package java.util. The interface is Comparator<T>.
  • The one abstract method: int compare(T a, T b) (negative: a first, zero: equal, positive: b first). Because there is only one, a Comparator can be written as a lambda.
  • Many ready-made helper methods (comparing, thenComparing, reversed, naturalOrder, nullsFirst...) build comparators in one line.
  • Pass it to list.sort(c), Collections.sort(list, c), Arrays.sort(a, c), new TreeSet<>(c), new TreeMap<>(c), new PriorityQueue<>(c) and stream.sorted(c).

Where Comparator sits

Comparator<T>
(I)
← implemented by
Lambda / method reference
(c)
← returned by
Comparator.comparing(...) results
(c)

(I) = interface, (c) = class. Comparator is a @FunctionalInterface.

Your first Comparator: three ways to write the same thing

  • Anonymous class: the long, classic form.
  • Lambda: (a, b) -> a.name().compareTo(b.name()).
  • Helper method: Comparator.comparing(Fort::name): shortest and clearest.

All Comparator methods at a glance

MethodWhat it does
compare(a, b)The one abstract method: orders two objects
Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor)Order by a field (any Comparable)
comparing(keyExtractor, keyComparator)Order by a field with your own comparator for it
comparingInt / comparingLong / comparingDoubleOrder by a primitive field, no boxing
thenComparing(...)Tie-breaker when the first order says equal
thenComparingInt / Long / DoubleTie-breaker on a primitive field
reversed()The opposite order
Comparator.naturalOrder() / reverseOrder()compareTo order / its opposite
Comparator.nullsFirst(c) / nullsLast(c)Handle null elements safely
Collections.reverseOrder()Reverse of the natural order (older style)
equals(obj)Inherited; rarely used

Benefits and advantages

For freshers: a Comparator lets you decide the order at the moment you sort, without touching the class.

  • Many orders for one class: name, height, trek time, each as its own comparator.
  • Works on classes you cannot edit, including String, library classes and records from other modules.
  • Short and readable: Comparator.comparing(Fort::name).thenComparing(Fort::district) reads almost like English.
  • Choose the order at run time: let the user pick "sort by price" or "sort by rating" from a menu.
  • Different order per collection: one TreeSet by name, another by height, same objects.

For experienced developers: comparators are values. You can store them in constants or a Map, compose them, pass them across layers, and unit-test each one. Being functional, they plug straight into streams, TreeMap and PriorityQueue constructors.

Disadvantages and when NOT to use it

  • You must remember to pass it. Forget it and Java uses the natural order, or throws ClassCastException when none exists.
  • Easy to build a wrong one: subtraction overflow, missing tie-breakers, a reversed() that flips more than you meant.
  • Scattered rules: if the same comparator is copied in ten places, they drift apart.
  • A TreeSet comparator decides duplicates, which surprises people who only wanted a display order.
  • If a class really has one obvious default order that everybody expects, implement Comparable as well and keep comparators for the extra orders.

For experienced developers: a comparator that reads mutable state or is inconsistent breaks TimSort ("Comparison method violates its general contract") or silently corrupts a TreeMap. Keep them pure and total.

When to use which: Comparator or Comparable

SituationPickWhy
Sort by name now, by height laterComparatorOne class, several orders
The class is from a libraryComparatorYou cannot add compareTo
Order is obvious and permanentComparableShorter calls, default for TreeSet
Sort a Map by its valuesComparatorMap.Entry.comparingByValue()
Case-insensitive, null-safe or custom text orderComparatorWrap or replace the natural order

intermediate.content:
Building comparators with comparing()

Name the field and let Java do the comparing.

1. Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor)

  • Signature: static <T, U extends Comparable> Comparator<T> comparing(Function<T, U> keyExtractor)
  • Returns: a Comparator
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: Pass a method reference to the field you want to sort by. The result orders objects by that field using its natural order (strings A to Z, numbers small to large).

For experienced developers: The key must be Comparable. For an int field prefer comparingInt (no boxing).

2. comparingInt, comparingLong and comparingDouble

  • Signature: static Comparator<T> comparingInt(ToIntFunction<T>); comparingLong(...); comparingDouble(...)
  • Returns: a Comparator
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: Same as comparing but for int, long and double fields, without boxing every value into an object. Use them for numbers.

For experienced developers: Numbers sort ascending by default: smallest first. Add .reversed() for largest first.

3. reversed()

  • Signature: default Comparator<T> reversed()
  • Returns: the opposite Comparator
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Turns any comparator around: ascending becomes descending. Call it on a ready comparator.

For experienced developers: With a lambda comparator, Java may not infer the type, so write Comparator.comparingInt(Fort::heightMetres).reversed() (works) rather than starting from an untyped lambda.

4. thenComparing(...) and thenComparingInt(...)

  • Signature: default Comparator<T> thenComparing(Comparator / Function); thenComparingInt(ToIntFunction)
  • Returns: a Comparator with a tie-breaker
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: Sort by one field first, then break ties with another: district, then name. Chain as many as you need.

For experienced developers: The later comparators are used only when all earlier ones return 0. Add .reversed() after a single step to reverse just that step, not the whole chain.

5. comparing(keyExtractor, keyComparator)

  • Signature: static Comparator<T> comparing(Function<T, U> key, Comparator<U> keyComparator)
  • Returns: a Comparator
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: Compare by a field using your own rule for that field, for example case-insensitive text or reverse order.

For experienced developers: String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER is a ready comparator for text that ignores upper and lower case.

6. naturalOrder(), reverseOrder() and Collections.reverseOrder()

  • Signature: static Comparator<T> naturalOrder(); static Comparator<T> reverseOrder(); Collections.reverseOrder()
  • Returns: a Comparator
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: naturalOrder() uses compareTo; reverseOrder() is its opposite. They are handy for TreeSet, PriorityQueue and sorting lists of strings or numbers.

For experienced developers: Collections.reverseOrder() does the same as Comparator.reverseOrder() (the older way). Collections.reverseOrder(c) reverses any comparator.
codeExamples:
// naturalOrder / reverseOrder with lists, TreeSet and PriorityQueue
import java.util.ArrayList;      // imports the ArrayList class
import java.util.Collections;    // imports the Collections class
import java.util.Comparator;     // imports the Comparator class
import java.util.List;           // imports the List class
import java.util.PriorityQueue;  // imports the PriorityQueue class
import java.util.TreeSet;        // imports the TreeSet class

public class ComparatorNaturalReverseDemo {         // class that holds the main method
    public static void main(String[] args) {        // program entry point
        List<Integer> altitudes = new ArrayList<>(List.of(800, 100, 1200, 400));  // creates an ArrayList filled with the listed values
        altitudes.sort(Comparator.reverseOrder());  // sorts using the given comparator
        System.out.println("List, high to low : " + altitudes);  // prints a label followed by the value

        TreeSet<String> cities = new TreeSet<>(Collections.reverseOrder());  // creates a TreeSet named cities copied from Collections.reverseOrder()
        cities.addAll(List.of("Pune", "Nagpur", "Mumbai"));   // adds every element of List.of("Pune", "Nagpur", "Mumbai... to the set
        System.out.println("TreeSet, Z to A   : " + cities);  // prints a label followed by the value

        PriorityQueue<Integer> queue = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());  // max-heap
        queue.addAll(List.of(5, 9, 2));  // adds every element of List.of(5, 9, 2) to the queue
        System.out.println("Max-heap poll     : " + queue.poll());  // prints the removed element
    }
}
// OUTPUT:
// List, high to low : [1200, 800, 400, 100]
// TreeSet, Z to A   : [Pune, Nagpur, Mumbai]
// Max-heap poll     : 9

intermediate.content:
7. nullsFirst(c) and nullsLast(c)

  • Signature: static Comparator<T> nullsFirst(Comparator<T>); static Comparator<T> nullsLast(Comparator<T>)
  • Returns: a null-safe Comparator
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Normal comparators throw NullPointerException on a null element or key. These wrappers place the nulls at the start or at the end and use your comparator for the rest.

For experienced developers: Use them whenever a sort key can be missing (an optional district, an unset date).

Where comparators are used

The same comparator works everywhere ordering is needed.

8. Sorted containers and streams

  • Signature: new TreeSet<>(c); new TreeMap<>(c); new PriorityQueue<>(c); stream.sorted(c); Collections.max(list, c)
  • Returns: ordered containers / sorted stream
  • Time: O(log n) per add, O(n log n) to sort

For freshers: Hand the comparator to the container or to the stream and it orders (and finds the biggest and smallest) by your rule.

For experienced developers: In a TreeSet or TreeMap the comparator also decides what counts as a duplicate, so include enough fields (a tie-breaker) to keep different objects apart.

9. A comparator as a reusable class

  • Signature: class ByHeight implements Comparator<Fort>
  • Returns: a named comparator
  • Time: O(1) per compare

For freshers: When the same order is used in many places, or has some logic, give it a name: a small class (or a static final constant) that implements Comparator.

For experienced developers: A named comparator can be unit-tested and reused. A static final Comparator<Fort> constant inside the class is a neat middle path.

Module: Sorting methods

For freshers: a Comparator is a ruler you hand to a sorting tool. Below is every method that builds or uses a comparator for sorting, each with one small program. For experienced developers: the builders (comparing, thenComparing, reversed) return new comparators and cost O(1) to create; the consumers (sort, sorted, TreeMap, PriorityQueue) invoke compare O(n log n) times in total.

10. compare(a, b): the one abstract method

  • Signature: int compare(T a, T b)
  • Returns: negative, zero or positive
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: You give it two objects and it tells which should come first. A lambda can supply it directly.

For experienced developers: Prefer Integer.compare(a, b) over a - b: subtraction can overflow and give the wrong sign.

11. Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor)

  • Signature: static Comparator<T> comparing(Function<T, U> keyExtractor)
  • Returns: a Comparator
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: Say which field to sort by with a method reference. Java compares that field in its natural order.

For experienced developers: The field must be Comparable; for primitives use the Int / Long / Double versions to avoid boxing.

12. comparingInt / comparingLong / comparingDouble

  • Signature: static Comparator<T> comparingInt(ToIntFunction<T>)
  • Returns: a Comparator
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: The number-friendly version of comparing. It reads an int, long or double straight from the object.

For experienced developers: No boxing means fewer allocations in a hot sort. comparingDouble uses Double.compare, so NaN and -0.0 are ordered consistently.

13. thenComparing(...)

  • Signature: default Comparator<T> thenComparing(Comparator<T> other) / thenComparing(Function key)
  • Returns: a Comparator with a tie-breaker
  • Time: O(1) to create

For freshers: When two objects tie on the first rule, the next rule decides. You can chain as many as you like.

For experienced developers: The second comparator runs only when the first returns 0, so cheap and selective rules should come first.

14. reversed()

  • Signature: default Comparator<T> reversed()
  • Returns: the opposite Comparator
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Flips ascending into descending. Call it on a finished comparator.

For experienced developers: It reverses the whole chain it is called on. To reverse only one step, wrap that step: thenComparing(Comparator.comparingInt(...).reversed()).

15. naturalOrder() and reverseOrder()

  • Signature: static Comparator<T> naturalOrder(); static Comparator<T> reverseOrder()
  • Returns: a Comparator
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Ready-made comparators for objects that are already Comparable: A to Z / small to large, and the opposite.

For experienced developers: Handy as the "key comparator" in comparing(key, keyComparator) and in nullsFirst.

16. nullsFirst(c) and nullsLast(c)

  • Signature: static Comparator<T> nullsFirst(Comparator<? super T> c); nullsLast(...)
  • Returns: a null-safe Comparator
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Normal comparators crash on null. These wrappers put missing values at the start or end of the order.

For experienced developers: Combine with a key extractor: comparing(Fort::district, nullsLast(naturalOrder())) handles a null field, not just a null element.

17. Map.Entry.comparingByKey() and comparingByValue()

  • Signature: static Comparator<Map.Entry<K,V>> comparingByValue()
  • Returns: a Comparator for map entries
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: A Map cannot be sorted itself, but its entries can. Sort the entries by value to build a "top list".

For experienced developers: Pass a comparator for the value: comparingByValue(Comparator.reverseOrder()) gives highest first.

18. list.sort(c) and Collections.sort(list, c)

  • Signature: void sort(Comparator<? super E> c); static void sort(List<T> list, Comparator<? super T> c)
  • Returns: void (list sorted in place)
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Two ways to say the same thing: sort this list using this comparator. list.sort is the modern one.

For experienced developers: Collections.sort(list, c) simply calls list.sort(c). Both are stable.

19. Arrays.sort(T[], c)

  • Signature: static <T> void sort(T[] a, Comparator<? super T> c)
  • Returns: void (array sorted in place)
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Sort an array of objects by your rule. It does not work on int[]: use Integer[] if you need a comparator.

For experienced developers: A comparator is not accepted for primitive arrays on purpose. Box the array or sort and then reverse.

20. stream().sorted(c)

  • Signature: Stream<T> sorted(Comparator<? super T> c)
  • Returns: a new sorted stream
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Gives you a sorted copy and leaves the source list alone. Chain limit for "top N".

For experienced developers: It is stateful and not lazy: it buffers everything. For only the top N of a huge stream consider a bounded PriorityQueue.

21. TreeSet / TreeMap with a Comparator

  • Signature: new TreeSet<>(c); new TreeMap<>(c)
  • Returns: a container sorted by your rule
  • Time: O(log n) per add

For freshers: Give the comparator to the constructor and the container keeps that order forever.

For experienced developers: The comparator also defines equality: compare == 0 means the same key. Include a tie-breaker or distinct items disappear.

22. PriorityQueue with a Comparator

  • Signature: new PriorityQueue<>(c)
  • Returns: a heap ordered by your rule
  • Time: O(log n) per offer / poll

For freshers: The element that comes first by the comparator leaves first. Use reverseOrder() for a max-heap.

For experienced developers: Only poll() and peek() follow the order; iteration and toString show the raw heap array.

Sorting with a Comparator: which one to pick

NeedUseNotes
Sort a list in placelist.sort(c)Stable; modern form
Sort an object arrayArrays.sort(array, c)Object arrays only
Sorted copy, keep sourcestream().sorted(c)Add limit(n) for top N
Always-sorted collectionnew TreeSet<>(c) / TreeMapComparator also defines duplicates
Repeatedly take the next onenew PriorityQueue<>(c)Heap: only poll is ordered
Sort a map by valueMap.Entry.comparingByValue()Sort the entry list, not the map
Build the comparatorcomparing, thenComparing, reversedCompose small pieces

Module: Finding (searching) methods

For freshers: the same comparator that sorts can also find the biggest, the smallest, or one exact item. For experienced developers: binary search must use the same comparator the list was sorted with; max / min are single passes; tree containers answer nearest-neighbour queries in O(log n).

23. Collections.max(c, comparator) and min

  • Signature: static T max(Collection<? extends T> c, Comparator<? super T> comp)
  • Returns: the largest / smallest by your rule
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: Gives the biggest or smallest object by any rule, with no sorting.

For experienced developers: Throws NoSuchElementException on an empty collection. The smallest by a reversed comparator is the largest by the original.

24. stream().max(c) and min(c)

  • Signature: Optional<T> max(Comparator<? super T> c)
  • Returns: an Optional
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: The streams version. The answer comes in an Optional, so an empty list is handled without an exception.

For experienced developers: Use orElse, orElseThrow or ifPresent to unwrap it.

25. filter + findFirst after sorted(c)

  • Signature: Stream.filter(p).sorted(c).findFirst()
  • Returns: an Optional
  • Time: O(n log n)

For freshers: Narrow the data, order it, take the first: "the quickest trek in Pune".

For experienced developers: For a single best element filter(p).min(c) is O(n) and does the same job cheaper.

26. Collections.binarySearch(list, key, c)

  • Signature: static int binarySearch(List<? extends T> list, T key, Comparator<? super T> c)
  • Returns: index, or -(insertion point) - 1
  • Time: O(log n) on ArrayList

For freshers: Fast exact search. The list must be sorted with the same comparator you pass here.

For experienced developers: Mismatched order gives silent wrong answers, not errors. The key only has to carry the fields the comparator looks at.

27. Arrays.binarySearch(T[], key, c)

  • Signature: static <T> int binarySearch(T[] a, T key, Comparator<? super T> c)
  • Returns: index, or -(insertion point) - 1
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: The array version. The array must be sorted by the same comparator.

For experienced developers: For a descending array pass a descending comparator, otherwise the search goes the wrong way.

28. TreeSet floor / ceiling with a Comparator

  • Signature: floor(e); ceiling(e); lower(e); higher(e)
  • Returns: an element or null
  • Time: O(log n)

For freshers: "Nearest" questions, in the order of the comparator you gave the TreeSet.

For experienced developers: The probe object only needs the fields the comparator reads.

Finding with a Comparator: which one to pick

QuestionUseSorted first?
Biggest / smallest by a ruleCollections.max / min(c) or stream.max / min(c)No
Smallest that passes a testfilter(p).min(c)No
Is this value present?binarySearch(list, key, c)Yes, same comparator
Nearest above / belowTreeSet(c).floor / ceilingKept sorted
Many lookups by one keyA HashMap indexed by that keyNot needed

expert.content:
Rules of a correct comparator

The same contract as compareTo, and the sorting algorithm depends on it.

  • Antisymmetric: sign(compare(a, b)) == -sign(compare(b, a)).
  • Transitive: if a < b and b < c then a < c.
  • A broken comparator can make sort throw IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract, or silently give a wrong order.
  • Avoid subtraction: a.x - b.x overflows. Use Integer.compare.
  • It should be consistent with equals when used in a TreeSet or TreeMap, or two "different" objects will be merged.
  • Sorting objects is stable (TimSort); sorting primitives is not stable but it does not matter there.
Trap: reversed() applies to the whole chain
Trap: a TreeSet comparator that is too loose

Real example: grouping and ranking

Comparators combine with streams to answer "rank the forts" questions in a few lines.

Comparator versus Comparable

ComparatorComparable
Methodcompare(a, b)compareTo(other)
WhereSeparate object / lambdaInside the class
Orders per classManyOne
Works on classes you cannot editYesNo
Helper methodscomparing, thenComparing, reversed, nullsFirst...None
Packagejava.utiljava.lang

Best practices

Build comparators from small pieces.

  • Prefer Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...) over hand-written compare methods.
  • Use comparingInt / Long / Double for primitive fields; never subtract.
  • Add a tie-breaker so the order is total, especially for TreeSet and TreeMap.
  • Use nullsFirst / nullsLast when keys can be null.
  • Keep reusable comparators as static final constants and give them clear names.
  • Remember that reversed() reverses the entire chain built so far.

Real-time examples

Three small, realistic programs where one class needs several orders. A Comparator makes each order a single line.

Example 1: Employees by department, salary and name

For freshers: the report groups by department, shows the highest paid first inside each, and uses the name when salaries are equal. For experienced developers: only the salary step is reversed, thanks to the nested reversed().

Example 2: Product catalogue with a sort menu

Each menu choice is just a different comparator stored in a map. The page picks one at run time.

Example 3: Student rank list with missing marks

Some students were absent, so their marks are null. They must appear at the bottom, not crash the sort.

Sample project: Employee Report Builder

What we build: a console report tool where every report is a named Comparator.

  • Step 1: define the Employee record (with a nullable bonus).
  • Step 2: build reusable comparators as constants and register them by name in a LinkedHashMap.
  • Step 3: run each report on a copy of the data using list.sort.
  • Step 4: answer questions with max / min and a top-N stream.
  • Step 5: sort by id and look an employee up with binarySearch; use a TreeSet to find the next salary band.

Practice questions

Now test yourself. Each question is harder than the examples above: read the problem, write your own solution, then compare it with the one shown. Every solution was compiled and run, and its output is real.

Practice question 1: Sort menu for a fort table (name, height, district then trek time)

Level: Medium

Problem: A web page shows a table of forts with a "Sort by" menu. Each menu choice is just a different Comparator held in a Map, so adding a new sort needs one line.

Your task:

  1. Keep the sort options in a LinkedHashMap<String, Comparator>.
  2. Build them with comparing / thenComparing / reversed.
  3. Apply the chosen comparator to the same list with list.sort.
  4. nullsLast keeps forts without a district at the bottom.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 2: Booking report with a custom status order

Level: Hard

Problem: Sort booking records by status priority (CONFIRMED, then WAITING, then CANCELLED: not alphabetical), then by trek date, newest first, then by name with missing names last.

Your task:

  1. Describe the status order with a list and indexOf, or with an enum.
  2. Build one Comparator with comparing, thenComparing, reversed and nullsLast.
  3. Print the sorted table.

Hints:

  • Enums compare by their declaration order, which is exactly the priority you want.
  • Put .reversed() on the date comparator itself, not at the end of the whole chain.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 3: Sort city names by length and then alphabet

Level: Easy

Problem: A signboard painter wants city names ordered shortest first, and alphabetical when the length is equal.

Your task:

  1. Create a list of six Indian cities.
  2. Sort it with Comparator.comparingInt(String::length).thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()).
  3. Print the list, then print it again in the exact opposite order using reversed().
  4. Print the longest city with Collections.max and the same comparator.

Hints:

  • The longest name that is alphabetically last wins under this order.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 4: Employees with an optional bonus

Level: Medium

Problem: Some employees have no bonus (null). Show the best bonuses first, people without a bonus last, and use salary then name for ties.

Your task:

  1. Create record Employee(String name, int salary, Double bonus).
  2. Build the comparator with comparing(Employee::bonus, nullsLast(reverseOrder())) followed by salary (high first) and name.
  3. Sort and print each employee with the bonus or "no bonus".
  4. Also print the employee with the highest salary using a stream max.

Hints:

  • Comparator.<Double>reverseOrder() gives the compiler the type it needs.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 5: Top 3 most frequent words

Level: Medium

Problem: Count how often each fort name appears in a list, then print the three most frequent. Ties are broken alphabetically.

Your task:

  1. Count the words into a HashMap<String, Integer> using merge.
  2. Copy the entries into a list.
  3. Sort the entries by value (high first) then by key, using Map.Entry.comparingByValue(Comparator.reverseOrder()).thenComparing(Map.Entry.comparingByKey()).
  4. Print the first three.

Hints:

  • HashMap order is not sorted, so the explicit tie-breaker is what makes the output stable.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 6: Natural file-name order: Fort2 before Fort10

Level: Hard

Problem: Plain text sorting puts "Fort10" before "Fort2". Write a Comparator<String> that splits a name into a text part and a number part, and compares the number numerically.

Your task:

  1. Write a static method that splits "Fort10" into the letters ("Fort") and the number (10).
  2. Compare the letters first; if equal, compare the numbers with Integer.compare.
  3. Sort a shuffled list (use new Random(7)) and print the result, next to the plain text sort.
  4. Check the contract: sort the same data from two different shuffles and show both results are identical.

Hints:

  • replaceAll("[0-9]+$", "") removes the trailing digits.
  • A correct comparator gives the same sorted result from any starting order.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.
codeExamples:
// Practice: a hand-written natural-order comparator
import java.util.ArrayList;    // imports the ArrayList class
import java.util.Collections;  // imports the Collections class
import java.util.Comparator;   // imports the Comparator class
import java.util.List;         // imports the List class
import java.util.Random;       // imports the Random class

public class CpPracticeNaturalOrder {        // class that holds the main method
    static String letters(String s) {        // method letters()
        return s.replaceAll("[0-9]+$", "");  // text before the trailing digits
    }

    static int number(String s) {                          // method number()
        String digits = s.substring(letters(s).length());  // stores the value in digits
        return digits.isEmpty() ? 0 : Integer.parseInt(digits);  // returns the result to the caller
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {  // program entry point
        Comparator<String> natural = Comparator.comparing(CpPracticeNaturalOrder::letters)
                .thenComparingInt(CpPracticeNaturalOrder::number);
        List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Fort10", "Fort2", "Fort1", "Gad3", "Fort21", "Gad10", "Fort3"));  // creates an ArrayList filled with the listed values

        List<String> first = new ArrayList<>(names);   // creates an ArrayList named first copied from names
        Collections.shuffle(first, new Random(7));     // shuffles the elements randomly
        first.sort(natural);                           // sorts using the given comparator
        List<String> second = new ArrayList<>(names);  // creates an ArrayList named second copied from names
        Collections.shuffle(second, new Random(99));   // shuffles the elements randomly
        second.sort(natural);                          // sorts using the given comparator

        List<String> plain = new ArrayList<>(names);       // creates an ArrayList named plain copied from names
        Collections.sort(plain);                           // sorts the list (natural order or the given comparator)
        System.out.println("Plain text sort : " + plain);  // prints a label followed by the value
        System.out.println("Natural order   : " + first);  // prints a label followed by the value
        System.out.println("Same result from another shuffle: " + first.equals(second));  // prints the comparison result
    }
}
// OUTPUT:
// Plain text sort : [Fort1, Fort10, Fort2, Fort21, Fort3, Gad10, Gad3]
// Natural order   : [Fort1, Fort2, Fort3, Fort10, Fort21, Gad3, Gad10]
// Same result from another shuffle: true

interviewQA: What is a Comparator?
A functional interface with compare(a, b) that defines an ordering outside the class; it can be passed to sort methods and sorted collections.
Comparable vs Comparator?
Comparable: one natural order inside the class (compareTo). Comparator: any number of external orders (compare), usable on classes you cannot modify.
Is Comparator a functional interface?
Yes (@FunctionalInterface): it has one abstract method, compare, so lambdas and method references work. equals is inherited from Object and does not count.
How do you sort by two fields?
Comparator.comparing(A::x).thenComparing(A::y).
How do you sort in descending order?
Add .reversed() to a comparator, or use Comparator.reverseOrder() for natural order. Be careful that reversed() reverses the whole chain built so far.
How do you sort a list containing nulls?
Wrap with Comparator.nullsFirst(c) or nullsLast(c).
Why use comparingInt instead of comparing?
It avoids boxing each int into an Integer, so it is faster and uses less memory.
What exception can a bad comparator cause?
IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract (from TimSort), or a wrong order without any error.
How does a Comparator affect a TreeSet?
It decides both the order and equality: elements for which compare returns 0 are duplicates and only one is kept.
How do you create a max-heap PriorityQueue?
new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder()) or Collections.reverseOrder().
Is sorting a list of objects stable?
Yes, list.sort and Collections.sort use TimSort, which is stable.

topics.name: Internal Working of HashSet

beginner.content:
The big idea: a HashSet is a HashMap

A HashSet does not have its own storage. Inside it holds a HashMap; every element you add becomes a key of that map, and the value is always the same dummy object. So "a Set has no duplicates" is really "a Map has no duplicate keys".

  • Field: private transient HashMap<E, Object> map;
  • Field: private static final Object PRESENT = new Object(); (the shared dummy value)
  • add(e) is map.put(e, PRESENT) == null: it returns true only if the key was new.
  • contains(e) is map.containsKey(e); remove(e) is map.remove(e) == PRESENT.
  • Everything you learnt about HashMap (buckets, collisions, resize, treeification) applies unchanged. See Internal Working of HashMap.

What each HashSet method really calls

HashSet methodDoes this insideTime
add(e)map.put(e, PRESENT) == nullO(1) average
contains(o)map.containsKey(o)O(1) average
remove(o)map.remove(o) == PRESENTO(1) average
size()map.size()O(1)
isEmpty()map.isEmpty()O(1)
clear()map.clear()O(capacity)
iterator()map.keySet().iterator()O(1) to start

Benefits of understanding how HashSet works inside

For freshers: you do not need this to use a HashSet, but it explains the rules you are told to follow, so they stop feeling like magic.

  • You will know why equals and hashCode must go together, instead of just memorising it.
  • You can explain the odd behaviour of order: the output order comes from buckets, not from adding order.
  • You will avoid lost elements: changing an object after adding it moves its "address", and the set cannot find it any more.
  • You can pick a good initial capacity and avoid needless resizing in big programs.
  • Interviews: "How does HashSet work internally?" is one of the most asked Java questions, and the answer is the same as HashMap.

For experienced developers: it lets you diagnose real problems: slow lookups from a degenerate hashCode, memory growth from a once-large set, and heisenbugs from mutable keys. The same model carries over to HashMap, HashTable and ConcurrentHashMap.

intermediate.content:
A HashSet built by hand

Wrapping a HashMap gives you a complete HashSet in a few lines.

1. MiniHashSet: add, contains, remove

  • Signature: class MiniHashSet<E> { private final HashMap<E, Object> map; }
  • Returns: a working set
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: This is almost exactly the real source of java.util.HashSet. The three core methods are one-line calls to the map; the shared PRESENT object saves memory because no per-element value is created.

For experienced developers: The real class has the same shape. Its constructors only differ in the capacity and load factor they pass to the backing map.

2. How a duplicate is detected

  • Signature: hash(e) -> bucket -> equals()
  • Returns: true / false
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: When you add an element, the backing map hashes it, goes to the bucket, and compares with every node there: first by hash, then by == or equals. A match means "duplicate": the map keeps the old key and add returns false.

For experienced developers: Note: when a duplicate is rejected, the old object stays in the set; the new one is thrown away. This matters if the two objects are equal but not identical.

3. Missing hashCode makes duplicates appear

  • Signature: equals() overridden, hashCode() not overridden
  • Returns: a set with duplicates
  • Time: wrong

For freshers: If you override only equals, two "equal" objects usually hash into different buckets, so the set never compares them and keeps both.

For experienced developers: Fix: always override hashCode with the same fields as equals. A record gets both for free.

Constructors and capacity

Each constructor just configures the backing map.

4. Constructors and the 0.75 / 16 defaults

  • Signature: new HashSet<>(); new HashSet<>(int cap); new HashSet<>(int cap, float load); new HashSet<>(Collection c)
  • Returns: a set
  • Time: O(1) / O(n)

For freshers: new HashSet<>() creates new HashMap<>() (capacity 16, load factor 0.75). The copy constructor sizes the map as max((int)(c.size() / .75f) + 1, 16) so that copying does not trigger a resize.

For experienced developers: Because the backing map has lazy allocation, the array of buckets is created only on the first add.

Ordering and iteration

The order of a HashSet is the order of the backing map's buckets.

5. Why the order looks random

  • Signature: iteration = map.keySet(): bucket 0 .. n-1
  • Returns: elements in bucket order
  • Time: O(n + capacity)

For freshers: Elements come out in bucket order, which depends on hash codes and the table size, not on the order you added them. After a resize the order can change.

For experienced developers: Never depend on this order. If you need one, use LinkedHashSet (insertion order, whose backing map is a LinkedHashMap) or TreeSet (sorted, backed by a TreeMap).

6. null in a HashSet and fail-fast iterators

  • Signature: add(null) and for-each + add()
  • Returns: allowed / ConcurrentModificationException
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: A HashSet allows one null element (HashMap allows a null key, stored in bucket 0). Its iterator is fail-fast through the map's modCount: adding or removing during a loop throws ConcurrentModificationException.

For experienced developers: Remove during iteration with iterator.remove() or removeIf.

expert.content:
The real source of java.util.HashSet (simplified)

The implementation is so small that its core fits in this list.

  • public boolean add(E e) { return map.put(e, PRESENT) == null; }
  • public boolean contains(Object o) { return map.containsKey(o); }
  • public boolean remove(Object o) { return map.remove(o) == PRESENT; }
  • public Iterator<E> iterator() { return map.keySet().iterator(); }
  • public int size() { return map.size(); }
  • clone() copies the backing map; serialization writes the elements, capacity and load factor (the map field is transient).
  • A package-private constructor HashSet(int, float, boolean dummy) creates a LinkedHashMap: that is how LinkedHashSet reuses all of HashSet.

Memory: why PRESENT matters

  • Each HashSet element costs one HashMap.Node (about 32 bytes: header, hash, key, value, next) plus its slot in the table. The value field points to the one shared PRESENT object, so it adds nothing.
  • A set of 1 million small objects therefore needs tens of megabytes just for the nodes. If memory is tight and keys are small integers, a BitSet or a primitive-collection library is far smaller.

Mutating an element after adding it

The bucket is chosen when the element is added. If the fields used by hashCode change afterwards, the element sits in the wrong bucket and contains cannot find it any more.

HashSet versus LinkedHashSet versus TreeSet: the map behind each

HashSetLinkedHashSetTreeSet
Backing mapHashMapLinkedHashMapTreeMap (via NavigableMap)
OrderNoneInsertionSorted
add / contains / removeO(1)O(1)O(log n)
Duplicate testhashCode + equalshashCode + equalscompareTo / Comparator
Null elementOneOneNo (natural order)
Extra memory per elementNodeNode + 2 linksTree node (larger)

Best practices

Everything about HashSet follows from the HashMap inside it.

  • Elements must implement equals and hashCode consistently (or be records / strings / numbers / enums).
  • Use immutable elements, or never change fields used by hashCode while the object is in a set.
  • Presize a large set: new HashSet<>((int) (n / 0.75f) + 1) (or HashSet.newHashSet(n) in Java 19+).
  • Do not rely on iteration order; choose LinkedHashSet or TreeSet if order matters.
  • For thread safety use ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() or Collections.synchronizedSet.

Real-time examples

Two classic production problems, shown on small data so you can see the cause.

Example 1: a bad hashCode makes every element collide

For freshers: hashCode picks the bucket. If every object returns the same number, all of them go into one bucket, and the set has to compare a new element with each one already there. It still works, but slowly.

For experienced developers: with 6 keys in one bucket the comparisons are 0+1+2+3+4+5 = 15. For n keys it is about n squared / 2 until the bin treeifies (at 8 nodes and 64 buckets), after which Comparable keys search in O(log n). Non-Comparable keys stay slow.

Example 2: the lost trek group (mutable element)

For freshers: a group object is added to a set. Later someone changes the group's city. The set stored the group in the bucket for the old city, so it cannot find it any more, though it is still inside.

For experienced developers: the safe pattern is to remove the element, change it, and add it again, or to use immutable elements. The element is not lost from memory, just unreachable by hash, so it is also a memory leak.

Sample project: a HashSet-like class with buckets

What we build: a tiny set of Strings written by hand, so you can see buckets, collisions and resizing.

  • Step 1: an array of buckets; each bucket is a chain (linked list) of nodes.
  • Step 2: a simple hash (sum of the characters) and index = hash % buckets.length.
  • Step 3: add checks contains first, then inserts at the head of the chain.
  • Step 4: when the set is more than 75% full, resize doubles the array and re-places every node.
  • Step 5: show prints each bucket so you can see collisions.

Practice questions

Now test yourself. Each question is harder than the examples above: read the problem, write your own solution, then compare it with the one shown. Every solution was compiled and run, and its output is real.

Practice question 1: Why a bad hashCode makes a HashSet slow

Level: Hard

Problem: Two key classes are identical except for hashCode: one returns the same number for every object, the other spreads the keys. Add 2000 keys to a HashSet of each and compare how many buckets are really used (estimate it from the hashes), then check that both sets still find every key.

Your task:

  1. Create BadKey (hashCode always 7) and GoodKey (hashCode from its number), both with correct equals.
  2. Count the distinct bucket indexes (h ^ (h >>> 16)) & 4095 that 2000 keys fall into.
  3. Check that contains still returns true for every key in both sets (the bad set is slow, not wrong).

Hints:

  • BadKey is Comparable, so Java 8+ turns the long chain into a tree: the set stays correct, and lookups are O(log n) instead of O(n).
  • In a real program you would measure the time with a benchmark tool such as JMH; do not trust one stopwatch run.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 2: Two different Strings with the same hash code

Level: Easy

Problem: The Strings "Aa" and "BB" have the same hashCode(). Add both to a HashSet and show that the set still keeps them apart.

Your task:

  1. Print the hash codes of both Strings.
  2. Add both to a HashSet and print the size.
  3. Check contains for each one, and explain in a comment which method separates them.

Hints:

  • The hash code only picks the bucket; equals decides "same or different" inside it.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

Practice question 3: Which bucket does each city go to?

Level: Medium

Problem: For a HashSet with 16 buckets, compute the bucket index of each city the way HashMap does: h = key.hashCode(), h ^ (h >>> 16), then index = (16 - 1) & h. Group the cities by bucket and report which buckets have a collision.

Your task:

  1. Write a method bucketOf(String key, int tableLength).
  2. Fill a TreeMap<Integer, List<String>> from bucket index to cities.
  3. Print each bucket and mark buckets that hold more than one city.

Hints:

  • The table length must be a power of two for the bit mask to work like a modulo.
  • Try changing tableLength to 8 or 64 and watch the collisions change.

Try it on your own first. The program below is one complete solution, with the real output it prints.

interviewQA: How does HashSet work internally?
It wraps a HashMap: each element is a key and the value is a shared dummy object PRESENT. add is map.put(e, PRESENT) == null.
How does HashSet avoid duplicates?
The backing HashMap cannot hold duplicate keys: it compares hashCode and then equals; if a match exists put returns the old value and add returns false.
What does HashSet.add() return and why?
true if the element was new (map.put returned null) and false if it already existed.
What is PRESENT?
A static final Object used as the value for every key, so no per-element value object is needed.
Why does a HashSet show duplicates when only equals is overridden?
Equal objects hash to different buckets, so they are never compared; hashCode must be overridden consistently with equals.
Is HashSet ordered?
No: iteration follows bucket order. Use LinkedHashSet for insertion order or TreeSet for sorted order.
Which map backs LinkedHashSet and TreeSet?
LinkedHashMap and TreeMap (through NavigableMap).
Can HashSet contain null?
Yes, one null (stored in bucket 0 of the backing map).
What happens if you modify an element after adding it?
If the change alters hashCode the element becomes unreachable via contains/remove while still taking space.
Time complexity of HashSet operations?
add, remove and contains are O(1) average; iteration is O(n + capacity).
Is HashSet thread-safe?
No. Use ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() or Collections.synchronizedSet.

topics.name: Internal Working of HashMap

beginner.content:
The big idea

A HashMap is an array of buckets. To store or find a key, Java turns the key into a number (the hash code), turns that number into an array index, and goes straight to that bucket. That is why get and put take about the same time whether the map holds 10 entries or 10 million.

  • The array is called table; each slot is a bucket holding a chain of Node objects (key, value, hash, next).
  • Default capacity 16 buckets, load factor 0.75: when more than 12 entries exist the table doubles.
  • Two different keys can land in the same bucket: a collision. They share a linked list there.
  • Since Java 8, a long chain (8 or more nodes, with capacity at least 64) becomes a red-black tree.

The four steps of put(key, value)

StepWhat happensCode idea
1. HashCall key.hashCode() and mix the high bits into the low bitsh ^ (h >>> 16)
2. IndexReduce the hash to a bucket number(n - 1) & hash
3. Search the bucketWalk the chain: same hash and equals(key) means "update this node"equals() decides
4. InsertNo match: add a new node at the end of the chain. Resize if size is above the thresholdsize > 0.75 x capacity

Why a power-of-two capacity?

  • When n is a power of two, (n - 1) & hash equals hash % n but is much faster (one AND instruction).
  • It also makes resizing cheap: after doubling, each entry either stays at its index or moves to index + oldCapacity.
  • That is why new HashMap<>(10) actually creates a table of 16: the capacity is rounded up to the next power of two.

Benefits and advantages

For freshers: knowing how a HashMap works makes you faster at spotting bugs and at answering interview questions.

  • Why it is fast: hash, index, then a short search. Lookups stay near O(1) even for millions of entries.
  • Flexible keys: any object with proper equals and hashCode can be a key.
  • One structure, many uses: caches, counters, indexes, grouping, de-duplication.
  • Self-tuning: the table doubles automatically, so you rarely manage the size yourself.
  • Tree buckets (Java 8+) protect against badly spread keys.

For experienced developers: amortised O(1) put / get, cache-friendly array of buckets, lazy allocation, and an order-preserving split on resize make HashMap the default map. The design explains the performance numbers you see in profiles.

Disadvantages and when NOT to use it

  • No order: iteration depends on hashes and capacity, not on insertion. Use LinkedHashMap or TreeMap if order matters.
  • Memory overhead: a Node object per entry plus the table array; costly for millions of small primitives (consider specialised maps).
  • Resizing pauses: one put can suddenly cost O(n).
  • Bad keys break it: missing hashCode, or a key changed after insertion, makes entries unfindable.
  • Not thread-safe: use ConcurrentHashMap for concurrent writes.
  • No range queries: for "all keys between A and B" a TreeMap is the right tool.

For experienced developers: iteration cost is O(size + capacity), and hash flooding can degrade buckets to O(log n) (tree) or O(n) (non-comparable keys).

Why learn the internals

SkillWhat the internals teachWhere it pays off
Correct keysequals and hashCode must agree; keys must not changeFixing "my map cannot find the key" bugs
PerformanceLoad factor, resize cost, presizingTuning large maps and caches
CollisionsChains, trees, hash spreadingExplaining O(1) vs worst cases
Choosing a mapWhy order is lost, why null is allowedPicking HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, ConcurrentHashMap
Interviewsput / get walk-through, Java 8 changesAnswering the classic "how does HashMap work" question

intermediate.content:
A HashMap built by hand

The best way to understand it is to write a small one. Each sample below adds one idea.

1. Node: key, value, hash, next

  • Signature: static class Node { final int hash; final K key; V value; Node next; }
  • Returns: one entry of a bucket chain
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: Every entry is a Node. It stores the key, the value, the key's hash (so it need not be recomputed) and a next pointer to the following node in the same bucket.

For experienced developers: In the real java.util.HashMap the class is HashMap.Node; a bucket that turned into a tree holds TreeNode objects instead.

2. put(): hash, index, search, insert

  • Signature: V put(K key, V value)
  • Returns: the old value or null
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: Compute the bucket, walk its chain looking for an equal key. If found, replace the value; otherwise add a node (this miniature adds it at the front of the chain for brevity; the real HashMap appends at the tail). It uses only 4 buckets so you can see collisions.

For experienced developers: The real code first compares hash (cheap int compare) and only then calls equals (possibly expensive). That is why a good hashCode matters.

3. Collisions and the role of equals() and hashCode()

  • Signature: int hashCode(); boolean equals(Object o)
  • Returns: int / boolean
  • Time: O(1) per call

For freshers: Two keys with the same hash end up in the same chain; equals then tells them apart. The contract: equal objects must have equal hash codes. If you override equals but not hashCode, equal keys land in different buckets and get fails.

For experienced developers: Mutable keys are dangerous: if a field used in hashCode changes after put, the entry sits in the wrong bucket and can never be found again.

4. Broken hashCode: equal objects in different buckets

  • Signature: class Fort { equals(...) without hashCode(...) }
  • Returns: a map that cannot find its keys
  • Time: O(1) wrong answer

For freshers: This is the most common HashMap bug. Without hashCode, the default (identity-based) hash is used, so two equal forts get different bucket numbers.

For experienced developers: Always override both together, and use the same fields in both. In modern Java a record does it correctly for you.

Resizing

When the table gets too full, it doubles and every entry is re-bucketed.

5. Load factor, threshold and resize()

  • Signature: threshold = capacity x loadFactor; if (++size > threshold) resize()
  • Returns: a table twice as big
  • Time: O(n) once, O(1) amortised

For freshers: With capacity 16 and load factor 0.75 the threshold is 12. The 13th entry triggers resize(): a new table of 32 buckets, with the threshold now 24.

For experienced developers: Resizing is the most expensive step of a HashMap. If you know the final size, create the map with enough capacity: new HashMap<>((int) (expected / 0.75f) + 1) (or HashMap.newHashMap(expected) in Java 19+).

6. The resize split: stay or move by oldCapacity

  • Signature: newIndex = oldIndex OR oldIndex + oldCapacity
  • Returns: each entry's new bucket
  • Time: O(n)

For freshers: When the capacity doubles from 16 to 32, only one more bit of the hash is used. That bit is 0 (the entry stays) or 1 (it moves exactly oldCapacity places up). Java 8 uses this to split each chain without recomputing.

For experienced developers: The order inside each bucket is preserved by the split, which is also why concurrent resizing no longer makes a cyclic list as in Java 7.

Java 8: chains become trees

Long chains are the only real threat to HashMap speed.

7. Treeification

  • Signature: TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8; MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64; UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6
  • Returns: a red-black tree bucket
  • Time: O(log n) worst case

For freshers: If a bucket reaches 8 nodes and the table has at least 64 buckets, the chain becomes a red-black tree, so lookups in that bucket cost O(log n) instead of O(n). With a smaller table, the map resizes instead. When a tree shrinks to 6 or fewer, it turns back into a list.

For experienced developers: Tree nodes are ordered by hash, then by compareTo if the key is Comparable, then by a tie-break. So Comparable keys are friendlier under heavy collisions. It also defends against hash-flooding attacks.

Null key and iteration

Two details that follow from the design.

8. The null key and iteration order

  • Signature: hash(null) = 0; iteration walks table[0..n-1]
  • Returns: bucket 0 / array order
  • Time: O(n + capacity) to iterate

For freshers: A null key has hash 0, so it always lives in bucket 0. Iteration visits buckets from 0 to n-1 and each chain in order, so the order depends on hashes and capacity, not on insertion order.

For experienced developers: Iterating costs O(size + capacity), so a huge capacity with few entries makes loops slow. The order can change after a resize.

Module: Finding and storing steps

For freshers: every HashMap method follows the same road: key, hash code, spread, bucket number, search the bucket with equals. Below each stop on that road is shown by itself, in a tiny program. For experienced developers: the samples mirror HashMap.hash, (n - 1) & hash, getNode and putVal; the real code compares the stored hash before calling equals.

9. Step 1: hashCode() turns a key into an int

  • Signature: int hashCode()
  • Returns: any int (can be negative)
  • Time: O(1) for most keys; O(length) for a String first time

For freshers: Every object can say a number for itself. Equal objects must give equal numbers.

For experienced developers: String caches its hash after the first call. The number alone is not a bucket yet; it can be negative or huge.

10. Step 2: spread the hash

  • Signature: h ^ (h >>> 16)
  • Returns: a mixed int
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: HashMap mixes the top bits of the number into the bottom bits, because only the bottom bits will choose the bucket.

For experienced developers: It costs one shift and one XOR, and rescues keys whose hashes differ only in high bits.

11. Step 3: pick the bucket

  • Signature: index = (n - 1) & hash
  • Returns: a number from 0 to n - 1
  • Time: O(1)

For freshers: The table has n buckets (a power of two). A single AND keeps just the bottom bits, so the answer is always a valid bucket number.

For experienced developers: Same as hash mod n for a power of two, but without the slow division, and never negative.

12. Step 4: walk the bucket and use equals() (get)

  • Signature: V get(Object key)
  • Returns: the value or null
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: The bucket may hold several keys. HashMap goes through the chain and returns the entry whose key is equals to yours.

For experienced developers: getNode checks hash == first (cheap) and then == or equals. A tree bucket is searched as a red-black tree.

13. Step 5: put() decides between update and insert

  • Signature: V put(K key, V value)
  • Returns: the old value, or null if the key was new
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: Same road as get. If an equal key is found its value is replaced; if the chain ends, a new node is added.

For experienced developers: The return value tells you which case happened, so put can double as a "was it new?" check.

14. containsKey(): the same search without returning the value

  • Signature: boolean containsKey(Object key)
  • Returns: true or false
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: Does the bucket chain hold an equal key? Unlike get, it can tell "missing" from "present with a null value".

For experienced developers: It calls the same getNode as get. Do not call containsKey then get in a loop: it hashes twice.

15. Step 6: the table doubles when it gets full (resize)

  • Signature: if (++size > threshold) resize()
  • Returns: a table of twice the size
  • Time: O(n) once

For freshers: After the 12th entry in a 16-bucket table, the 13th makes the table 32 buckets wide, so chains stay short.

For experienced developers: Each old chain is split in two: nodes either stay at the same index or move to index + oldCapacity.

16. remove(): find the node, then unlink it

  • Signature: V remove(Object key)
  • Returns: the removed value or null
  • Time: O(1) average

For freshers: Same search as get; once the node is found, the link from the previous node is changed to skip it.

For experienced developers: Removal increments modCount and never shrinks the table.

Which lookup method to pick

GoalUseWhy

expert.content:
The exact source, in plain words

What java.util.HashMap does for put(key, value) (putVal):

  • hash(key) = key == null ? 0 : (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16).
  • If table is null or empty, resize() creates it (lazy allocation: no array until the first put).
  • Bucket = table[(n - 1) & hash]. If empty, place a new Node there.
  • Otherwise: if the first node matches (hash == and key == or equals) remember it; else if it is a TreeNode use putTreeVal; else walk the chain and, at the end, append a node and call treeifyBin when the chain length reaches 8.
  • If an existing node matched: replace its value (and return the old one); do not change modCount.
  • Else: ++modCount, and if ++size > threshold then resize().
  • New nodes are appended at the tail of the chain in Java 8+ (Java 7 inserted at the head).

Why the hash is spread with h ^ (h >>> 16)

  • The bucket number only uses the low bits of the hash (4 bits for 16 buckets). Many hash codes differ only in their high bits.
  • XOR-ing the top 16 bits into the bottom 16 lets high bits influence the index, spreading keys more evenly at almost no cost.

Fail-fast iterators: modCount

Every structural change (add a new key, remove) increments modCount. An iterator remembers the value it started with and throws ConcurrentModificationException if it differs. Updating the value of an existing key is not structural.
Sizing a HashMap to avoid resizes

HashMap versus ConcurrentHashMap internals

HashMapConcurrentHashMap
TableNode[] tableNode[] table (volatile reads)
Writing a bucketPlain writeCAS into an empty bucket, otherwise synchronized on the bucket's first node
ReadingPlain readLock-free
Sizeint sizeStriped counters (CounterCell)
ResizeOne threadSeveral threads help migrate buckets
null key / valueAllowedNot allowed
IteratorsFail-fastWeakly consistent (never throw CME)

Best practices

What the internals tell you to do.

  • Override equals and hashCode together, using the same immutable fields (or use a record).
  • Use immutable keys: String, Integer, enums, records.
  • Presize the map when the final size is known.
  • Make keys Comparable if many may collide: the tree bin can use it.
  • Never share a plain HashMap between threads that write; use ConcurrentHashMap.
  • Do not rely on iteration order.

Real-time examples

Three problems that every Java team meets sooner or later. Each program is small and prints what really happens.

Example 1: A bad hashCode piles everything into one bucket

For freshers: if every key gives the same number, all of them land in one bucket and the map behaves like a slow list. For experienced developers: the sample counts bucket sizes with the same index formula HashMap uses, so the damage is visible without any timing.

Example 2: A mutable key gets lost

A key is stored in the bucket for its hash at that moment. If a field used in hashCode changes later, the lookup goes to a different bucket and the entry is stranded.

Example 3: Resizing and presizing

Every time the table doubles, all entries are moved. When you know the final size, ask for enough room once.

Sample project: SimpleHashMap with buckets

What we build: a small generic hash map written by hand, following the real HashMap steps.

  • Step 1: a Node class with key, value, hash and next.
  • Step 2: an array of buckets, starting with 4 slots, and a load factor of 0.75.
  • Step 3: put hashes the key, finds the bucket, updates an equal key or appends a node, then resizes if needed.
  • Step 4: get and remove use the same search.
  • Step 5: resize doubles the table and re-buckets every node. A demo run prints the table after each phase.

Practice questions

Now test yourself. Each question is harder than the examples above: read the problem, write your own solution, then compare it with the one shown. Every solution was compiled and run, and its output is real.

interviewQA: How does HashMap work internally?

An array of buckets. put hashes the key, picks the bucket with (n-1) & hash, searches the chain using hash and equals, then updates or appends a node; the table doubles when size exceeds capacity x 0.75.
What is a collision and how is it handled?
Two different keys mapping to the same bucket. They are stored in a linked list in that bucket (a red-black tree when it reaches 8 nodes and the table has 64+ buckets); equals() distinguishes them.
Why must you override hashCode when you override equals?
Equal keys must go to the same bucket; with the default identity hashCode they do not, so get() misses.
What are the default capacity and load factor?
16 and 0.75. The table is allocated lazily on the first put and the threshold is 12.
Why is the capacity always a power of two?
Index = (n - 1) & hash is a fast modulo, and resizing splits each bucket into "stay" and "move by oldCapacity".
What changed in HashMap in Java 8?
Treeification of long chains (O(log n) worst case), tail insertion instead of head insertion, an order-preserving resize split, and no more cyclic-list bug.
It mixes the high 16 bits into the low bits that the index uses, reducing collisions for hashes that differ mostly in high bits.
Where is the null key stored?
Bucket 0, because hash(null) is 0.
What happens if a key is mutated after being put?
Its hash changes, so it is looked up in a different bucket and becomes unreachable: effectively lost.
Is HashMap thread-safe? What happens with concurrent writes?
No. Concurrent writes can lose entries or corrupt the table (Java 7 could loop forever when resizing). Use ConcurrentHashMap.
What is the time complexity of get / put?
O(1) average, O(log n) worst case with treeification (O(n) before Java 8 or for non-comparable colliding keys in a tree bin).
What is modCount?
A counter of structural changes; iterators compare it to the value they saw at creation and throw ConcurrentModificationException if it changed.
